papers.title: A Community-Driven Single-Cell PBMC Reference Integrating Landmark Datasets Spanning Health and Disease
papers.authors: Cujba, A.-M.; Aguilar-Fernandez, S.; Antoinette, A.; Said, W.; Mueller, M. F.; Kock, K. H.; Nestor, J.; Sonthalia, R.; Buyamin, E. V.; Rawat, P.; Predeus, A.; Kretschmer, L.; Fei, L.; Slowikowski, K.; Sen, P.; Cosgriff, C. V.; MGH COVID-19 Collection & Processing Team, ; Dufva, O.; Askari, M.; Kimler, K.; Futey, M.; Zucchi, I.; Chatzigeorgiou, A.; Nejad, P.; Jin, L.; Bowen, B.; Yang, A.; Lindeboom, R. G. H.; Normand, R.; Megas, S.; Ando, Y.; Chatterjee, A.; Park, J.-E.; Majumder, P. P.; Matangkasombut, P.; Charoensawan, V.; Shin, J. W.; Park, W.-Y.; Asian Immune Diversity Atlas (AIDA) Network
papers.abstract: Blood provides an accessible window into human health, yet the absence of a peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) reference with standardized immune cell annotations has constrained comparisons between single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) studies. Here, we present HARP (Human Cell Atlas Reference for PBMCs), an integrated atlas of ~9 million PBMCs from >2,600 donors across 15 studies spanning four continents, encompassing diverse populations, neonates to 97 years, across health and diverse immune-related diseases. We developed optimized integration workflows, including novel label-free metrics to assess integration quality, and generated community-driven consensus annotations for 192 immune cell subsets, identifying rare populations representing as few as 0.004% of PBMCs. HARP reveals coordinated cellular modules associated with age, sex, and disease, identifies female-biased interferon and inflammatory gene programs and their perturbation by COVID-19, and uncovers a novel sexual dimorphism in prostaglandin signaling. Finally, we introduce scTiger, a hierarchical label-transfer framework that accurately projects these 192 cell annotations onto ~18 million additional PBMCs, providing a robust and transferable reference for harmonizing future PBMC studies. HARP provides a high-resolution community-driven reference atlas for PBMC annotation and analysis, as a basis for emerging clinical applications of single-cell genomics.

papers.title: Single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis of inflammation-metabolism programs and the tumor microenvironment of colorectal cancer liver metastasis.
papers.authors: Ma Z, Jiang W, Zhang J, Kong L, Zhao C, Ma F, Wu C.
papers.abstract: Background Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) is a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC) and develops within a heterogeneous tumor microenvironment (TME). How immune, stromal, and metabolic programs differ between primary CRC and matched liver metastases remains incompletely resolved. Methods We analyzed publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from GSE178318 (15 specimens from six patients: six primary CRC samples, six matched liver metastases, and three peripheral-blood mononuclear cell samples) together with bulk RNA-seq data from GSE50760 (54 samples from 18 patients spanning normal colon, primary CRC, and liver metastasis). The single-cell workflow included quality control, score-based cell-type annotation, patient-level pseudobulk differential expression, pathway/module scoring, ligand-receptor co-expression analysis, and diffusion-map pseudotime. Bulk data were assessed using within-patient paired comparisons, co-expression analysis, and program-level scoring. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction was applied for multiple testing. Results After quality control, 132,915 single cells were retained. Liver metastases showed higher patient-level T/NK-cell fractions and lower malignant epithelial and B/plasma-cell fractions than primary tumors. In paired single-cell pseudobulk analysis, no gene remained significant at the prespecified FDR threshold, although nominal differences suggested extracellular-matrix and metabolic changes. Glycolysis scores were modestly higher and oxidative-phosphorylation scores modestly lower in liver metastases, whereas inflammatory and glycolytic scores were not correlated at the patient-tissue level. Ligand-receptor co-expression was strongest for MIF-CD74, VIM-CD44, and HLA-A-CD8A, with CAF/stromal and myeloid/TAM populations showing high aggregate outgoing scores. Diffusion pseudotime showed increasing EMT/invasion scores and decreasing glycolysis along the inferred transcriptomic ordering; this ordering is descriptive and not a longitudinal lineage. In the bulk cohort, 654 genes differed between liver metastasis and primary tumor, while cross-platform rank concordance was weak (Spearman rho=0.106). Conclusions Public single-cell and bulk datasets support compartment-associated differences in cellular composition and transcriptional programs in CRLM, with prominent stromal, myeloid, and metabolic features. However, limited patient numbers, cross-sectional sampling, weak cross-platform concordance, and the absence of experimental validation mean that the ligand-receptor and trajectory findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than causal or clinically validated.

papers.title: An interpretable machine learning model integrating mucosal and cellular immunity to predict SARS-CoV-2 reinfection: a multicenter cohort study.
papers.authors: Ran J, Zhang W, Zhang W, Huang H, Gong L, Yin S, Chen Y, Wang A, Min H, Zhu L, Chu J, Qin Y, Huang R, Wu C, Chen Y.
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 reinfection remains a significant public health challenge that requires accurate risk assessment across populations. Using prospectively collected data from two independent cohorts, we developed and externally validated an interpretable machine learning model for predicting symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 reinfection. The cohort comprised 1,156 adults from Wuxi and Nantong, China, with a median follow-up duration of 10 months. Reinfection occurred in 128 participants (11.1%). The model integrated eighteen clinical and immune features, and ultimately identified spike-specific nasal secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) and spike-specific CD4 + central memory T cells (T CM ) as key predictors. Developed using the extreme gradient boosting (XGB) algorithm, the prediction model achieved an AUC of 0.835 in the internal validation cohort and demonstrated strong discrimination in the external validation cohort. SHAP analysis revealed that higher nasal spike-specific sIgA was associated with lower risk, while spike-specific CD4 + T CM cells exhibited a non-linear association with reinfection. This interpretable immune-based model provides a framework for immune-informed risk stratification, enabling better prediction and management of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection risk in settings with heterogeneous population immunity.

papers.title: Machine learning-derived intracellular protein-based prognostic model reflecting a senescence-associated secretory phenotype-driven immunosuppressive microenvironment in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Chang X, Jiang L, Zhang L, Ren T, Fan C, Li P.
papers.abstract: Background This study aimed to investigate the associations of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-related genes with the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and clinical outcomes in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and to develop and evaluate a prognostic signature for risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. Methods Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) was conducted to identify distinct molecular subtypes. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), Random Forest, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) were utilized to identify core prognostic SASP genes. The expression patterns of selected SASP-related genes were explored using multi-omics datasets, LUAD cell lines, and clinical specimens. Results Cluster 1 was associated with significantly shorter overall survival (OS), enhanced senescence pathway activity, and computationally inferred immunosuppressive and immune-exclusion features. Five intracellular SASP regulators- ANGPTL4 , CDKN2A , H2AX , MMP1 , and CCL20 -were selected through machine learning to construct the SASP Protein Regulator Score (SASP-PRS). A high SASP-PRS was associated with the activation of senescence/SASP and cell-cycle pathways, suppression of antitumor immune signatures, and distinct immune-checkpoint and chemokine expression profiles. A higher SASP-PRS was also associated with advanced disease stage, poorer OS, predicted lower responsiveness to immunotherapy, lower predicted sensitivity to erlotinib, and higher predicted sensitivity to selected chemotherapeutic agents. The nomogram incorporating the SASP-PRS demonstrated discriminatory ability and calibration for predicting 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS in the analyzed LUAD cohorts. Conclusion These findings suggest that SASP-related gene-expression patterns are associated with LUAD molecular subtypes, senescence signaling, computationally inferred immune features, and treatment-related outcomes. The SASP-PRS may serve as a potential biomarker for prognostic stratification in LUAD. However, its utility for treatment-response assessment remains exploratory. Prospective external validation and functional studies are required to establish its clinical applicability and clarify the mechanisms linking SASP-related networks to the LUAD immune microenvironment.

papers.title: Heterogeneous nanoplastic exposure induces integrated immunometabolic transcriptional responses in human monocytes under continuous flow.
papers.authors: Kovacevic V, Dimitrijević NM, Zivanovic M, Ivanovic M, Zivic A, Gazdic Jankovic M, Kovacevic A, Prosenc Zmrzljak U, Puac F, Filipović N, Mihailovich M, Ljujic B.
papers.abstract: Nanoplastics interact continuously with circulating immune cells, yet how particle size and exposure complexity shape immune transcriptional responses under dynamic exposure conditions remains poorly understood. Here, controlled microfluidic exposure was combined with single-cell RNA sequencing to investigate the effects of size-defined polystyrene nanoplastics (PSNPs; 40 nm, 200 nm, and 40 + 200 nm) on primary human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) under continuous flow conditions. Across immune populations, PSNP exposure induced a conserved ribosome-associated and RNA-regulatory transcriptional program, indicating a shared intracellular transcriptional response. Monocytes displayed particularly prominent transcriptional remodeling, characterized by coordinated modulation of ribosome-associated, metabolic, and inflammatory signaling pathways across exposure conditions. Exposure to 40 nm PSNPs showed negative enrichment of mitochondrial metabolic pathways, whereas 200 nm PSNPs showed enrichment of inflammatory signaling programs. Heterogeneous particle-size exposure induced concurrent metabolic and inflammatory pathway engagement without evidence of major inter-lineage connectivity disruption or discrete inflammatory state transitions. Orthogonal flow cytometry measurements in PBMCs from three donors showed trends towards increased frequencies of IL-6- and TNF-α-positive monocytes following PSNP exposure. In contrast, adaptive immune cells exhibited comparatively modest and lineage-preserving transcriptional modulation. Together, these findings indicate that size-defined PSNP exposure conditions and exposure composition are associated with coordinated immunometabolic transcriptional responses in human immune cells under continuous flow conditions and establish a framework for studying dynamic material-immune interactions at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Single-cell-level digital twins for preterm birth prevention strategies.
papers.authors: Einhaus J, Neidlinger P, Fondeur O, Sato M, Anronikov S, Miyazaki K, Maechler A, Amar JN, Ando K, Badea V, Gaudilliere DK, Sabayev M, Feyaerts D, Diop M, Tsai AS, Cambriel A, Ganio EA, Lagarde R, O'Kelly E, Stelzer IA, Hedou J, Wong RJ, Blumenfeld YJ, Lyell DJ, Shaw GM, Oskotsky TT, Sirota M, Giudice LC, Stevenson DK, Aghaeepour N, Gaudilliere B.
papers.abstract: Digital twin models can accelerate therapeutic development by enabling low-risk testing of candidate interventions. In preterm labor (PTL), a major pregnancy complication where clinical trials face ethical and financial barriers, digital twins are especially valuable for evaluating new therapies targeting immune dysfunctions driving PTL. Yet, current models lack single-cell resolution, limiting detection of cell type-specific mechanisms, off-target effects, and the design of personalized interventions. We present Simulated Immunome Modeling of Clinical Outcomes (SIMCO), a single-cell-level digital twin framework that models immunomodulatory treatment effects on the timing of labor using immunome-wide, single-cell simulations. SIMCO's digital twins are trained and validated on a newly generated mass cytometry atlas of the pregnant immunome exposed to nine candidate drugs preselected for PTL prevention. Applying SIMCO to an independent cohort of pregnant individuals, we simulate treatment effects on gestational length, screening for candidate drugs that delay labor timing and providing system-level mechanistic insight for each drug candidate. Tetrahydrofolate and the combination of aspirin and lansoprazole emerged as top candidates for PTL prevention, delaying labor onset primarily through enhanced mTOR signaling in innate immune cells and attenuated JAK/STAT signaling in naïve CD4 + T cells.

papers.title: Identification of Immuno-Diagnostic and Therapeutic Markers in Tumors and Inflammatory Diseases Based on Single-Cell and Machine Learning Methods.
papers.authors: Tang J, Yuan D, Wu Z, Xie Y, Xu J.
papers.abstract: Background Chemotherapy is the mainstay of systemic treatment for colorectal cancer (CRC), but drug resistance and tumor heterogeneity markedly limit survival. Mitochondrial metabolism is increasingly recognized as a regulator of tumor progression, immune contexture, and therapeutic response. However, the prognostic relevance of mitochondrial metabolism-related transcriptional patterns and their relationships with chemotherapy-response signatures and immune features in CRC remain incompletely understood. Methods Clinical and transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas colorectal cancer cohort (TCGA-CRC) and Gene Expression Omnibus cohorts GSE17537 and GSE104645 were analyzed. A curated set of mitochondrial metabolism-related genes (MMRGs) were used to calculate an MMRG score, whereas genes upregulated in chemotherapy-sensitive cases in GSE104645 were used to derive a drug-sensitivity gene-set score by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA), differential expression analysis, univariate Cox regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, and multivariate Cox regression were used to construct a five-gene RiskScore. Prognostic associations were assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves, external validation, and subgroup analyses. Immune-cell enrichment and pRRophetic-predicted half-maximal inhibitory concentration values were evaluated, and CD36 was examined using in vitro phenotypic assays. Results Tumors showed lower MMRG scores than normal tissues, and higher MMRG scores were associated with better overall survival (OS). The drug-sensitivity gene-set score was higher in tumors but was not significantly associated with OS. A five-gene signature (CD36, CPA3, FCRL2, POU2F2, and S100B) generated a RiskScore that separated OS outcomes in the TCGA training, testing, and overall cohorts, as well as GSE17537, although its time-dependent discrimination varied across cohorts and follow-up periods. Similar survival associations were observed within subgroups defined by stage, age, and sex; however, independent or incremental prognostic value was not evaluated. High-risk tumors exhibited altered immune-cell enrichment, and the RiskScore was correlated with pRRophetic-predicted drug IC50 values after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. CD36 expression was higher in SW1116 than in NCM460 cells, and its knockdown inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mitochondrial function was not directly measured in these experiments. Conclusion The five-gene RiskScore was associated with OS, immune-cell enrichment, and in silico drug-sensitivity estimates in CRC. It may serve as a candidate tool for prognostic stratification, but its incremental clinical value and treatment-predictive utility require prospective validation. The CD36 knockdown experiments support a tumor-promoting phenotype in SW1116 cells but do not establish dependence on mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming.

papers.title: FABP4 Couples Lipid Metabolism to PD-L1 Stabilization in Immunosuppressive Myeloid Cells.
papers.authors: Yu J, Shilyansky J, Hao J, Avellino A, Sun Y, Jiang X, Han X, Curry M, Sugg SL, Li B.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysregulation in obesity reshapes immune function, but how lipid signals drive immune suppression remains unclear. Herein, we identify a FABP4-PD-L1 axis that links lipid metabolism to immune checkpoint regulation in myeloid cells. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed a distinct FABP4high immunosuppressive splenic macrophage subset enriched under high-fat diet (HFD) conditions, characterized by impaired antigen presentation and elevated PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, palmitic acid (PA) was shown to induce FABP4 and promote PD-L1 palmitoylation, leading to its stabilization on the cell surface independent of transcriptional regulation. FABP4 was essential for this process, which enabled PD-L1 surface stabilization, immunosuppression and mammary tumor progression. In humans, a conserved CD14intCD16⁺ monocyte population exhibited elevated FABP4-PD-L1 signaling and correlated with obesity and invasive breast cancer. These findings establish PD-L1 as a metabolically regulated protein and reveal a mechanism by which lipid excess drives immune evasion, suggesting FABP4 as a potential therapeutic target in cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages in breast cancer: from myeloid plasticity and tumor-promoting programs to CAR-macrophage therapy.
papers.authors: Heydari F, Derakhshani M, Naghinezhad J.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer develops within spatially organized, multicellular microenvironments in which particular tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) states can influence immune access and stromal remodeling. Conventional M1/M2 classification and total macrophage density fail to capture the developmental, transcriptional, metabolic, and spatial heterogeneity that determines TAM function. This macrophage-focused review examines breast cancer within its multicellular microenvironment, integrating lineage-tracing, single-cell, spatial, mechanistic, and clinical evidence while distinguishing breast-specific findings from hypotheses extrapolated from other tumors. We examine how tissue-resident and monocyte-derived macrophages are recruited, retained, expanded, and reprogrammed across primary and metastatic sites, emphasizing interactions with malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, vasculature, adipose tissue, and lymphoid populations. In defined breast-tumor contexts, TAM programs have been implicated in immune exclusion, invasion, metastatic dissemination, and adaptation to systemic treatment, although evidence strength varies across mechanisms and therapeutic modalities. Small and heterogeneous clinical studies have not established a benefit from broad CSF1/CSF1R-axis targeting in breast cancer, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Accordingly, we highlight a shift toward state-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated targeting. Emerging approaches include restoring phagocytosis, disrupting chemokine and fibrotic circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and converting suppressive TAMs into inflammatory, antigen-presenting effectors. A major focus is chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy, which combines antigen-directed phagocytosis with tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and recruitment of endogenous immunity. Although early clinical data support manufacturing feasibility, tumor trafficking, and acceptable initial safety, limited antitumor activity underscores challenges involving antigen heterogeneity, persistence, metabolic fitness, biodistribution, and scalable production. We propose a translational roadmap integrating spatial biomarkers, quantitative target selection, macrophage-adapted CAR design, checkpoint-resistant phagocytosis, metabolic engineering, safety switches, and biomarker-guided combination therapy. This framework positions macrophage reprogramming as a context-dependent strategy for modifying selected breast-tumor niches, with therapeutic targets chosen according to the macrophage program and its surrounding cellular architecture.

papers.title: Diverse infection models demonstrate robust resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to innate immunity.
papers.authors: Fairgrieve MR, Brydon EC, Chavez RA, Kotov DI, Vance RE.
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is a robust activator of innate immunity. While innate immune activation of macrophages can impact Mtb replication in vitro, there is little in vivo evidence that the innate immune system controls Mtb before the onset of adaptive immunity. Prior work has generally used specific pathogen-free (SPF) mouse models and relatively large infectious doses, which may obscure the capacity of innate immunity to control Mtb. Here, we performed ultra-low dose Mtb infections and found that the initial innate immune response was unable to curb even minimal Mtb infectious doses. Additionally, we primed the immune systems of C57BL/6 mice by co-housing with "pet shop" mice prior to Mtb exposure. Co-housed mice were as susceptible to Mtb infection as SPF mice. To pre-activate innate immunity at the site of Mtb infection more specifically, we also infected the lungs of mice with Legionella pneumophila (Lp) prior to Mtb. Innate immunity alone can clear large doses (>100,000 CFU) of Lp from the lung within a few days. However, priming the mouse lung by pre-infection with Lp only modestly reduced Mtb CFU compared to mice infected with only Mtb, indicating that Mtb can robustly replicate even in the presence of a strong anti-bacterial innate response. We performed single-cell RNA-sequencing on myeloid cells from mice either infected with Mtb alone or mice primed with Lp. We found that Lp priming before Mtb infection induced measurable changes in myeloid cells responding to Mtb, but these changes had little effect on innate control of Mtb. Together, these data demonstrate the robust resistance of Mtb to innate immune clearance under diverse experimental conditions.

papers.title: Immune-related Plasma Proteins Associated with Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis Identified by Mendelian Randomization and Clinical Validation.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Che J, Guan C, Guo H.
papers.abstract: Purpose To identify immune-related plasma proteins causally associated with susceptibility to recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) through two-sample Mendelian randomization, and to validate their biological and clinical relevance using integrative multi-omics analyses and clinical samples. Materials and methods Two-sample Mendelian randomization was performed using protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) data for immune-related plasma proteins from the deCODE genetics database and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for RAS to identify proteins with potential causal associations. Candidate proteins were further evaluated by Gene Ontology (GO)/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), and colocalization analyses. Single-cell transcriptomic data from oral mucosa were integrated to characterize the cellular expression patterns of the corresponding genes. Finally, plasma levels of the candidate proteins were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in 35 patients with RAS (sampled during both the ulcerative and healing phases) and 35 healthy controls to validate their clinical relevance. Results A total of 28 immune-related plasma proteins were identified as having potential causal associations with RAS through two-sample Mendelian randomization. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these proteins were mainly involved in immune and inflammatory pathways, including natural killer (NK) cell-mediated cytotoxicity, Th1/Th2 cell differentiation, and the IL-17 signaling pathway. SMR and colocalization analyses highlighted IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA as key candidate genes, with IL17A showing the strongest genetic evidence. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further revealed distinct cell-type-specific expression patterns of these genes in the oral mucosa. Clinical validation confirmed statistically significant alterations in the plasma levels of IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA across different stages of RAS. Conclusions This integrative study combining genetic analysis, single-cell transcriptomics, and clinical validation identified IL17A, MMP1, and IL2RA as key immune-related molecules associated with RAS. Among them, IL17A showed the strongest genetic evidence and may serve as a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target for RAS.

papers.title: Lineage-specific X chromosome inactivation escape and skew underlie sex-biased immune gene dosage and deleterious variant exposure
papers.authors: Kavanagh, D.; Steel, A.; King, H. E.; Vieira, H. G. S.; Kumar, K. R.; Masle-Farquhar, E.; King, C.; Weatheritt, R. J.; Skvortsova, K.
papers.abstract: The X chromosome carries an unusually high density of immune genes and is a major contributor to sex differences in immune function and autoimmune diseases. In females, X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) has two major functional consequences: it shapes X-linked gene dosage through XCI escape and determines the cellular exposure of heterozygous X-linked variants through XCI skew. Yet because XCI creates a mosaic of cells expressing different parental X chromosomes, these properties have remained largely inaccessible in individual women, becoming measurable only where XCI is non-random or after aggregation across large cohorts. Consequently, how X-linked variation contributes to sex-biased immunity and differs between individual women has remained unresolved. Here we present scDaisyChain, a graph-based framework that reconstructs chromosome-scale X haplotypes directly from heterozygous SNPs and single-cell long-read transcriptomes. scDaisyChain achieves near-ground-truth accuracy in highly polymorphic mouse hybrids and shows strong concordance with orthogonal long-read whole-genome phasing in human samples. Applied to peripheral blood immune cells from healthy women, it reveals a lineage-specific escape program in which lymphoid cells escape XCI more broadly than monocytes, with corresponding gains in the inactive X chromatin accessibility and female-biased expression. Lineage-specific skew further alters the proportion of cells expressing each heterozygous X-linked variant, a property we term variant exposure. Predicted deleterious variants are preferentially found in low-exposure states, exemplified by a splice-altering TLR8 variant expressed in few cytotoxic T cells. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), the monocyte compartment - which has the lowest escape in health - shows reproducible inactive X dysregulation converging on a trained-immunity programme linked to disease flare and synovial macrophage activation, with elevated escape of IL13RA1 and HDAC8. These findings establish lineage-specific escape, skew and variant exposure as quantifiable, patient-resolved determinants of sex-biased immune gene dosage and X-linked variant penetrance in health and autoimmune disease, resolving a dimension of female biology that has been previously inaccessible in individual donors.

papers.title: A CAR T cell-amplified suppressive B cell circuit in AML
papers.authors: Gottschlich, A.; Kavaka, V.; Janert, T. A.; Igl, V.; Carlini, E.; Rohrbacher, L.; den Hartog, W.; Harwood, J.; Trefny, M. P.; Sogukcelik, S.; Penovici, P.; Ransmayr, B.; Rausch, C.; Brauneck, F.; Frenz-Wiessner, S.; Goek, I.; Haenel, G.; Zucchinetti, C.; Oner, A.; Zwicker, P. S.; Gruenmeier, R.; Delahais, S.; Schnell, P. M.; Nandi, S.; Thomas, M.; Brabenec, R.; Briukhovetska, D.; Michaelides, S.; Mueller, R. D.; Ballheimer, L. Y.; Tsiverioti, C. A.; Hoffmann, G. V.; Stock, S.; Piseddu, I.; Mueller, P. J.; Kruppa, M.; Fiedler, W.; Rade, M.; Kreuz, M.; Kehl, N.; Bhagwat, A. S.; Thiel, J. T.; Ste
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is constrained by a hostile bone marrow niche. Here we identify atypical memory B cells (Batyp) as a suppressive population within this microenvironment. Across single cell and flow cytometry cohorts, Batyp were expanded in AML, and their molecular and phenotypic profiles resembled those of atypical B cells associated with chronic inflammatory conditions. Batyp were polarized within the AML microenvironment, and this was amplified by CAR T cell-AML interactions. Mechanistically, polarization was dependent on Toll-like receptor, interferon and CD70-CD27 signaling. Batyp suppressed T cell and CAR T cell responses via PD-1- and TGF-beta signaling, and were enriched in non-responding patients with AML and myeloma. CD180-directed CAR T cells, targeting an antigen shared by Batyp and AML blasts, resisted suppression in vitro and cleared disease in B cell-humanized xenografts while sparing hematopoietic stem cells, with B cell engagement further enhancing their expansion. CAR T cells thus reinforce their own suppressive niche through Batyp polarization, a constraint that can be relieved by dual blast- and B cell-targeting strategies.

papers.title: An immune world model with multi-agent orchestration for peptide vaccines
papers.authors: Chen, L.; Luan, H.; Yu, G.
papers.abstract: Peptide-vaccine design requires a connection between vaccine-induced priming and recognition of the antigen naturally displayed by a tumor. We present an immune world model that preserves this connection through separate vaccine and tumor branches, endpoint-specific evidence and multi-agent orchestration. Native-recognition constraints held an altered peptide despite its higher presentation score, and targeted perturbations removed antigen-dependent benefit when required tumor-recognition conditions were absent. Public dendritic-cell data distinguished donor from antigen-source transfer: a context ranker achieved Recall@20 of 0.483 and 0.333 under the respective holdouts. Structure-informed receptor prediction added candidate-ranking evidence while preserving functional constraints and matched scenario trajectories. An assay observation model further concentrated a cross-presentation coefficient around its known value in a synthetic conditioning experiment. Together, these results establish a computational framework for linking molecular predictions, native-target requirements and conditional immune dynamics. The framework provides a reproducible basis for choosing peptide-vaccine candidates and the experiments needed to resolve their biological dependencies.

papers.title: Cardiovascular Toxicity Across the Cancer Immunotherapy Spectrum: Mechanisms and Management in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) and Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell (CAR-T) Therapy.
papers.authors: Lushington J, Wilson JM, Lalwani S, Makker S, Kandala A, Ghose A, Shaw H, Northend M, Frazer RD, Ghosh AK.
papers.abstract: Purpose of review This review evaluates the evolving landscape of cardiovascular toxicities associated with two pillars of modern cancer treatment: immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. It examines their distinct immune-mediated pathophysiologies, clinical manifestations, and management frameworks. Recent findings While ICIs carry a clinical trial incidence for cardiotoxicity of approximately 1%, real-world data suggest rates of 3-5%, with myocarditis sometimes manifesting early as part of a high-mortality "Triple M" or overlap syndrome. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occur in nearly 50% of ICI-myocarditis cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) using the modified Lake Louise criteria, with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) detection sensitivity increasing from 21.6% to 72.0% when imaged after four days of symptoms. Conversely, CAR-T cardiotoxicity is predominantly driven by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which affects 49-93% of patients with currently licensed products. Severe CRS more than doubles the risk of cardiovascular events, including a 6-10% incidence of LVEF decline and a 4-18% incidence of arrhythmias. Recent advancements include machine learning models to predict MACE and structured screening programs to risk-stratify candidates. Cardiotoxicity remains a significant complication, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring and early intervention. Management relies on baseline risk assessment and rapid deployment of targeted therapies, such as high-dose methylprednisolone for ICI-myocarditis and IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab) for CAR-T-related CRS. A multidisciplinary cardio-oncology approach is essential to mitigate risks. With early diagnosis and appropriate immunosuppressive strategies in a multidisciplinary setting, these complications can be better managed, optimising oncological benefits whilst reducing treatment-related morbidity and mortality in majority of patients.

papers.title: Evolution-Informed Viroinformatics Identifies Conserved Immune Targets with Predicted Lower Mutational Vulnerability Across Betacoronaviruses.
papers.authors: Alshammari J, Alqahtani HA, Alonaizan R, Rahman IU, Alzhrani K, Al-Hoshani N, Alwaili MA, Aziz T.
papers.abstract: The extensive evolutionary diversity and continuous mutational adaptation of betacoronaviruses represent a major challenge to the development of broadly protective countermeasures. This study applied an evolution-informed Viroinformatics framework to systematically identify conserved and immune targets with predicted lower mutational vulnerability across betacoronaviruses. The workflow integrated comparative sequence conservation and phylogenetic analysis with immunoinformatics-based epitope screening, HLA population coverage, mutational escape profiling, structural modeling, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Conserved cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and helper T-lymphocyte epitopes were prioritized based on immunogenicity, antigenicity, safety, HLA binding potential, evolutionary conservation, and predicted resistance to mutational escape. Combined MHC class I and II analysis predicted a theoretical global population coverage of 99.92%, which requires experimental validation. The resulting 409-amino-acid multiepitope construct was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, and physiochemically stable. Structural validation showed that 99.7% of the residues were located within favored or additionally allowed regions. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable interaction of the vaccine construct with TLR7, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation supported persistence of the predicted vaccine-receptor association. Overall, these findings provide a computational framework for prioritizing evolutionarily conserved immune targets and developing pre-emptive candidate epitopes showing predicted cross-betacoronavirus conservation within the analyzed dataset. Experimental studies evaluating HLA binding, cellular and humoral immunogenicity, recombinant expression, cross-reactivity, and in vivo protection are required to validate the predicted immunological potential and determine whether the proposed construct can provide broad protection against diverse betacoronaviruses.

papers.title: Vascular Cell Adhesion Molecule 1 Is Associated With Immune Remodeling, Glioma Progression, and Tumor Cell Survival in U87 and U251 Cells.
papers.authors: Liu M, Jiang SC, Chen W, Zhang J, Wei Z.
papers.abstract: The immunosuppressive microenvironment of glioma remains a major barrier to effective treatment. Vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) regulates leukocyte adhesion and inflammatory signaling, but its relevance to glioma remains unresolved. Clinical and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), gene co-expression information from LinkOmics, and protein expression data from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) were integrated. Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and nomogram construction were used to evaluate prognostic value. Computational deconvolution was used to characterize immune cell composition, and small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated knockdown in U87 and U251 glioma cells was performed to evaluate VCAM1 function. VCAM1 expression was higher in glioma tissues than in normal brain tissues and increased with tumor grade. Overall survival (OS) was shorter in patients with higher VCAM1 expression, and similar findings were observed for disease-specific survival (DSS) and progression-free interval (PFI). Macrophage, regulatory T-cell, and dendritic-cell infiltration estimates were associated with VCAM1 expression, and programmed cell death 1 ligand 2 (PDCD1LG2/PD-L2) expression showed a further positive association. In cell-based assays, VCAM1 depletion reduced IL-4, IL-10, and TNF-β expression; increased IFN-γ expression; reduced MMP2, MMP9, and N-cadherin transcript levels; increased E-cadherin transcript levels; enhanced apoptosis; and reduced phosphorylation of p65, AKT, and ERK. These findings suggest that VCAM1 is associated with immune composition, inflammatory signaling, glioma cell survival, and an invasion-associated transcriptional phenotype, supporting further evaluation as a prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: A Photocurable Hydrogel Cardiac Patch Incorporating Formononetin-Loaded Lipid Nanoparticles for Myocardial Repair After Acute Ischemia.
papers.authors: Yang J, Cheng Z, Zhang H, Kong L, Dai T, Ding X, Zhao X, Jin X, Li T, Qi Z, He C, Liu Z.
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) induces ventricular dysfunction through ischemic necrosis and fibrotic remodeling, progressing to heart failure and constituting a major global cardiovascular burden. To address this, we developed a photocurable, hydrogel-based cardiac patch (Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel) with favorable mechanical robustness. The patch is composed of methacryloylated carboxymethyl chitosan (CACSMA) and methacryloylated gelatin (GelMA), incorporating Formononetin-loaded lipid nanoparticles (FMN@LNPs) for myocardial restoration. In vitro studies demonstrated that the Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel not only inhibited cardiomyocyte apoptosis by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) but also promoted migration and tube formation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Moreover, when a co-culture system of the Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel and heart-forming organoids (HFOs) was subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) conditions, the system effectively inhibited HFO apoptosis and suppressed HFO fibrosis. In vivo experiments in MI model rats revealed that the Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel group preserved a higher left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF: 67.2 ± 1.9%) compared to the MI group (LVEF: 41.7 ± 4.7%) at 28 days post-MI, thereby improving cardiac function. Histological analysis showed that the Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel reduced myocardial fibrosis in the infarct border zone, promoted angiogenesis, and facilitated macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) identified pathways associated with metabolic regulation (PPAR signaling pathway), myocardial protection (PI3K-Akt signaling pathway), anti-fibrosis (inhibition of extracellular matrix remodeling), and anti-inflammatory immune regulation (TNF signaling pathway). Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) revealed that the Gel-CS/FMN@LNP hydrogel promoted post-MI cardiac repair through a multi-target network involving circadian rhythm remodeling, matrix regulation, immune balance, and vascular protection. Our hydrogel system, which combines facile injectability, sustained release of active factors, and synergistic therapeutic effects, represents a promising therapeutic approach for post-MI repair.

papers.title: The Crosstalk Role of Intestinal Barrier Damage in the Gut-Organ Axis and its Potential Therapeutic Implications.
papers.authors: Feng J, Xie W, Lu H, Tian L, Shi X, Huang J, Zeng X, Zhou Y, Zhao M, Cheng B, Zeng H.
papers.abstract: Intestinal barrier damage is a pivotal mediator of gut-organ crosstalk and a key contributor to systemic disease. This review systematically summarizes the structural organization of the intestinal barrier, including the mucus layer, epithelial tight junctions, and the lamina propria immune network, and highlights their coordinated roles in regulating intestinal barrier dysfunction and immune homeostasis. Disruption of barrier integrity facilitates the translocation of microbial products, cytokines, and metabolites, thereby promoting systemic inflammation and the pathogenesis of multi-organ diseases, including liver injury, pancreatitis, and cardiovascular disorders. Emerging evidence underscores the critical roles of gut microbiota, immune signaling pathways, and metabolic factors in barrier regulation. Advances in single-cell and spatial omics, together with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven multi-omics integration, are providing novel insights into the cellular heterogeneity and molecular mechanisms underlying barrier dysfunction. Therapeutic strategies targeting barrier restoration-including microbiota-based interventions and pharmacological approaches-show promising potential but require further clinical validation. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding intestinal barrier biology and its translational relevance.

figure.label: Fig. 1
figure.caption: Schematic overview of the structural organization of the intestinal barrier and its coordinated role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis. The intestinal barrier comprises three interconnected functional components: the outer mucus layer, the intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) monolayer, and the underlying mucosal immune compartment within the lamina propria. The mucus layer, enriched with mucins, secretory IgA, and antimicrobial peptides, limits microbial adhesion and restricts luminal antigens from contacting the epithelium. Adjacent IECs are sealed by intercellular junctional complexes, including TJs, AJs, and desmosomes, thereby regulating paracellular permeability and preserving epithelial integrity. Goblet cells continuously replenish the mucus layer, whereas immune cells residing in the lamina propria, including dendritic cells, macrophages, T cells, and B cells, coordinate innate and adaptive immune responses. Collectively, these integrated structural and immune components function synergistically to prevent microbial translocation, maintain intestinal barrier integrity, and support bidirectional communication along the gut-organ axis

papers.title: Granuloma-Like Structures in Tuberculosis A Critical Review of Their Biology, Quantitative Behavior, and Translational Use.
papers.authors: Mastrostefano E, Delogu G, Stamilla A, Segafreddo G, Palucci I, Degiacomi G, Boldrin F, Ravoni A, Moretti D, Onofri E, Molin MD, Rybniker J, Sorze D, Campagnaro E, Cioetto-Mazzabo L, Tieri P, Ramón-García S, Pasca MR, Manganelli R.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) granulomas are complex multicellular structures central to disease pathogenesis and treatment challenges, notably due to bacterial persistence and immune modulation. Existing animal and in vitro models do not fully capture granuloma heterogeneity and immune complexity. Here, we review the biology and applications of Granuloma-Like Structures (GLS) derived from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which recapitulate key features of early granuloma formation, including macrophage differentiation, lymphocyte involvement, and cytokine dynamics. Quantitative analysis identifies conserved bacterial growth trajectories and recurrent aggregate sizes, despite protocol diversity and donor variability. Furthermore, a minimal theoretical model illustrates how aggregate size may influence drug efficacy, through physical and biological mechanisms. Although underutilized in drug screening, GLS offer a promising intermediate platform by bridging simple cell monolayers to animal models, particularly for evaluating host-directed therapies. Standardized metrics and integration with computational models are needed to enhance reproducibility and translational relevance. GLS thus represent a valuable tool to investigate host-pathogen interactions and advance TB drug development under controlled immune conditions.

papers.title: In vivo Gene Writing with engineered retrotransposons.
papers.authors: Li D, De Iaco A, Ngan KC, Smyshlyaev G, Kumbhojkar N, Steinberg BE, Kalani Z, Xia L, Dolbee A, Kibbler ES, Duncan MC, Lin I, Benczkowski MS, Venkatesan L, Calabria A, Carter TA, Corsi GI, Kristiansen TA, McAllister G, Bolt CC, Harris KA, Boucher JI, Zeng C, Dakhara IS, Wang X, Sothiselvam S, Akinci E, Strickland J, Mathur A, Ferren C, Desmond J, Rodriguez J, Rottman JB, Gupta M, Liu L, Palchaudhuri R, Wang ZJ, Citorik RJ, Rubens JR, Pujar NS, Holmes MC, Cotta-Ramusino C.
papers.abstract: Efficient integration of gene-length cargos in vivo remains challenging. Non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons, which naturally mobilize large DNA segments through an RNA intermediate, could potentially address these limitations. Here, we developed a computational pipeline to systematically identify a diverse set of non-LTR retrotransposons. Extensive engineering generated elements capable of the efficient and stable insertion of reporter genes in human cells using RNA templates introduced in trans, which we term Gene Writers. Gene Writers successfully generated CD19 and CD20 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells ex vivo with robust antitumor activity. Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enabled in vivo CAR-T cell generation and stable B cell depletion in a humanized mouse model. Our study delineates a comprehensive framework for the discovery, engineering, and application of non-LTR retrotransposons and demonstrates their utility for gene-sized cargo delivery in vivo, thereby bridging a critical gap in existing gene therapy modalities.

papers.title: SARS-CoV-2 variant-dependent alterations in nasopharyngeal microbiota and host inflammatory response.
papers.authors: Maulen M, Pezoa-Soto I, León D, Dominguez EM, Martin AJM, Díaz-Vásquez WA.
papers.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic saw multiple outbreaks occur over short periods. This was linked to the virus's high infectivity and rapid mutation rate, which hindered the development of effective treatments and a comprehensive understanding of COVID-19 pathophysiology. The nasopharyngeal tract, the main entry site of SARS-CoV-2, interacts with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors via the viral spike glycoprotein, triggering pro-inflammatory responses that affect both tissue integrity and the resident microbiota. Viral infection induces dysbiosis by modulating microbiome diversity. Although distinct variants produce independent symptoms and viral loads, their impact on the nasopharyngeal microbiota and host inflammatory profile remains poorly understood. To address this, we analyzed nasopharyngeal samples from Chilean individuals collected during different phases of the pandemic. The microbiota was characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region), and cytokine expression was quantified by RT-qPCR. Finally, applied rigorous data processing and machine-learning models, Random Forest and K-Nearest Neighbors, to identify associations between SARS-CoV-2 variants, inflammatory markers, and opportunistic bacterial genera. Our results reveal that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with distinct immunomicrobial signatures marked by increased TNF-α expression and the expansion of opportunistic taxa. These variant-dependent alterations indicate that host inflammatory responses and microbial dysbiosis are closely intertwined in the nasopharyngeal environment. This study provides a comprehensive framework integrating microbial and host factors to better understand the mechanisms underlying COVID-19 pathogenesis and highlights the potential of combining microbiome and cytokine profiling with machine-learning approaches to differentiate infection outcomes across viral variants.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding how SARS-CoV-2 infection alters the upper respiratory microbiota and host immune responses is essential to uncover the mechanisms underlying COVID-19 severity. In this study, we integrate bacterial 16S rRNA sequencing, inflammatory markers, and machine learning to identify key descriptors of infection such as TNF-α, Acinetobacter , Prevotella , and Staphylococcus . These markers define a conserved immunomicrobial signature across viral variants, linking inflammatory activation with microbial dysbiosis in the nasopharyngeal environment. Our findings highlight the value of the correct and robust application of machine learning models and nested cross-validation strategies in high-dimensional (wide) data sets to improve variant discrimination, reveal host-microbe interactions, and support the development of therapeutic strategies for respiratory viral infections.

papers.title: Decoding autoimmune diseases through the adaptive immune receptor repertoires.
papers.authors: Wang X, Zhu H, Li Z, Cao L.
papers.abstract: The adaptive immune receptor repertoire (AIRR), composed of T-cell receptors (TCRs) and B-cell receptors (BCRs), underpins antigen-specific immunity through extensive diversity generated by V(D)J recombination and junctional modification. Advances in high-throughput AIRR sequencing have enabled comprehensive characterization of clonal diversity, gene usage patterns, and antigen-driven selection at unprecedented resolution. In autoimmune diseases, breakdown of immune tolerance permits the persistence and expansion of autoreactive lymphocyte clones, and is associated with characteristic repertoire remodeling. Reported alterations include changes in repertoire diversity, oligoclonal expansion, biased V(D)J gene usage, and convergent CDR3 motifs. Notably, repertoire changes exhibit spatial and temporal heterogeneity across peripheral blood and target tissues, highlighting the compartmentalized nature of adaptive immune responses. This review synthesizes current evidence on TCR and BCR repertoire alterations across major autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's disease, type 1 diabetes, and ankylosing spondylitis. We summarize emerging computational frameworks for AIRR analysis and highlight machine learning approaches for clonotype classification and antigen specificity prediction. Furthermore, we discuss the diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications of AIRR profiling, particularly the potential for identifying disease-associated clonotypes and guiding antigen-specific immunotherapies. Despite ongoing technical and biological challenges, continued advances in sequencing technologies and computational modeling are strengthening the role of AIRR analysis as a valuable framework for elucidating autoimmune pathogenesis and advancing precision immunology.

papers.title: Long-lived plasma cells in rheumatic and selected antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases: biology, evidence, and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.authors: Guo H, Xiang W, Zeng L, Xiao W, Sun L.
papers.abstract: Persistent autoantibody production after conventional immunosuppression or B-cell depletion has focused attention on antibody-secreting cells that survive without ongoing proliferation. Long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs) are indispensable for durable protective immunity, but autoreactive members of this compartment may also maintain pathogenic antibodies in selected autoimmune diseases. Interpretation is complicated because longevity is usually inferred from population kinetics, anatomical persistence, transcriptional state, or treatment resistance rather than demonstrated by lineage tracing in humans; neither CD19 loss nor any single surface phenotype is a definitive identifier. We conducted a structured narrative review focused on rheumatic diseases and selected antibody-mediated disorders. We integrate developmental routes, CXCR4-dependent homing, adhesion, BAFF/APRIL receptor biology, stromal contact, proteostatic and metabolic adaptation, and single-cell heterogeneity. Systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis receive dedicated consideration because renal antibody-secreting-cell signatures distinguish active plasmablast-rich inflammation from LLPC-like persistence in refractory disease. Across diseases, the evidence ranges from direct kinetic or tissue studies to indirect serological observations and therapeutic inference. Plasma-cell-directed therapies-including proteasome inhibition, CD38 depletion, BCMA-directed T-cell engagers or cellular therapy, and immune reconstitution-have produced clinically important signals, but most autoimmune data remain uncontrolled, early-phase, or disease-specific. Niche disruption, apoptosis or autophagy inhibition, and antigen-specific deletion remain preclinical or conceptual. A useful translational framework is therefore not that LLPCs are universal master drivers, but that persistent autoreactive plasma cells may constitute one treatment-relevant disease module whose importance should be demonstrated with tissue, clonal, and longitudinal evidence before intervention.

papers.title: Bidirectional Regulatory Mechanisms of T cell-microglia Interactions in Cerebral Ischemic Disease: Molecular Crosstalk, Experimental Techniques and Therapeutic Implications.
papers.authors: Zheng Y, Cheng J, Li F, Ren Z, Chen C, Zhang Z, Lan X, Zhang C, Zhao Y, Han J, Li J, Cheng F, Wang Q, Li C, Wang X.
papers.abstract: Cerebral ischemic diseases, such as ischemic stroke (IS) and vascular dementia (VaD), are major causes of neurological disability and mortality. Neuroinflammation acts as a pivotal driver of secondary brain injury, mediated by intricate bidirectional interactions between peripheral T cells and central nervous system (CNS)-resident microglia. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms underlying T cell-microglia crosstalk in cerebral ischemia, emphasizing their dual roles in exacerbating neurotoxicity and promoting repair. Direct interactions involve antigen presentation via MHC-TCR engagement and co-stimulatory checkpoints (e.g., CD80/CD86-CD28, PD-L1-PD-1), which regulate T cell activation and microglial polarization. Direct signaling through cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-10) further modulates microglial phenotypes: Th1/Th17 cells drive pro-inflammatory M1 polarization via STAT1/NF-κB pathways, while Tregs/Th2 cells induce anti-inflammatory M2 states through STAT6/SMAD signaling. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell omics reveal spatiotemporal dynamics of these interactions, identifying STAT1/STAT6 imbalance as a critical determinant of neuroinflammatory outcomes. Advanced methodologies, including two-photon intravital microscopy and microfluidic blood-brain barrier (BBB) models, enable real-time visualization of immune cell trafficking and synaptic communication. Therapeutically, targeting immune checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1) or cytokine pathways (e.g., IL-4 mimetics) shows promise in recalibrating neuroimmune responses. However, challenges such as blood-brain barrier impermeability to biologics and interspecies immune heterogeneity necessitate innovative delivery strategies. This review integrates molecular, cellular, and technological insights to propose a framework for precision immunomodulation. By elucidating context-dependent signaling nodes and leveraging emerging tools, the study underscores the potential of harnessing T cell-microglia crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and enhance neural repair, offering transformative avenues for stroke and dementia therapy.

papers.title: Single-cell analysis reveals CXCL16 + dendritic cells and clonally expanded GZMK + CD4 T cells driving joint inflammation in psoriatic arthritis.
papers.authors: Mullins BJ, Shwetar J, Herrera A, Cheng AY, Yang KL, Hernández AJ, Tumang K, Mimitou EP, Sahimi A, Alvarado L, Medina R, Haberman RH, Girija PV, Boehringer T, Ivanova E, Borbet TC, Eichman S, Cunningham I, Hillier K, Bajwa S, Carvalho CC, Schwab SR, Attur MG, Ruggles K, Scher JU, Koralov SB.
papers.abstract: Objective Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic immune-mediated arthritis affecting approximately 30% of individuals with psoriasis. The mechanisms driving PsA joint inflammation remain incompletely defined. Methods To address this gap, we performed multimodal single-cell sequencing of immune cells from matched peripheral blood and synovial fluid (SF) from 6 PsA patients, with comparisons to a rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patient and 6 healthy controls (HC). Results SF CD4 and CD8 T cells displayed elevated expression of TOX, PDCD1, CTLA4, GZMK, CXCR3, and CXCR6, reflecting a tissue-specific activation state. CD4 T cell sub-clustering revealed clonally expanded populations enriched for GZMK and cytotoxic gene programs, suggesting antigen-driven activation. In contrast, CD8 T cell clonality showed a significant correlation with GZMK expression, however GZMK + CD8 T cells in the joint exhibited a transcriptional signature consistent with functional exhaustion. Concurrently, SF was enriched for CD141 + , CD1c + , CCR7 + , and SIGLEC6 + dendritic cells (DCs), characterized by increased CXCL16 expression and antigen presentation pathways. Flow cytometry and ELISA in an additional 25 PsA patients and 16 HCs confirmed protein-level enrichment of key chemokines and GZMK + T cells. Cell-cell communication analysis highlighted CXCR6-CXCL16 and CXCR3-CXCL10 chemokine axes as mediators of immune cell recruitment and retention, while in vitro assays showed enhanced migration of PsA SF T cells toward a CXCL16 gradient relative to paired blood. Conclusion Together, these findings suggest that clonally expanded GZMK + CD4 T cells in PsA are cytotoxic and antigen-responsive, contributing to joint inflammation following recruitment by CXCL16-producing dendritic cells.

papers.title: The evolution of immunotherapy resistance in mismatch repair-deficient colorectal cancer: A spatiotemporal perspective.
papers.authors: Lv Y, Ding Y, Zhao Z, Song S, Zang D, Zhang J, Ji Y, Zhong J.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the therapeutic landscape for mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) colorectal cancer; however, primary and acquired resistance remain significant challenges in clinical practice. This review proposes a working hypothesis that resistance can be conceptualized as following an evolutionary trajectory from a dynamic spatiotemporal perspective: commencing with early immune evasion by tumor cells, progressing through an adaptive immunosuppression phase, and culminating in advanced metastatic resistance characterized by spatial heterogeneity. Within this framework, we critically evaluate combination therapeutic strategies targeting resistance signals at each stage, including dual immune checkpoint blockade, tumor microenvironment modulators, novel bispecific antibodies, and neoantigen vaccines. We further emphasize that future breakthroughs will depend on leveraging single-cell multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics technologies to unravel resistance heterogeneity. This will drive the development of dynamic, personalized sequential combination therapies, delivering sustained benefits for patients.

papers.title: NU-1025 modulates immunogenic cell death in bladder cancer: A multi-omics insight.
papers.authors: Li Y, Zuo L, Dong X, Sun R, Liu H.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has shown limited efficacy in bladder cancer, underscoring the need for therapeutic strategies that enhance tumor immunogenicity. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) can stimulate adaptive immunity and remodel the tumor microenvironment, yet its comprehensive landscape and druggable potential in bladder cancer remain unexplored. Here, we performed integrative bioinformatics analysis of transcriptomic data from TCGA and GEO bladder cancer cohorts to characterize ICD-associated subtypes, construct a prognostic risk model, and analyze immune infiltration. Connectivity Map (CMap) database and the XSum algorithm were employed for computational drug screening. Molecular docking was used to predict interactions between candidate compounds and immune checkpoint proteins. In silico ADMET and toxicology profiles were evaluated. The clinical relevance was assessed through independent CT urography imaging and PD-L1 immunohistochemistry data. Two ICD molecular subtypes were identified with distinct prognostic and microenvironment features. An eight-gene ICD risk model was established and validated, effectively stratifying patients into high- and low-risk groups with differential survival, immune cell infiltration, and tumor mutational burden. Through computational screening, NU-1025 was nominated as a top candidate capable of reversing the high-risk gene expression pattern. In silico profiling indicated favorable drug-like properties and low toxicity risk. Clinical data analysis revealed that high-grade bladder tumors frequently exhibit low PD-L1 expression, aligning with the predicted need for ICD-inducing agents. Overall, this research decodes the ICD landscape in bladder cancer and, via a computational drug repurposing pipeline, nominates NU-1025 as a novel candidate with predicted ICD-inducing and/or immune checkpoint modulatory activity.

papers.title: The Characteristics of Tumor Microenvironment by the Single Cell Profile in Endometrial Cancer of no Specific Molecular Profile (NSMP) Subtype.
papers.authors: Yuan X, Zhai Z, Jing C, Zhang W, Tian W, Ren Y.
papers.abstract: Endometrial cancer (EC) of no specific molecular profile (NSMP) subtype lacks specific molecular features, and the relationship of tumor microenvironment (TME) and relapse in NSMP EC remains incompletely understood. This study integrates single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex immunohistochemistry to elucidate the TME and mechanisms of relapse in NSMP EC. The results showed reduced immune infiltration and increased immune-suppressive cells, including SPP1+ macrophages and regulatory T cells (Tregs) in NSMP EC. More epithelial cell clusters with high stemness scores are observed in primary NSMP EC tumors collected before recurrence. In NSMP EC, tip endothelial cells and MMP11+ LEF1+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are linked with angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and CD4+ T cells remain in a stress-response state and are functionally impaired. Interestingly, a subset of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) characterized by SPP1 expression is discovered, which may remodel the tumor microenvironment by potentially promoting CD4+ T cells stress and maintaining epithelial cells stemness through SPP1-CD44, thereby potentially contributing to the proliferation and migration of tumor cells, which has verified by in vitro experiments. This study advances the mechanistic understanding of recurrence-related TME and provides a foundation for the development of personalized treatments for NSMP EC patients.

papers.title: Microglia in Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders: Pathogenic Mechanisms and Emerging Concepts of Microglial Heterogeneity.
papers.authors: Wang H, Wang X, Ai Q, Pei D.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) comprise a spectrum of cognitive disturbances after anesthesia and surgery, affecting learning, memory, and executive function. Although systemic inflammation, surgical trauma, anesthetic exposure, and patient vulnerability have been implicated in PND, the mechanisms linking perioperative stress to persistent cognitive changes remain incompletely understood. Microglia, as resident immune cells of the central nervous system, are important regulators of neuroimmune interactions and may contribute to PND through alterations in inflammatory signaling, synaptic regulation, vascular function, metabolism, and epigenetic programs. In this Overview, we summarize current evidence regarding microglial involvement in PND across five interconnected domains: neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, microglia-neuron communication, mitochondrial and metabolic regulation, and epigenetic remodeling. We further discuss emerging single-cell transcriptomic and multi-omic studies indicating that microglial responses are heterogeneous, dynamic, and context dependent rather than adequately described by the traditional M1/M2 framework. We propose that PND involves complex interactions among peripheral immune activation, neurovascular dysfunction, microglial state transitions, and neuronal vulnerability. Finally, we highlight current challenges in translating microglial mechanisms into clinical applications and discuss future directions for identifying biomarkers and developing context-specific perioperative neuroprotective strategies.

papers.title: PLCB3 as a causal regulator linking ferroptosis and immune remodeling in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
papers.authors: Zhu H, Qin C, Yang J, Luo S, Guo Y.
papers.abstract: Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a complex syndrome lacking effective targeted therapies, but its causal genes and mechanisms remain poorly defined. Objective To investigate the role of PLCB3 and its association with ferroptosis in HFpEF. Methods We integrated transcriptomic data and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) data and employed differential expression analysis, mendelian randomization (MR), summary data-based mendelian randomization (SMR), and colocalization analysis to identify key genes associated with HFpEF. Furthermore, functional validation was performed using a HFpEF mouse model and siRNA mediated PLCB3 knockdown in AC16 cardiomyocytes. Cell viability, reactive oxygen species (ROS), lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis related protein expression were subsequently assessed to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying PLCB3-mediated ferroptosis. Results Phospholipase C beta 3 (PLCB3) was identified as a candidate causal gene for HFpEF. PLCB3 expression was significantly reduced in HFpEF cardiac tissue and a mouse model induced by high-fat diet and l-NAME. Knockdown of PLCB3 decreased cell viability and induced ferroptosis, as indicated by reduced GPX4 and FTH1 expression, increased ACSL4 levels, and elevated lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species. These effects were significantly reversed by the ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1. In vivo, ferroptosis-related markers were similarly altered in HFpEF mice. In addition, immune infiltration analysis revealed significant differences in multiple immune cell populations between HFpEF and controls. Single-cell eQTL-based MR analysis further suggested that PLCB3 expression is associated with specific immune cell subsets, including B cells, CD4 + naïve T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. Conclusion PLCB3 is a potential regulator of HFpEF and may contribute to disease progression through its role in regulating ferroptosis and immune alterations. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of HFpEF and suggest that targeting PLCB3 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: UBL3 modification reduces nuclear POLE levels to potentiate antitumor immunity in aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas.
papers.authors: Dong Z, Huang W, Zhang L, Guo Q, Zhang X, Yang Y, Wang X, Liu Z, Yin Y, Ma G.
papers.abstract: While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized treatment of the patients with aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), including esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), only a subset of patients benefit from ICIs, therefore entailing exploration of the mechanisms to regulate treatment responsiveness. POLE, as a subunit of DNA polymerase ε, possesses 3'-5' proofreading activity, and its mutations have been associated with favourable response to ICIs in several solid tumors. However, post-translational modification (PTM) of POLE and its impact on the therapeutic efficacy of ICIs are unknown. Here, this study demonstrates that ubiquitin-like protein 3 (Ubl3), whose expression is markedly downregulated in SCCs, covalently binds to Pole, reduces nuclear Pole levels, triggers DNA damage, and activates cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Notably, Ubl3 modification of Pole significantly primes the local immune microenvironment to mitigate the growth of murine aero-upper digestive SCC cells and boost the efficacy of αPD-1 treatment in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis further revealed that UBL3 expression is positively correlated with better clinical outcomes in a cohort of ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with αPD-1. Together, our findings unravel UBL3 modification as a novel PTM mechanism governing subcellular location of POLE and its influence on immunotherapy responsiveness, thus making UBL3 modification as a promising immunomodulatory approach to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in patients with aero-upper digestive SCCs.

papers.title: Early transcriptional divergence and spatial remodeling toward immune activation and evasion shape lung adenocarcinoma precancer evolution.
papers.authors: Li JR, Zhu B, Chi Y, Chen H, Chen P, Hemaych JV, Tian Y, Hu X, Qin K, Nilsson MB, Zhang J, Cheng C.
papers.abstract: Tumor heterogeneity is a universal feature of cancer and may arise as early as precancer stages during lung adenocarcinoma evolution, yet the emergence of aggressive transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity across hyperplasia, adenoma, and invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) in a genetically engineered mouse model (129S4/Sv Kras LSL-G12D/+ ). Disease progression was accompanied by coordinated remodeling of epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments, along with dynamic changes in proliferation, immune response, and metabolic pathways. Notably, lesions of the same histological stage exhibited substantial transcriptional heterogeneity. By quantifying dedifferentiation states, we identified a subset of adenomas that had already diverged toward highly proliferative and metabolically active programs despite lacking invasive features. These lesions were further marked by early chromosome 6 amplification, whose corresponding human ortholog signature recapitulated aggressive proliferation-associated programs in early-stage human lung adenocarcinoma. Spatial analyses further revealed pronounced intratumoral heterogeneity within IAC, with tumor core regions showing increased proliferation and metabolism but reduced immune signaling compared to peripheral regions. In addition, immune checkpoint gene expression in T cells was transiently elevated at the hyperplasia stage, suggesting early immune modulation prior to overt malignancy. Together, these findings indicate that aggressive transcriptional divergence can emerge early during lung adenocarcinoma evolution and that spatial organization critically shapes tumor and immune programs before and after invasion.

papers.title: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor in CD8+ T cells inhibits GVHD through transcriptional modulation of differentiation and exhaustion.
papers.authors: Basu S, Massalee R, Mustapha HA, Alzubi M, Choi CY, Fan X, Cao X.
papers.abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) is an effective therapy for selected hematologic diseases. However, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) limits broader application of allo-HCT. The catecholaminergic sympathetic nervous system modulates immune cells. Beta-2 adrenergic Receptor (β2AR) acts as an immune checkpoint, yet its role in CD8+ T cells remains poorly understood. We used an MHC-mismatched model of acute GVHD to study how β2AR activity on donor CD8+ T cells affects GVHD severity. Host mice receiving β2AR+/+ (WT) CD8+ T cells demonstrated less severe GVHD, lower inflammatory cytokines in peripheral circulation, decreased donor CD8+ T cell expansion, and reduced central memory formation compared to host mice receiving β2AR-/- (KO) CD8+ T cells. Single cell RNA-seq and flow cytometry analyses revealed that donor-derived KO CD8+ T cells had an increased Tc1/Tc17 signature (T-Bet, IFNγ, TNFα, RORγT, and IL23r), expressed lower levels of Eomes and Gata3, and expressed inhibitory PD1, Tim3, Lag3, and CTLA4 less frequently than β2AR WT counterparts. In addition, host mice receiving KO CD8+ T cells exhibit a stronger graft-versus-lymphoma effect than host mice receiving β2AR WT CD8+ T cells. Together, these results indicate that β2AR activity in donor CD8+ T cells inhibits GVHD through transcriptional modulation of T cell differentiation and exhaustion, including a T-Bet/Eomes and PD1 relevant process.

papers.title: An improved protocol to isolate enriched immune cells from murine intestinal epithelium and lamina propria.
papers.authors: Crotts SB, Shapiro VS.
papers.abstract: The intestine is home to more immune cells than any other non-lymphatic peripheral tissue, but research of these cells is stymied by the technical difficulties involved in isolating them. Here, we describe a protocol to isolate highly viable immune cells from murine intestinal epithelium and lamina propria. This protocol can be used to characterize cells by flow cytometry or single-cell transcriptomics, as in Crotts et al., or by other analysis methods.

papers.title: Cytokine context shapes antigen-presenting and matrix-producing states of cancer-associated fibroblasts.
papers.authors: Song F, Chen Q, Huang D, Zhang Y, Han D, Rao W, Li M, Gao Y, Zhang R, Zhu H, Wang S, Jiang X, Lin S, Bi D, Zhang H, Wei Q, Qin H.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) exhibit remarkable functional heterogeneity, with conserved subtypes observed across diverse malignancies. However, their shared roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their dynamic plasticity remain incompletely understood. In this study, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling across four cancer types, we identified two distinct immunomodulatory CAF states, termed antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) and matrix-producing CAFs (mCAFs). Across multiple solid tumors, apCAFs were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immune features and favorable prognosis, whereas mCAFs were associated with immunosuppressive characteristics and poorer clinical outcomes. Spatial analyses revealed distinct localization patterns of apCAFs and mCAFs within the TME. Functionally, patient-derived apCAFs promoted T-cell migration, proliferation, and activation, whereas mCAFs suppressed these responses in vitro. Pan-cancer analyses further revealed a strong inverse correlation between apCAF and mCAF abundance across tumor tissues. Mechanistically, IFN-γ and TGF-β-associated signaling contexts were linked to distinct CAF transcriptional programs, with IFN-γ promoting apCAF-associated features and TGF-β favoring mCAF-associated features, suggesting a potential role of cytokine context in shaping CAF state heterogeneity. Clinically, apCAFs correlated with favorable immunotherapy response, whereas mCAFs predicted poor therapeutic outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify conserved immunomodulatory CAF subtypes across cancers, reveal distinct cytokine-associated CAF programs, and support stromal reprogramming as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

papers.title: A gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene score for subtyping and predicting the treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis: integrative analysis with in silico knockout validation.
papers.authors: Sun XF, Yang YJ, Li CL, Huang T, Wang Q, Yu Q.
papers.abstract: Background The pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves a complex interplay between immune dysregulation and metabolic disturbance, with the gut microbiota and its metabolites playing pivotal roles. However, integrated biomarkers based on the "gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene" regulatory axis that can quantify its impact on RA stratification and therapeutic response are lacking. Methods We integrated multiple RA transcriptomic datasets to screen for host genes explicitly associated with the gut microbiota and metabolites using the gutMGene database. A gut microbiota-metabolite-host score (GMS) was constructed via principal component analysis (PCA). Immune infiltration patterns were evaluated using CIBERSORT. Furthermore, scRNA-seq was employed to map the cellular origins of key genes, and in silico knockout analysis using scTenifoldKnk was performed to simulate the functional ablation of core host genes within this regulatory axis. Additionally, molecular docking was conducted to validate the binding affinities between the key host proteins and the optimal small molecule. Results We identified seven microbiota-metabolite-host hub genes (FOS, JUN, IDO1, PEMT, EGFR, ABCC4, and FADS3) and constructed the GMS. The GMS stratified patients with RA into two distinct functional subtypes: an adaptive immune activation subtype and an inflammatory-metabolic composite subtype. Notably, the GMS demonstrated superior performance in predicting responses to anti-TNF and rituximab therapies. The scRNA-seq analysis revealed high expression of FOS and JUN in T cells and NK cells. In silico knockout analysis further revealed the central transcription factors FOS and JUN as key executors of this axis, as their ablation significantly affected osteoclast differentiation and the enrichment of TNF/MAPK inflammatory pathways. These computational findings support the core mechanism by which gut microbiota-metabolite signalling drives RA joint pathology via FOS/JUN. Molecular docking results confirmed strong binding interactions between the identified active molecules and their respective target proteins. Conclusion This study establishes a GMS based on the gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene regulatory axis as a robust tool for molecular subtyping and predicting biological therapy responses in patients with RA. Crucially, through integrated computational modelling, including in silico knockout and molecular docking validation, we identified FOS/JUN as critical executor genes linking the gut microenvironment to RA bone destruction, providing novel targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at the gut-joint axis.
