papers.title: Exploratory Single-Cell Analysis of NK-Annotated Cells Across Marrow Compartments in Prostate Cancer Bone Metastasis.
papers.authors: Pan K, Xing N.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer preferentially colonizes bone, where marrow compartments differ in tissue structure and immune composition. We reanalyzed a 920,521-cell integrated prostate cancer atlas containing 38,842 NK-annotated cells from 126 sample identifiers, focusing on one bone-marrow cohort of 16 subjects and 32 samples. Distal marrow from patients with bone metastasis was compared with nonmalignant marrow from unrelated hip-replacement controls, while complete within-patient pairs were used for local comparisons. Sample- or subject-level composition, pseudobulk expression, pathway, and microenvironment analyses treated biological units, not cells, as replicates. The inherited CytokNKs_GZMH label was more frequent in distal marrow than in controls (25.4% versus 2.0%; centered log-ratio effect 2.82; false-discovery rate 0.0367). Paired tumor-versus-distal comparisons showed higher relative abundance of ImmSuppNKs_CREM and lower proportions of several other inherited labels at the 10% false-discovery threshold. A pooled comparison identified 62 differential genes within RegNKs_IL7R and generated a 24-gene exploratory program; distal-only models had no genes meeting the joint cutoff. Frequent T-cell- and myeloid-marker detection precluded assignment of this population as a validated NK subset. Program separation within the discovery cohort was subject to gene-selection bias and did not establish predictive performance. Full-atlas analyses described compartment-associated composition differences and candidate ligand-receptor expression pairs. Donor characteristics, treatment, sampling site, specimen processing, and annotation uncertainty remain unresolved sources of confounding. These findings are hypothesis-generating associations in recovered NK-annotated cells, not evidence of a metastasis-specific field effect, a regulatory NK population, or clinical utility.

papers.title: A syngeneic murine glioma model recapitulates key molecular, immunologic, and functional features of human glioblastoma to enable therapeutic development.
papers.authors: Grausam KB, Pioso MS, Sanchez JC, Li M, Rincon Fernandez Pacheco D, Hatanaka EA, Herrera G, Lai TJ, Lu E, Linesch PW, Kobritz N, Phan TL, Ashley S, Andrade AA, Markus L, Yao J, Fan X, Yu B, Diaz AA, Liau LM, Danielpour M, Nathanson DA, Prins RM, Breunig JJ, Shiao SL.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

papers.title: Targeting CCR1/CCR2 attenuates cytokine release syndrome while preserving CAR T-cell antitumor activity.
papers.authors: Li YR, Chen Y, Zhu Y, Zhao AS, Shen X, Yuen T, Yeh S, Padua DM, Zou K, Qiu Z, Huang J, Yang L.
papers.abstract: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major dose-limiting toxicity of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, yet the upstream mechanisms driving macrophage activation remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a xenograft model of human CAR T-cell therapy that recapitulates key features of CRS and combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with pharmacological intervention to define the inflammatory programs underlying CRS. CAR T-cell treatment induced dose-dependent systemic inflammation and remodeled the host myeloid compartment, leading to the accumulation of a distinct population of CRS-associated macrophages. Analysis of clinical scRNA-seq datasets from CAR T cell-treated glioblastoma patients confirmed enrichment of the CRS-associated macrophage gene signature following therapy in patients, supporting the clinical relevance of our findings. Transcriptomic analyses identified marked upregulation of the chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR2 together with activation of CCL3- and CCL2-associated signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1 and CCR2 significantly reduced clinical CRS, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage activation while preserving CAR T-cell expansion, effector cytokine production, and in vivo antitumor efficacy. These findings identify CCR1/CCR2-dependent chemokine signaling as a critical regulator of macrophage-driven CRS and support chemokine receptor blockade as a promising strategy to improve the safety of CAR T-cell therapy without compromising therapeutic efficacy.

papers.title: Cross-omics mapping of the human HIV restrictome across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses.
papers.authors: Maghembe RS.
papers.abstract: Host restriction factors can block HIV at multiple stages, but they are often studied as individual genes or within a single molecular layer. I performed an evidence-structured computational reanalysis of three independent public datasets to determine how the human HIV restrictome varies across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses. The analysis used bulk monocyte RNA sequencing (GSE157198), PBMC single-cell/CITE-seq data (GSE256089), and primary CD4 T-cell proteomics (PXD012263) within a prespecified restrictome-immunometabolism framework. In GSE157198, ART-naive monocytes had higher core-restrictome activity than healthy controls (difference = 1.154, p = 0.000746), and core scores were strongly correlated with interferon/innate-sensing scores (Spearman r = 0.800, p = 7.47 × 10^-11). Core-lipid/cholesterol correlation was weaker and was not independent of interferon after conditional analysis. In GSE256089, participant-paired core-restrictome scores were enriched in NK cells relative to B cells, monocytes, and T cells, and matched random-gene-set analyses supported enrichment beyond background expression structure. FCGR3A monocytes also had higher participant-paired core scores than CD14 monocytes. Exploratory sensing/death-gene analysis identified cell-type-specific expression patterns but did not establish pathway activation, pyroptosis, or apoptosis. In PXD012263, the historical q < 0.05 proteomic selection contained 19 curated genes and retained mixed response polarity; sensitivity thresholds q < 0.01 and q < 0.10 selected 10 and 25 genes, respectively. Together, the results show that HIV restrictome activity varies across clinical and immune-cell contexts and is embedded within broader interferon-linked and immunometabolic states. Because the datasets are independent and not subject matched, the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

papers.title: CD74 as a Potential Adjunctive Tissue Biomarker for Bullous Pemphigoid Lesions: A Retrospective Study Integrating Bioinformatics Analysis and Experimental Validation.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Zhang X, Dong F, Zhang C, Jin Z, Mao Y, Zhu H, Zhang Q, Yin D, Yang C, Mei X.
papers.abstract: Background Bullous pemphigoid (BP), an autoimmune blistering disorder that primarily afflicts the geriatric population, poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, particularly in patients with comorbidities. This retrospective study aimed to identify and validate potential adjunctive tissue biomarkers for BP and explore their association with immune-related mechanisms through integrated bioinformatics analysis and experimental validation. Methods Transcriptomic data from the GEO dataset were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), which were further cross-referenced with immune-related gene signatures. CD74 was selected as a candidate biomarker and its expression was validated by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in paraffin-embedded skin tissues from patients with BP, healthy controls (HC), and disease controls, including pemphigus vulgaris (PV), psoriasis (Pso), atopic dermatitis (AD), and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Diagnostic performance was evaluated by ROC curve analysis. Single-cell RNA sequencing and immunofluorescence staining were performed to investigate the cellular distribution and immune association of CD74. Results CD74 was identified as an immune-related DEG associated with CCL13 expression. CD74 expression was increased in BP lesions and exhibited a characteristic linear distribution along the dermoepidermal junction. Quantitative ROC analysis based on CD74 expression area percentage showed moderate diagnostic performance, while the linear staining pattern demonstrated potential value as an adjunctive diagnostic feature. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed predominant CD74 expression in MHC-II-enriched cells, and immunofluorescence confirmed CD74/HLA-DR colocalization. CD74 expression was positively correlated with peripheral blood eosinophil counts, suggesting an association with systemic immune activation in BP. Conclusion CD74 may represent a promising adjunctive tissue biomarker for BP diagnosis. Its characteristic tissue distribution and association with immune-related features suggest that CD74 may reflect immune alterations within BP lesions. Further validation in larger independent cohorts is required.

papers.title: Effects of Paeonia-derived Catechin on Neutrophil-associated Inflammation in Pneumonia.
papers.authors: Bo W, Zhang J, Jiang N.
papers.abstract: Pneumonia in children is frequently accompanied by excessive inflammatory responses and immune dysregulation, which may lead to severe clinical outcomes. Catechin has shown anti-inflammatory activity in multiple disease settings, but its role and molecular mechanisms in pneumonia remain unclear. Public bulk RNA-sequencing data from pediatric pneumonia (GSE261482) and public mouse lung single-cell RNA-sequencing data from an experimental pneumonia model (GSE295484) were analyzed using weighted gene co-expression network analysis, differential expression analysis, cell-type annotation, and gene set enrichment analysis. Interactions between catechin and selected proteins were assessed using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. A key gene module associated with pneumonia-related traits was identified, and 18 candidate genes, primarily enriched in inflammatory and immune-related pathways, were screened. Single-cell analysis showed that these genes were predominantly enriched in neutrophils and alveolar macrophages, with increased neutrophil proportions under inflammatory conditions. MMP9, PYGL, and GADD45A were selected as candidate genes. Docking and dynamics simulations supported stable predicted interactions between catechin and these selected proteins. Catechin may be associated with pneumonia-related inflammatory pathways by modulating neutrophil-associated pathways and interacting with key immune-related proteins. This study provides a systems-level view of catechin action in pneumonia and highlights potential targets for further experimental validation.

papers.title: RNA evidence supports clinical stage antibody drug targets in oncology
papers.authors: Pozzobon, D.; Khusial, N.; Spreafico, R.; Csala, A.
papers.abstract: Background: The selection of efficacious and safe antibody-based oncology targets depends on tumor specificity and normal-tissue expression, and remains challenging. Bulk RNA-seq can identify tumor-enriched surface genes, but may obscure tumor specificity and normal-cell expression patterns that are relevant to the therapeutic window. We evaluated whether single-cell RNA-seq-derived expression features improve retrospective prioritization of clinically pursued antibody targets. Methods: We developed a bulk and single-cell RNA expression-based ranking framework across six solid tumor indications. 4,532 candidate surfaceome targets were scored using tumor Specificity, normal Safety, and blood Sink features derived from bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, or a combined modality. Ranking performance was evaluated against a curated validation set of tumor-associated antibody-based oncology targets using logistic regression, with odds ratios (ORs) reported per one-standard-deviation increase in score. Results: Higher Specificity scores were associated with clinical-stage target selection across all modalities. In cross-indication meta-analysis, single-cell Specificity showed higher ORs than bulk Specificity across clinical phase thresholds, including Phase [≥] 1 (OR 2.56 versus 1.81), Phase [≥] 2 (OR 2.77 versus 1.88), Phase [≥] 3 (OR 3.53 versus 2.04) and Approved targets (OR 3.51 versus 1.74). Combined bulk-and-single-cell Specificity showed intermediate enrichment. Specificity score alone did not consistently show a significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons, except for Phase [≥] 3 targets. After adding normal-cell Safety and blood Sink features, the single-cell general score showed the strongest enrichment across thresholds (Phase [≥] 1 OR 3.61, Phase [≥] 2 OR 4.16, Phase [≥] 3 OR 5.57, and Approved targets OR 4.25). This general score also showed consistently significant single-cell advantage over bulk in paired indication-level comparisons. Safety contributed most strongly in the single-cell modality, increasing meta-analytic ORs by an average of ~36% across thresholds compared to Specificity alone. Performance varied by indication, with breast cancer showing weaker Specificity-based enrichment. Conclusion: Expression-derived ranking features are retrospectively enriched among clinically pursued tumor-associated antibody targets. Single-cell evidence is most informative when tumor Specificity is combined with normal-cell Safety information, supporting its use as an interpretable component of early antibody target prioritization. These findings are in alignment with recent evidence that single-cell RNA-based cell-type specificity supports clinical-stage targets and demonstrate that expression-driven ranking can systematically recover clinically relevant oncology targets.

papers.title: Deep-learning-driven tumor microenvironment profiling improves immunotherapy response prediction
papers.authors: Wang, R. H.; Benard, B. A.; Ilerten, I.; Zdravkovic, S.; Al-Humadi, R.; Nasr, S.; Howitt, B.; Gentles, A. J.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the management of many cancers, such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), yet durable clinical benefit is achieved in only a subset of patients. Immunotherapy outcomes are governed by the multicellular tumor microenvironment (TME), through the structured and directional interplay of regulatory programs and ligand-receptor communications. Yet most existing methods for immunotherapy response prediction rely on independent signatures or cell types and fail to model the structured and directional signaling network within the TME. To address this gap, we introduce EcoNet, a computational framework that first models ecosystems consisting of co-occurring cell states, then constructs intercellular and intracellular signaling networks based on the ecosystems, and applies a graph attention network to derive embeddings from the signaling network for immunotherapy response prediction. Pretrained on 2,532 pan-cancer immunotherapy samples across multiple cohorts, EcoNet outperformed existing prediction methods by 7.5-19.9% and marker-based signatures by 4.4-21.2% in AUC, and its high-attention genes were enriched among those required for T-cell-mediated tumor killing in an independent CRISPR screen; applied to ccRCC with disease-specific fine-tuning, it stratified an independent ccRCC cohort by clinical outcome (P=0.024). Biologically, high-attention genes capture an interferon-responsive program that enhances antigen presentation and immune infiltration. To validate these findings, we curated a ccRCC clinical cohort profiled with CosMx single-cell spatial transcriptomics (46 samples, ~450,000 cells) and found the response-associated TME configuration identified by EcoNet localized to immune-enriched niches, supporting the response stratification. These results establish EcoNet as a generalizable framework for TME-informed therapeutic response prediction, readily extensible to other cancer types and therapeutic contexts.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation.
papers.authors: Cao Z, Zheng P, Qi Z, Yao Y, Xie D, He Y, Zong S, Zhang Z, Shi FD.
papers.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being evaluated to integrate clinical, imaging, immunological, and molecular data for decision-making in neuroimmunology. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.

papers.title: The osteoimmune cell atlas of peri-implantitis: A narrative scoping review.
papers.authors: Cafferata EA, Sculean A, Schwarz F.
papers.abstract: Background/aim Peri-implantitis represents a complex osteoimmune disorder characterized by dysregulated cellular ecosystems that drive chronic inflammation and accelerated peri-implant bone loss. Materials and methods This article was designed as a narrative scoping review to map and integrate the available evidence from transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics, flow cytometry, and immunohistochemistry to construct a comprehensive cellular atlas of peri-implantitis. Key findings Current evidence suggests that peri-implantitis lesions contain expanded and activated neutrophil, macrophage, T-cell, and B-lineage compartments, together with stromal and vascular cell populations that may contribute to inflammatory amplification and osteoclastogenic signaling. Reported features include CXCR2 + neutrophil subsets with NETosis-associated activity, inflammatory macrophage states, altered Th17/Treg-related immune responses, and expanded B-cell/plasma-cell compartments forming organized adaptive immune niches. Proposed molecular mechanisms include NF-κB-related inflammatory activation, CXCL13-associated adaptive immune organization, NETosis-related pathways, and RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenic signaling. However, several of these pathways remain incompletely validated in human peri-implantitis tissue. Critical knowledge gaps include limited direct evidence for NLRP3 inflammasome activation, uncharacterized type I interferon signaling, unresolved hierarchies of cellular RANKL sources, and limited functional data for rare immune populations. Conclusions The peri-implantitis osteoimmune microenvironment constitutes a highly organized, self-reinforcing inflammatory ecosystem. Progress toward precision therapeutic strategies requires spatial multiomics at subcellular resolution, longitudinal human studies, and functional ex vivo validation models to interrogate the self-sustaining circuits identified here.

papers.title: FGFR pathway inhibition enhances PD-1 blockade and modulates antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer models.
papers.authors: Shang Z, Jing C, Liu J, Zhang B, Rúbies Bedós M, Papakyriacou I, Mao Y, Chen Y.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has demonstrated limited efficacy in microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC). The fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling pathway contributes to tumor immune evasion, yet its role in CRC remains insufficiently understood. We investigated the immunomodulatory effects of FGFR inhibition in combination with PD-1 blockade in murine CRC models. In vitro co-culture systems were used to evaluate T cell activation upon FGFR3 blockade. RNA sequencing and bioinformatics analyses, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset evaluation, were conducted to elucidate molecular mechanisms and clinical relevance. Combined FGFR inhibition and PD-1 blockade significantly reduced T cell exhaustion and promoted macrophage repolarization toward an antitumor phenotype. Transcriptomic profiling revealed upregulation of immune-related pathways and activation of immune-stimulatory genes. In vitro, FGFR3-specific monoclonal antibody treatment enhanced IFNg release following PD-1 blockade. Moreover, analysis of TCGA data demonstrated that high FGFR3 expression correlates with worse prognosis in CRC patients. Our findings suggest that FGFR pathway inhibition may enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade and provide a rationale for further investigation of FGFR-targeted combination strategies in MSS CRC.

papers.title: CUE domain-containing 2 promotes diffuse large B-cell lymphoma progression via PP2A-B55β degradation and shapes macrophage-mediated immune responses.
papers.authors: Zeng LJ, Lu WX, Liang YZ, Yang J, Zhu JY, Wang L.
papers.abstract: CUE domain-containing 2 (CUEDC2) regulates ubiquitin-mediated protein turnover, cell-cycle progression, and inflammatory signaling, but its role in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) remains unclear. DLBCL is the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and a substantial proportion of patients develop relapsed or refractory disease. Here, by integrating clinical bioinformatics, immunohistochemistry, and functional studies in DLBCL cell lines, we demonstrate that CUEDC2 is overexpressed in DLBCL and is associated with advanced disease stage and poor prognosis. Mechanistically, proteomic and ubiquitination analyses revealed that CUEDC2 interacts with the protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) regulatory subunit B55 and promotes its ubiquitination-associated proteasomal degradation, accompanied by activation of NF-κB and mTOR signaling. Rescue studies support the role of PP2A-B55 as a downstream effector contributing to CUEDC2-associated proliferation and chemoresistance, and isoform-specific experiments identify PP2A-B55β as a preferentially regulated isoform. In addition, CUEDC2 knockdown in macrophages promoted M1-like polarization, enhanced phagocytosis, and supported CD8 + T cell activation and lymphoma cell apoptosis in vitro, without a detectable change in PP2A-B55 protein abundance. These immune effects were accompanied by changes in cellular metabolism and histone lactylation, although their causal relationships remain unresolved. Together, these findings support a tumor cell-intrinsic CUEDC2-PP2A-B55β-NF-κB/mTOR axis in DLBCL and suggest a potentially distinct immunomodulatory role for CUEDC2. Further mechanistic studies and in vivo validation are required to establish its therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Dietary Curcumin Protects Common Carp ( Cyprinus carpio ) Against Potassium Permanganate-Induced Toxicity: Hematological, Immunological, Oxidative, and Molecular Docking Evidence.
papers.authors: Eroğlu M, Mişe Yonar S, Tanrıkulu D, Uslu H, Yonar ME.
papers.abstract: Potassium permanganate treatment can adversely affect fish physiology despite its usefulness in aquaculture. This study evaluated the protective effects of dietary curcumin against potassium permanganate-induced disturbances in common carp (Cyprinus carpio). Fish were fed a basal diet or diets supplemented with 1%, 2%, or 4% curcumin for eight weeks, with or without subsequent exposure to potassium permanganate at 2 mg/L for 30 min daily for seven days. Hematological and immune parameters and oxidative status in the liver, kidney, spleen, and gill were assessed. Potassium permanganate exposure altered blood and immune parameters, increased lipid peroxidation, and weakened antioxidant defenses. Curcumin supplementation alleviated these effects, with protection evident at 1%, the lowest dietary inclusion level tested, and further improvements in selected parameters at 4%. Inclusion levels below 1% were not evaluated, so the minimum effective level remains unknown. Molecular docking predicted interactions between curcumin and the antioxidant enzymes SOD, CAT, GPx, and GST at structurally plausible binding sites. These computational findings were interpreted alongside the biological results as supportive, hypothesis-generating evidence rather than confirmation of functional effects on these enzymes in vivo. Overall, dietary curcumin showed potential to reduce the physiological disturbances associated with repeated potassium permanganate exposure. Further dose-response studies should evaluate inclusion levels below 1% to identify effective and economically viable supplementation rates and determine whether curcumin affects the antiparasitic or antibacterial efficacy of potassium permanganate.

papers.title: Unveiling a dual-pathway prognostic model: Integrating T cell-related and ubiquitination-related genes in lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Zeng S, Gao H, Liang H, Zhang D.
papers.abstract: The prognosis of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is closely associated with T-cell function and ubiquitination; however, the underlying mechanisms have remained elusive. Therefore, there is an urgent need to identify robust prognostic biomarkers. Using The Cancer Genome Atlas (n=515) and the Gene Expression Omnibus Series GSE31210 (n=226) datasets, an integrated differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression were performed to identify a prognostic signature. Based on an eight-gene risk model, patients were stratified into high-risk and low-risk groups. The model was subsequently evaluated through immune infiltration analysis, drug sensitivity assessment and reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) validation. Although the RT-qPCR validation cohort was relatively small (n=20), limiting statistical power, the observed expression trends were consistent with the bioinformatics findings. An eight-gene signature comprising RNF180, MAP3K3, TRIM2, RNF125, RWDD3, RNF144B, KCTD5 and TRIM27 was identified. In the training cohort, the risk model achieved area under the curve values of >0.6 for 1-, 3- and 5-year survival and was successfully validated in the independent GSE31210 cohort. A nomogram incorporating the risk score and M stage showed potential clinical utility within a limited threshold probability range. The high-risk group exhibited distinct immune infiltration patterns and significantly higher Tumour Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion scores. Drug sensitivity analysis identified 125 agents, including axitinib, with significantly different half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) values between the two risk groups. Specifically, high-risk patients exhibited higher IC 50 values for certain drugs, indicating lower sensitivity, whereas low-risk patients were more likely to respond to these agents. RT-qPCR analysis of an expanded cohort of 20 paired LUAD and adjacent normal tissues confirmed the differential expression of five key genes: KCTD5, MAP3K3, RNF144B, TRIM2 and TRIM27 . In conclusion, this novel prognostic model integrating T cell-related and ubiquitination-related genes provides a potential tool for risk stratification and personalized treatment in LUAD. It may also help clinicians identify high-risk patients who could benefit from closer follow-up or targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Identification of shared cuproptosis- and mitophagy-related hub genes and construction of a diagnostic model in sepsis-induced acute lung injury.
papers.authors: Tan R, Jin Y, Yuan Y, Zhang S, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Background Sepsis-induced acute lung injury (SI-ALI) is a life-threatening complication of sepsis. It is characterized by complex pathophysiology and the absence of reliable early biomarkers. Cuproptosis and mitophagy are both closely linked to mitochondrial homeostasis, but their potential molecular association in SI-ALI remains insufficiently characterized. Methods Transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analyzed, with GSE32707 serving as the discovery dataset and GSE10361 as an independent validation dataset. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were intersected with cuproptosis- and mitophagy-related gene sets to identify candidate genes. Biological functions were explored using Gene Ontology/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses and a protein-protein interaction network. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression and random forest were used to identify hub genes. A three-gene logistic regression model and nomogram were constructed and internally evaluated in the GSE32707 discovery cohort using receiver operating characteristic analysis, bootstrap calibration, and decision curve analysis. The individual hub genes were further evaluated in GSE10361. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT, and single-cell RNA-sequencing data from GSE151263 were used to characterize cell-type-specific expression of the hub genes. Results From 296 DEGs, 24 cuproptosis- and mitophagy-related candidate genes were identified. Machine learning identified RPL22, FTH1, and MMP8 as hub genes. MMP8 was upregulated, whereas RPL22 and FTH1 were downregulated. In the discovery cohort, the individual areas under the curve (AUCs) of RPL22, FTH1, and MMP8 were 0.826, 0.762, and 0.720, respectively, whereas the combined three-gene model achieved an AUC of 0.911. The individual hub genes showed preliminary discriminatory performance in the independent validation cohort. Immune-cell infiltration analysis showed higher estimated proportions of neutrophils and monocytes and lower proportions of selected T- and NK-cell subsets in SI-ALI. Single-cell analysis revealed cell-type-specific expression patterns of RPL22 and FTH1. Conclusion This study identifies RPL22, MMP8, and FTH1 as candidate hub genes associated with both cuproptosis- and mitophagy-related molecular signatures in SI-ALI. The three-gene model showed promising discriminatory performance in the discovery cohort, while the identified genes represent candidate molecular features associated with SI-ALI that require further validation.

papers.title: Potential molecular links between triclosan exposure and osteoarthritis: An integrative systems toxicology study.
papers.authors: Tang X, Xu H, Liu X, Yang Y, Li Z.
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic disease affecting the entire joint, influenced by a combination of inflammatory, metabolic, immune, and environmental factors. Triclosan (TCS), a commonly used antimicrobial compound, has been linked to oxidative and immune disturbances; however, its molecular relevance to OA remains to be elucidated. This study integrated network toxicology, bulk transcriptomics, cross-cohort machine learning prioritization, immune infiltration analysis, single-cell transcriptomic analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and primary chondrocyte experiments. Thirty candidate genes related to both TCS and OA were identified, with CBR3, MAOA, MMP13, and AVPR1A being prioritized. Among these, CBR3 exhibited the most stable contribution to model predictions, widespread expression across OA chondrocyte subpopulations, and significant associations with inferred immune-cell composition. Supporting molecular docking and dynamics analyses indicated structural compatibility and dynamic feasibility between TCS and the four candidate proteins. In primary rat chondrocytes, low-dose TCS heightened reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, upregulated Cbr3 and Mmp13, downregulated Col2a1, Maoa, and Avpr1a, and increased CBR3 protein levels, with specific redox-related and matrix-related alterations becoming more pronounced under IL-1β stimulation. These findings contribute to a model that links TCS-associated redox disturbances to OA-relevant chondrocyte stress and matrix remodeling, providing candidate molecular connections for future mechanistic validation.

papers.title: β-Hydroxybutyrate alleviates intestinal aGVHD via remodeling gut microbiota-bile acid axis and inhibiting TLR4-NF-κB-driven Th1/Th17 differentiation.
papers.authors: Tian R, Deng C, Liu K, Lai H, Liao C, Tu H, Li J.
papers.abstract: The intestine is a major target organ in acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD), and its microbial homeostasis critically influences disease pathogenesis and progression. Emerging evidence indicates that beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) can remodel the gut microbiota and dampen pro-inflammatory immune activity. To investigate the therapeutic potential of BHB in aGVHD, we first reanalyzed publicly available transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing data from patients with aGVHD, which revealed that genes involved in ketone body metabolism and transport were significantly decreased in intestinal tissues. We then used a murine model of aGVHD to evaluate the therapeutic effects of BHB by clinical scoring and intestinal histopathological examination. To define the immunological and microbial mechanisms, we integrated flow cytometry and ELISA for Th1/Th17, intestinal tissue-resident T and circulating T cells assessment, and with multi-omics analyses, including fecal 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal metabolomics, and intestinal transcriptomics. We further explored whether BHB directly regulates T-cell migration and differentiation and therefore assessed its effects on Th1 and Th17 differentiation in vitro. BHB treatment reduced the clinical score of aGVHD, alleviated intestinal injury in mice, and showed effects similar to those of methotrexate (MTX). BHB also corrected gut microbial dysbiosis, enriched Akkermansia muciniphila, and ameliorated bile acid metabolism dysregulation. Moreover, BHB inhibited intestinal T cell migration and Th1/Th17 differentiation both in vivo and in vitro. Mechanistically, transcriptome sequencing suggested that suppression of the TLR4-NF-κB pathway may underlie these anti-inflammatory effects. In summary, BHB effectively alleviates intestinal damage in aGVHD mice, likely through coordinated microbial, metabolic, and immunological regulation, and may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for aGVHD.

papers.title: 3D-printed fish-skin-derived composite dECM hydrogel patch for immunomodulatory and pro-angiogenic diabetic wound repair.
papers.authors: Lee SH, Moon JS, Noh S, Yi HS, Lee H.
papers.abstract: Diabetic wounds are sustained by persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, infection susceptibility, and impaired angiogenesis, highlighting the need for bioactive dressings with manufacturable architectures. Here, we developed a methacrylation-free and photopolymerization-free fish-derived composite decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) hydrogel scaffold by blending tilapia skin-derived dECM (TdECM) with carp skin-derived dECM (CdECM). Rheology-guided screening identified TdECM/CdECM-2, a 1:2 (v/v) blend of TdECM and CdECM, as a printable formulation that combined shear-thinning behavior, thermally induced collagen fibrillogenesis, and extrusion printability. Post-print stabilization with 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide (EDC) and N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) preserved lattice architecture and generated highly porous scaffolds with a porosity of 90.3 ± 3.9%. In vitro , the composite scaffold (TdECM/CdECM-2) supported fibroblast, keratinocyte, and endothelial cell growth; promoted keratinocyte migration and endothelial network formation; and reduced Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa survival to 10.5 ± 1.3% and 13.3 ± 3.3%, respectively, in direct-contact assays. Macrophage studies indicated attenuated pro-inflammatory gene expression, increased pro-regenerative macrophage-associated markers, and reduced oxidative stress-associated reactive oxygen species accumulation. In mice with streptozotocin-induced diabetes, TdECM/CdECM-2 increased wound closure to 91.2 ± 3.9% at day 14, compared with 73.2 ± 9.7% in the untreated control and 79.3 ± 12.5% in the porcine skin-derived dECM (PdECM) group, together with improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, and cluster of differentiation 31 (CD31)-positive neovascularization, and reduced inflammatory myeloid cell accumulation and macrophage activation. Exploratory single-cell transcriptomic profiling suggested treatment-associated modulation of immune and stromal/endothelial gene programs related to inflammation and angiogenesis. These findings support fish-derived composite dECM scaffolds as printable bioactive wound dressing platforms for diabetic wound repair.

papers.title: CD200 + fibroblasts prime the immunoregulatory function of granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells in inflammatory arthritis.
papers.authors: Angeli MR, Schütz C, Schmidt H, Demmler R, Chang J, Labinsky H, Raimondo MG, Lalazi B, Stergioula K, Huang K, Fedorchenko V, Li M, Winter Z, Tsiami S, Lienert A, Rütten S, Weber S, Luber M, Bäuerle T, Bahrami R, Boehm H, Schett G, Rauber S, Baraliakos X, Ramming A.
papers.abstract: Granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) are immunoregulatory cells of the neutrophil lineage. Here, we show that immunoregulation by G-MDSCs is imprinted by the joint tissue microenvironment in patients with axial spondyloarthritis and in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. We demonstrate that the suppressive function of G-MDSCs is significantly enhanced in the joint tissue, but not in the circulation. Analysis of public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets was consistent with Cd200r1 high Hmgb2 + precursors differentiating into G-MDSCs following interaction with Cd200 + fibroblasts. In hTNFtg/Il23mc mice, treatment with a CD200R1 agonist promoted an immunoregulatory signature associated with PD-L1 expression, whereas CD200 blockade reversed the phenotype. Following adoptive transfer of G-MDSC precursor cells into arthritic mice, administration of a CD200-blocking antibody impaired the differentiation of PD-L1 + G-MDSCs and exacerbated disease severity. These findings reveal a tissue-intrinsic program that facilitates resolution of inflammation through fibroblast-myeloid crosstalk that enhances G-MDSC function.

papers.title: Pulmonary Disease and NF-κB-Associated Responses in Mice Infected with Two Klebsiella pneumoniae Isolates.
papers.authors: Song R, Xu J, Pu D, Wang N, Syed MA, Zhao J, Cao B.
papers.abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKP) causes invasive disease, but pulmonary macrophage responses remain incompletely defined. We compared strain 55055, used as a classical K. pneumoniae (cKP) comparator, with strain 46274, operationally classified as hvKP, using a pneumonia model, single-cell RNA sequencing of pooled lungs, and RAW 264.7 macrophages. At the same inoculum, strain 46274 had higher lung burdens and greater mortality than strain 55055; representative sections showed more extensive inflammatory-cell infiltration, whereas no pairwise difference in animal-level H&E scores remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment. Because neither pulmonary burden nor disease stage was matched, immune-response differences cannot be separated from effects of unequal bacterial exposure or differences in disease progression. Descriptive pooled-library analysis showed differences in immune-cell composition and CellChat-inferred communication. In the single day-2 strain 46274 pooled library, SPP1 + macrophages comprised a larger fraction than in the corresponding strain 55055 pooled library and had high inflammatory-response, chemokine, and bacterial-recognition gene-set scores; this library-level observation was not independently validated in individual animals. Tissue-level staining showed numerical day-2 differences in CD86- and CD206-positive-cell abundance, but adjusted pairwise comparisons did not confirm strain-specific differences and the data do not demonstrate M1/M2 macrophage polarization. NF-κB-associated imaging findings remained qualitative. In vitro, strain 46274 showed lower adhesion to and phagocytosis by RAW 264.7 macrophages, but higher IL-6 and TNF-α readouts and stronger qualitative late p65 nuclear localization. These in vitro observations were obtained in RAW 264.7 cells within one experimental run and should not be extrapolated directly to primary pulmonary macrophages. Overall, in this strain-pair murine model, strain 46274 was associated with more severe pulmonary disease and NF-κB-associated inflammatory readouts.

papers.title: Transcriptomic profiling of psychological stress-related genes uncovers prognostic subtypes in colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Tao R, Tu Y, Shen D.
papers.abstract: Background Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a major malignancy of the gastrointestinal tract with substantial global morbidity and mortality. Mounting evidence underscores the pivotal role of chronic psychological stress in the pathogenesis of gastrointestinal cancers. Psychological stress-related genes have been implicated in modulating tumor progression and represent promising prognostic biomarkers. Nevertheless, their precise prognostic significance in CRC remains incompletely characterized. Methods We initially identified prognostic genes through univariate Cox regression analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset. An optimal prognostic signature was subsequently constructed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariate Cox analysis. Predictive accuracy was assessed via Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, and calibration curves. Furthermore, immune microenvironment characterization and chemotherapeutic response profiling were performed across risk-stratified subgroups to elucidate underlying biological mechanisms. Results Of 374 psychological stress-related genes examined, 62 demonstrated significant associations with overall survival (OS). The resulting 11-gene signature achieved area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.711, 0.768, and 0.800 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS prediction in the TCGA training cohort, respectively. External validation in three GEO cohorts showed attenuated but reproducible prognostic stratification, with AUCs ranging from approximately 0.56 to 0.63. High-risk patients exhibited significantly reduced survival probability. Computational analyses suggested a higher estimated M2 macrophage fraction and reduced predicted sensitivity to oxaliplatin. Conclusion We developed and externally evaluated an 11-gene transcriptomic signature related to stress-associated tumor biology in CRC. The signature stratified survival in retrospective cohorts, although external discrimination was moderate. This signature should be regarded as an exploratory research tool rather than a clinically validated assay. Computational analyses generated hypotheses regarding immune contexture and oxaliplatin sensitivity, and UBP1 emerged as a candidate tumor-suppressive regulator. Prospective multicenter validation and mechanistic studies are required before clinical application.

papers.title: Interpretable AI model reveals spatial codes of cell recruitment in tissues.
papers.authors: Yao J, Shim JS, Wong K, Zhu J, Liu Y, Kang SW, McCord K, Burt BM, Choi JM, Lee C, Lubo Julio IC, Solis Soto LM, Hernandez S, Colbert Maresso K, Liu Y, Dai Y, Chu T, Lu W, Khan K, Mansfield PF, Jang HJ, Hudson WH, Yue T, Zhang B, Li C, Wang L, Zhu H, Lee HS, Wang T.
papers.abstract: Understanding which molecular signals recruit specific cells to precise tissue locations is fundamental to tissue biology, immunity and disease. Existing computational tools for spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) describe where cells reside but cannot explain why. Here we introduce SPACER, a fully interpretable multi-instance learning framework that decodes gene-level recruitment rules directly from SRT data. Applied to 37 SRT datasets spanning multiple human tumour types and mouse heart, SPACER achieved 4-21-fold improvement over existing methods in various tasks of recovering biologically meaningful recruitment signals. SPACER revealed (1) that tumour-expressed mucins are associated with physical barriers to T cell engagement, which predicts resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors and patient prognosis, (2) that local antigen presentation is the dominant correlate of T cell engagement across cancer types and (3) that Cd4 + T cells are the dominant functional effectors in severe immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis. These findings establish SPACER as a discovery engine for cellular recruitment biology with direct translational applications.

papers.title: Structure-based discovery of a novel Granzyme A (GZMA) inhibitor for autism spectrum disorder through integrative transcriptomics, virtual screening, and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.authors: Alharbi M, Alshammari A, Al Shabanah O, Mufadhe Alanazi M, Altuwaijri A, F Alasmari A, Alshammari T.
papers.abstract: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a trypsin-like serine protease expressed in cytotoxic lymphocytes that cleaves gasdermin B (GSDMB) to release a pore-forming N-terminal fragment, thereby inducing pyroptosis, a lytic and pro-inflammatory form of programmed cell death. This pathway has been implicated in immune dysregulation reported in a subset of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). In this study, we reanalyzed the peripheral blood transcriptome dataset GSE26415 using an integrative computational framework comprising outlier-aware quality control, differential expression analysis, functional enrichment profiling, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and protein-protein interaction network centrality scoring. These orthogonal evidence layers were integrated into a composite prioritization score, in which GZMA ranked first among candidate genes, followed by KLRK1 and KLRB1. Querying the Drug-Gene Interaction Database revealed no approved small-molecule inhibitors targeting GZMA, indicating that it remains pharmacologically undrugged. To explore druggability at the structural level, we performed structure-based virtual screening of a ZINC similarity library against the active site of GZMA (PDB ID: 1ORF). This yielded three drug-like candidates (T1, T2, and T3) with docking scores of -9.3, -9.1, and -8.9 kcal/mol, respectively, compared with -7.4 kcal/mol for the co-crystallized reference ligand (0G6). Each drug-protein complex and apo enzyme was studied in 500 ns molecular dynamics to verify the binding stability and conformational persistence compared to the unliganded protein. Among the screening compounds, T2 was able to occupy the catalytic pocket for the entire simulation, with a stable protein-ligand interaction and one low-energy conformational basin. T1, despite a better docking score, was able to detach from the pocket after around 400 ns, while T3 was able to do so in 50 ns. The overall order of binding persistence was T2 > T1 > T3. Collectively, these results prioritize GZMA as a key ASD-associated immune effector candidate and identify T2 as the most credible lead compound. Importantly, the findings underscore the limitation of docking scores alone and demonstrate that long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations and binding free energy are essential for distinguishing kinetically stable binders from transient docking poses. We note that GZMA was transcriptionally downregulated in peripheral blood; its selection rests on network centrality and on the premise that granzyme pathology is governed by enzymatic activity at tissue sites rather than by circulating transcript abundance, a mechanistic hypothesis to be tested at the activity level.

papers.title: Robust ORF Deconvolution from Multiple Ribo-seq Datasets with Group LASSO Penalty
papers.authors: Maidhof, K.; Schlosser, A.; Erhard, F.
papers.abstract: Ribo-seq has provided compelling evidence that there are many translated but unannotated ORFs. Despite a growing body of peptidomic support for cryptic ORFs, the computational discovery of weakly translated, short and mutually overlapping ORFs has remained a major bottleneck. Here we introduce PRICE 2, a method designed to resolve these challenging translation events by adapting concepts from isoform deconvolution. PRICE 2 employs a generative model combined with group LASSO regularized regression to jointly infer active ORFs across multiple sequencing runs. In a comprehensive benchmark, PRICE 2 outperformed thirteen state-of-the-art tools in detecting short and overlapping ORFs. Orthogonal validation via immunopeptidomics demonstrated that ORFs identified by PRICE 2 enable the discovery of [~]40% more cryptic MHC-I peptides than the best-performing competing tool at a fixed false discovery rate. By analyzing public ribo-seq data across 45 distinct cell and tissue types, we constructed ORF-stock, a comprehensive database of non-canonical ORFs for immunopeptidomic studies.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal profiling of T cell repertoires in Lynch syndrome reveals convergent immune responses through neoplastic progression
papers.authors: Edwards, P.; Swinyard, O.; Ronel, T.; Jiang, Y.; Nageswaran, G.; Sakr, C.; Yasmin, S.; Grant, H.; Smith, E.; Braeutigam, K.; Braeutigam, K.; Varughese, S.; Datt, P.; Martinez, A.; Fisher, J.; Chain, B.; Shiu, K. K.; Jansen, M.; Baker, A.-M.; Monahan, K. J.; Graham, T. A.
papers.abstract: Surveillance of individuals with Lynch syndrome (LS), who are carriers of heterozygous inactivating mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations that predispose to colorectal cancer, enables the study of tumour-immune coevolution during tumour initiation. Somatic loss of MMR activity in the LS colon leads to the accrual of cancer driver mutations, and also of neoantigens likely to generate an adaptive immune response. However, the spatial and temporal immune dynamics in colon and peripheral blood are uncharacterised. Here we show that the neoplastic evolution of mismatch repair deficient (MMRd) clones leads to large-scale and sustained reorganisation of the T-cell repertoire in colon and peripheral blood. We performed dense spatiotemporal profiling of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires from 109 colonic biopsies (11 tumour samples, 98 normal bowel) from seven individuals, with eight matched blood repertoires. We additionally analysed 13 colorectal polyp repertoires from eight participants, 286 cross sectional blood repertoires from 242 participants (198 LS and 44 non-LS) and 52 longitudinal peripheral blood samples from 26 individuals with LS. We detected tumour-associated T cell clones, some of which were widely present in normal bowel tissue and also detectable in peripheral blood. Sequence similarity analysis revealed conserved TCR architectures across tissue compartments and recurrent clustering patterns between patients, that were not present in non-Lynch controls, consistent with convergent MMRd-associated antigen-driven immune selection. We identified systemic signatures associated with local tumour immune activity and revealed evidence of structured repertoire remodelling before overt malignancy. Longitudinal profiling revealed frequent turnover of low-abundance clonotypes, whereas highly abundant clonotypes persisted for several years. Collectively, our data defines the local and circulating TCR landscape associated with colonic neoplasia in LS, and provides a framework for LS blood-based immune monitoring, early interception and biomarker development.

papers.title: Addition of chemotherapy to radiotherapy promotes progenitor-exhausted CD8⁺ T-cell clonal dominance in head and neck cancer.
papers.authors: Chan Wah Hak C, Patrikeev A, Rullan A, Patin EC, Roulstone V, Hubbard LC, Guelbert M, Appleton ES, Foo S, Dean I, Burley A, Kyula-Currie JN, Baldock H, Lee JY, Nenclares P, Nanapragasam H, Murano C, Pedersen M, Cheang MCU, Bhide SA, Ono M, Harrington KJ, Melcher AA.
papers.abstract: Concomitant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is a standard-of-care treatment for unresectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-SCCHN), but its immune effects, particularly relative to radiotherapy (RT) alone, remain incompletely understood. Using syngeneic murine models, we integrated Nr4a3-Tocky reporter analysis with single-cell transcriptomics and T cell receptor clonotyping to comprehensively profile intratumoural CD8⁺ T-cell responses following RT and CRT. We show that CRT uniquely drives robust clonal expansion of antigen-engaged CD8⁺ T-cells and biases differentiation toward progenitor-exhausted (TPEX) states, whereas RT favours terminal exhaustion (TEX). Single-cell analyses further reveal preferential clonal dominance within TPEX populations following CRT. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients treated with CRT, TEX populations predominated early after treatment, followed by delayed expansion of circulating TPEX-like populations at 3 months, suggesting phased recovery of progenitor-like T-cell states. Together, these findings demonstrate that CRT and RT induce distinct CD8⁺ T-cell differentiation trajectories and clonal architectures, providing insight into treatment-induced immune remodelling in LA-SCCHN.

papers.title: Computational design and translational development of TCR-mimic scFv antibodies for peptide-HLA neoantigen targeting.
papers.authors: Niazi SK, Magoola M, Mariam Z.
papers.abstract: Single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) penetrate tissue more effectively than full antibodies and are simpler to produce, but the mutant proteins that define a tumor are predominantly intracellular and therefore inaccessible to conventional antibodies. What is accessible is the mutation-derived peptide displayed on cell-surface HLA. This review concerns TCR-mimic scFvs directed at those peptide-HLA complexes. It separates three questions that are frequently conflated: which mutations are predicted to be presented, which presented complexes are genuinely targetable given surface density and cross-reactivity risk, and how immunogenic the resulting therapeutic molecule will itself be. We review computational strategies spanning target identification, AI-driven structure prediction, de novo design, affinity and specificity engineering, half-life extension and deimmunization, and distinguish throughout between the scFv as a recognition module and the effector architecture, such as a CD3 bispecific, a chimeric antigen receptor binding domain or an Fc-containing format, in which it must ultimately be deployed.

papers.title: Deciphering the crosstalk between cancer stemness and the immune microenvironment in melanoma: a single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
papers.authors: Xing J, Chen M, Tao R.
papers.abstract: Background Tumor stemness fuels cutaneous melanoma (CM) progression and therapeutic resistance, posing a major challenge in clinical management. However, the spatial architecture of the stem cell niche and the causal genetic drivers orchestrating its maintenance remain elusive. Methods We employed an integrative multi-omics framework combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) to map the melanoma stem-like cell (CSC) ecosystem. Computational algorithms, including CytoTRACE (for cellular differentiation inference) and hdWGCNA (for spatial gene network detection), were leveraged to delineate stemness trajectories and their spatially co-localized modules. Furthermore, Mendelian Randomization (MR), a genetic epidemiology method, was applied to evaluate the potential causal roles of candidate genes, thereby moving beyond observational correlations. These findings were validated through immune landscape profiling and pharmacogenomic sensitivity analysis. Results We identified a stem-like subpopulation confined within a distinct hypoxic niche. MR analysis identified IGFBP7, LGALS1, and RPL10A as potential causal drivers of CM. Mechanistically, we reveal a dual mode of maintenance, IGFBP7 and LGALS1 act extrinsically to construct immune-excluded microenvironments via vascular remodeling and myeloid barriers, whereas RPL10A functions intrinsically to secure biosynthetic capacity via enhanced translation. Pharmacogenomic profiling further supports a mechanism-based therapeutic stratification, revealing subtype-specific vulnerabilities to MAPK inhibitors, taxanes, and platinum agents. Conclusion By defining the causal spatial architecture of melanoma stemness, this study provides a translational rationale for biomarker-driven patient stratification and mechanism-based therapeutic selection, offering specific strategies to disrupt the CSC niche and overcome therapeutic resistance.

papers.title: Multi-omics insights into immune dysregulation and candidate biological programs in kawasaki disease: toward precision immunomodulation.
papers.authors: Han Y, Liu J, Song C, Fu L, Gu Y, Zeng Y, Zou Z.
papers.abstract: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an immune-mediated pediatric vasculitis characterized by dynamic interactions among genetic susceptibility, innate and adaptive immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular remodeling. Although intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy substantially reduces coronary complications, 10%-20% of patients show persistent or recurrent fever after initial IVIG treatment, and reliable clinically validated molecular approaches for diagnosis, treatment-response prediction, and coronary-risk stratification remain unavailable. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, single-cell sequencing, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiome profiling, have expanded our understanding of KD-associated immune dysregulation. However, the clinical interpretation of these molecular findings remains challenging because of limited cohort sizes, heterogeneous control populations, treatment-related confounding, and insufficient external validation. In this review, we integrate evidence across multiple molecular layers and propose a framework in which current KD multi-omics findings converge into candidate biological programs rather than fixed molecular subtypes. These programs may represent temporally dynamic biological states along a shared inflammatory trajectory, influenced by disease phase, cellular composition, genetic background, and treatment exposure. Synthesized from convergent multi-omics evidence rather than derived from formal molecular classification, these candidate biological programs include myeloid inflammatory activation characterized by S100A8/A9 and IL-1/NF- κ B signaling, interferon-associated immune responses, and vascular injury/remodeling responses involving endothelial activation and extracellular matrix regulation. Current evidence supports biologically meaningful molecular programs that may contribute to clinical heterogeneity, but prospective validation is required before molecular signatures can be applied as clinical classifiers or treatment-selection tools. Integrating multi-omics approaches with functional validation, longitudinal sampling, and multicenter studies may facilitate the development of precision immunomodulation strategies for Kawasaki disease.

papers.title: Macrophage fate decisions during AKI-CKD transition insights from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Feng Z, Li X, Li Z, Yan X, Wei J.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an established risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the cellular events that determine recovery or maladaptive repair remain incompletely defined. Macrophages are central regulators of this transition because their functional states change with time and tissue context. Recent single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic studies show that renal macrophages cannot be adequately described by a simple M1/M2 scheme. Instead, inflammatory, cycling, reparative and profibrotic programs emerge in a model- and niche-dependent manner. Experimental studies identify early S100A8/A9-associated inflammatory macrophages, cycling states and repair-associated programs involving TREM2, MRC1/IGF1 and efferocytosis. Together, these changes define a transient reparative phase in which inflammation can resolve and tubular repair can proceed. Failure to sustain this phase is associated with persistent inflammation, fibro-inflammatory niches, CD38-high and scar-associated macrophages, and progression towards fibrosis. Spatial transcriptomics further shows that interactions with injured tubular cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells and platelets shape macrophage function. Although the timing and dominant populations differ across experimental models, several pathway-level programs recur. Human datasets support selected inflammatory and fibrotic macrophage states but show limited one-to-one conservation of cell subsets across species. Clinical translation will therefore require conserved macrophage programs, treatment windows and biomarkers that distinguish reparative from maladaptive responses.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics analysis identifies CCDC69 as a marker associated with germinal center B-cell infiltration in TNBC: development and validation.
papers.authors: Li J.
papers.abstract: Although coiled-coil domain containing 69 (CCDC69) has been implicated in tumor biology, its role in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and immune regulation remains unclear. Bulk transcriptomic data, single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, and spatial transcriptomics were used to investigate the role of CCDC69 in TNBC. Germinal center B-cell (GCB) signatures were quantified using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), and their associations with CCDC69 expression were assessed using correlation, ROC, and logistic regression analyses. An independent external TNBC cohort (GSE58812) was used to validate the association between CCDC69 expression, GCB infiltration, and survival outcomes. CCDC69 expression was significantly downregulated in breast cancer tissues but was associated with favorable survival outcomes in TNBC patients. CCDC69 expression positively correlated with multiple immune cell populations, particularly B cells and plasma cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrated that CCDC69 expression was enriched in B-lineage cells, especially GCB. Spatial transcriptomic analyses further showed that CCDC69-high regions were spatially co-localized with B-cell-rich and germinal center-like immune niches. In the TCGA TNBC cohort, CCDC69 expression was strongly associated with GCB infiltration and effectively distinguished GCB-high tumors. Logistic regression analysis confirmed that CCDC69 was independently associated with GCB enrichment. Findings were validated in the GSE58812 cohort. CCDC69 expression correlated with GCB-related signatures, showed good discriminative performance in identifying GCB-high tumors, and was associated with improved patient outcomes when combined with GCB enrichment. CCDC69 is closely associated with B-cell-mediated immune responses and germinal center niches in TNBC. Our findings suggest that CCDC69 may serve as a robust biomarker of immune activation and favorable prognosis.

papers.title: Spatial heterogeneity in glioblastoma: linking single-cell and spatial multi-omics to vaccine immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Yuan J, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most lethal primary brain tumor, with survival still limited despite advances in multimodal treatment. The tumor's profound heterogeneity--across patients, within individual tumors, and over time--has frustrated every class of therapeutic intervention. Recent developments in single-cell and spatial omics technologies have substantially advanced our understanding of this heterogeneity. No longer viewed as a uniform mass, GBM is now recognized as a spatially organized ecosystem of distinct malignant cell states, immune neighborhoods, and metabolic niches that interact across macroscopic distances. Spatial transcriptomics has revealed that malignant cells exist along a continuum of transcriptional programs--from neural progenitor-like to mesenchymal-like--that are not randomly distributed but organized into structured regions with a multi-layered architecture associated with hypoxia. Spatial proteomics and imaging mass cytometry have complemented these findings by mapping protein-level immune landscapes, uncovering cellular neighborhoods associated with survival and identifying spatially defined immunosuppressive niches. This review summarizes current knowledge from single-cell and spatial multi-omic studies of GBM, with an emphasis on the spatial organization of malignant cell states, the architecture of the tumor immune microenvironment, and the implications of these findings for therapeutic development, particularly vaccine immunotherapy. We argue that spatial technologies do not replace existing therapeutic pipelines but address a critical blind spot: the spatial dimension that bulk measurements cannot see.

papers.title: Integrative single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis identifies monocyte/macrophage senescence-associated candidate genes in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
papers.authors: Chen X, Wu W, Liu Y, Lian G, Liu Q.
papers.abstract: Background Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vascular disorder characterized by immune dysregulation and vascular remodeling. Cellular senescence modulates immune responses, but its role in PAH, particularly in monocytes/macrophages, remains unclear. Here, we integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data to identify senescence-associated candidate genes associated with monocytes/macrophages in PAH. Methods Publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data from PAH and control pulmonary vascular tissues were analyzed. A senescence-associated score was calculated for each cell based on MSigDB gene sets. Senescence-associated genes in monocytes/macrophages were identified through correlation and differential expression screening, and further examined in bulk transcriptomic datasets. Bulk transcriptomic discovery used GSE113439, GSE117261, and GSE254617. A sample-title audit identified 68 shared PHBI identifiers between GSE117261 and GSE254617; therefore, the merged data represented 257 expression profiles from 189 unique subjects. LASSO, Random Forest, and XGBoost were used as complementary feature-selection approaches, and genes jointly retained by the three algorithms were defined as candidates for evaluation in independent cohorts. Results Single-cell RNA-seq identified 14 cell types in PAH pulmonary vascular tissues, with dendritic cells, T cells, and monocytes/macrophages exhibiting the highest senescence-associated scores. Integrative screening identified 405 senescence-associated genes enriched in monocytes/macrophages. Multi-algorithm screening prioritized 10 candidate genes for subsequent evaluation. After within-cohort multiple-testing correction, external cohort analyses reproduced the discovery-stage expression directions for RGS1 , PHLDA1 , MAFB , and RNF13 in lung tissue cohorts, and for MAFB in a PBMC cohort. With nominal P values, RGS1 was significantly upregulated in GSE48149 and GSE53408 (both lung), and PHLDA1 was upregulated in GSE48149 (lung). MAFB was significantly downregulated in GSE33463 (PBMC) and GSE48149 (lung), whereas RNF13 was downregulated in GSE15197 and GSE48149 (both lung). Functional analysis revealed significant enrichment of immune-inflammatory and phagocytosis-related pathways among the candidate genes. Consensus clustering based on the candidate genes classified PAH patients into two exploratory transcriptomic groups with distinct expression and pathway activity profiles. In vivo evaluation in an MCT-induced PAH rat model showed seven significant direction-consistent changes, two direction-consistent nonsignificant trends, and one discordant gene ( PDE4B ), supporting tissue-level expression concordance. Conclusion These analyses identify a Mono.Macs-associated senescence-related candidate gene set in PAH. Independent expression analyses provide additional support for RGS1 , PHLDA1 , MAFB , and RNF13 as candidate genes for subsequent mechanistic and functional validation.

papers.title: Functional single-cell omics in gynecological cancers immunotherapy: from heterogeneity dissection to clinical translation.
papers.authors: Li DM, Pei KG, Yang BW, Qie MR, Xu JF, Zhong L, Song L.
papers.abstract: Ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers represent major threats to women's health worldwide. The profound heterogeneity of their immune microenvironments has rendered immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, particularly PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, far less effective than anticipated in gynecological malignancies. Conventional research approaches, constrained by coarse analytical resolution, are insufficient to unravel the underlying mechanisms of this therapeutic shortfall. Functional single-cell omics technologies, including single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and multi-omics integration, have provided a new framework for systematically studying the tumor immune microenvironment across three progressive dimensions: cellular identity, functional state, and spatial localization. This review systematically synthesizes the applications of this technological toolkit in the three major gynecological cancers. It reveals distinct bottlenecks across the three dimensions. In ovarian cancer, the core obstacle lies in the spatial dimension, where cancer-associated fibroblast-mediated physical barriers and pro-angiogenic macrophage subsets together construct a "spatial exclusion" microenvironment. In cervical cancer, the principal bottleneck resides in the functional dimension, where HPV status and histological subtype drive a "functional disability" phenotype, in which T cells infiltrate but fail to achieve effective activation, with therapy resistance-associated immune evasion clones further exacerbating functional impairment. In endometrial cancer, however, the immune fate is governed by the identity dimension, where molecular subtypes dictate the baseline nature of immune infiltration, and autophagy-related cellular subpopulations may offer new insights into intratumoral heterogeneity. Although single-cell omics has identified immunologically actionable targets with translational potential, including TREM2 + macrophages and the LAG-3/TIM-3 dual-target axis, clinical translation remains constrained by technical and biological bottlenecks, including stringent requirements for tissue sample quality, high assay costs, lack of standardized analytical pipelines, and the discordance between transcriptomic profiles and protein-level functionality.

papers.title: Tumor antigens across cancer progression: from immune recognition and selection to precision cancer immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Leong SP.
papers.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: Neurotensin modulation of immune and oxido-inflammatory homeostasis targeting TGF-β activated kinase 1/Nuclear factor-kappa βeta pathway: an integrated in vivo and in silico study.
papers.authors: Mishra S, Mohanty B.
papers.abstract: Background Neurotensin (NTS) is a brain peptide and is known to regulate several brain pathways. Subsequently NTS involvement in psychosis was administered having its promising therapeutic effects as an antipsychotic drug. Therefore, it has been deduced that targeting the NTS system in the regulation of the immune organs would prove to be a productive strategy for developing the novel immune modulatory drugs. Objective The present study elucidated the potential anti-inflammatory properties of NTS receptor 1 (NTSR1) agonist PD149163 (PD) in modulation of immune organs specifically, spleen and thymus investigating the potential immunomodulatory mechanisms targeting NF-κB /TAK1 signaling pathway. Methods Swiss albino female mice were randomly grouped: Group I-control, treatment groups- Group II, Group III and Group IV were intraperitoneally exposed with NTSR1-agonist PD low dose/ PD 50 (50 µg /kg bw), PD high dose/ PD 100 (100 µg /kg bw) and NTSR1-antagonist SR48692 (500 µg /kg bw), respectively for 28 days. Biochemical, hematological, histopathological, and bioinformatics analyses were performed. Differences were considered statistically significant at P Results The levels of Nuclear factor kappa beta/NF-κB, Tumor necrosis factor- alpha/TNF-α, Interleukine-6/IL-6, Corticosterone/CORT and pro-oxidant, Lipid-peroxidation/LPx were visibly similar to control after the treatment of PD 100 as well as PD 50 dose however the elevation was observed with the SR. PD 100 dose has a prominent effect on the plasma Interleukine-10/IL-10, CORT, NTS levels and tissue anti-oxidants superoxide dismutase/SOD, catalase/CAT as well as positively regulated the hematological and histological parameters, clearly deciphering NTS's immunomodulatory effects. Furthermore, in silico molecular docking analyses showed that PD exhibited high binding affinity with TGF-β activated kinase 1/TAK1 inflammatory protein, indicating inhibition of TAK1/NF-κB downstream signaling pathways. Conclusion NTS receptor 1 analogs might provide a better understanding of the mechanisms by which NTS regulates immune-system and could be further exploited for managing various immune-related disorders.
