papers.title: Colorimetric/chemiluminescent vertical flow immunoassay based on multifunctional cobalt-gold bimetallic nanoclusters for Brucella antibody detection and deep learning-assisted semiquantitative analysis.
papers.authors: Bi H, Zhao X, Wei M, Li X, Wu J, Wang Y, Zhang X, Ma H, Zhou H, Xu Z, Guo K, Jiang Y, Shi F.
papers.abstract: A colorimetric/chemiluminescent vertical flow immunoassay (VFI) for Brucellosis was developed using glutathione-protected cobalt-gold nanoclusters conjugated with staphylococcal protein A (GSH@Co-AuNCs-SPA) as multifunctional catalytic immunoprobes. The nanocluster probe integrates antibody recognition with peroxidase-like catalytic activity, enabling three complementary signal readouts within a common immunorecognition architecture: direct colorimetric visualization, TMB-H₂O₂-amplified colorimetry, and luminol-H₂O₂ chemiluminescence.The prepared GSH@Co-AuNCs exhibited H₂O₂-mediated catalytic activity and sustained chemiluminescent emission, with a detectable visual signal persisting for more than 150 min, thereby providing a broad acquisition window for low-background imaging. Serial-dilution experiments showed experimentally determined signal-discrimination thresholds of 0.5 IU mL⁻¹ for direct colorimetry and 0.2 IU mL⁻¹ for both TMB-amplified colorimetry and chemiluminescence. For the chemiluminescent mode, analysis of 20 independent blank measurements yielded a statistical limit of detection of 0.134 IU mL⁻¹. Under the same analytical dilution-series conditions, a commercial colloidal-gold lateral-flow assay produced a visually distinguishable signal down to 20 IU mL⁻¹.To improve the consistency of image interpretation, shared-weight dual-branch ResNet-18 regression models were established for both TMB and chemiluminescent images. Grouped five-fold cross-validation yielded mean R² values of 0.8746 ± 0.0784 and 0.8907 ± 0.0588, with four-level grading accuracies of 96.25 ± 2.10% and 93.00 ± 6.28% for the TMB and chemiluminescent models, respectively. In a preliminary evaluation of 30 clinical serum samples, TMB-amplified colorimetry showed 95.0% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity, and 93.3% overall agreement with the serum agglutination test (SAT), whereas chemiluminescence showed 95.0%, 100%, and 96.7%, respectively.The proposed platform integrates catalytic signal amplification, complementary optical readouts, and regression-based semiquantitative interpretation within a single VFI system. This strategy provides a practical framework for improving weak-signal discrimination and standardized interpretation in rapid anti-Brucella antibody screening, while further validation in larger independent clinical cohorts remains necessary.

papers.title: EBV-positive Hodgkin lymphoma with an immunosuppressive microenvironment during guselkumab (interleukin-23 inhibitor) therapy for chronic plaque psoriasis.
papers.authors: Shah B, Franco-Barraza J, Cai KQ, Dmitrieva M, Messmer M, Yang Y, Wasik M, Cukierman E, Nejati R.
papers.abstract: Background Psoriasis is an independent risk factor for classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL). Guselkumab has a favorable malignancy safety profile in clinical trials. Purpose To report the first documented Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive cHL arising in a biologic-naive patient with psoriatic arthritis during guselkumab therapy for chronic plaque psoriasis, and to describe its tumor microenvironment. Methods Excisional biopsy with immunohistochemistry, EBER in situ hybridization, and targeted sequencing, plus spatial single-cell proteomics (9-plex sequential immunofluorescence) of the diagnostic lymph node. Results A man in his early 40s developed night sweats, syncope, and bulky right cervical lymphadenopathy 7 months after starting guselkumab. Biopsy showed mixed-cellularity EBV-positive cHL (latency IIa: EBER+, LMP1+, EBNA-2-). HRS cells were weak PAX5+, CD20 negative, CD15+, strong CD30+, OCT2 negative/weak, BOB1 negative/weak, and strong CD200+. The microenvironment contained CTLA4+ immunosuppressive T cells (10.15%), M2 macrophages (10.35%), modest Th2 cells (0.38%), a low Th1/Th2 ratio (~0.39), and Th17 cells (~13%). GATA3 and CCR4 immunohistochemistry confirmed modest Th2 skewing. After guselkumab was stopped, he achieved a complete metabolic response with ABVD and involved-site radiotherapy and remains in remission on apremilast. Conclusions The short latency and atypical Th2-skewed, myeloid-enriched microenvironment, in contrast to the typical Th1-dominant profile of EBV-positive cHL, raise the possibility of immune-milieu alteration under IL-23 inhibition. This case supports continued pharmacovigilance for rare lymphomas in patients receiving IL-23 inhibitors and the need for larger studies to clarify potential class effects.

papers.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals vascular heterogeneity and cell-cell communication remodeling in the glioma blood-tumor barrier.
papers.authors: Zhao Z, Lang J, Gu H, Wang L, Luo J, Lang J, Yao Q, Qiao X, Wang Z, Yin L, He C.
papers.abstract: Background The blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts drug delivery in glioma, yet its pathologically remodeled counterpart, the blood-tumor barrier (BTB), is a promising therapeutic target. A comprehensive view of the cellular composition and transcriptional heterogeneity of the vascular compartment across the BBB-to-BTB transition is essential for improving glioma therapy. Methods We performed a secondary single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of the public GSE242044 dataset (7 patients; 13 tumor and adjacent non-tumor surgical specimens, comprising IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas and IDH-wild-type gliomas). After stringent quality control, doublet removal, Harmony batch correction, and annotation with SingleR plus canonical markers, we dissected vascular cell heterogeneity and performed differential expression, Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA), pseudotime (Monocle/Slingshot), and CellChat ligand-receptor inference, with sample-level statistical comparisons (Kruskal-Wallis and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests on per-specimen values). Findings were assessed in three independent glioma scRNA-seq cohorts (GSE162631, GSE117891, GSE174554) and in the CGGA bulk cohort. Results Vascular cell composition (relative representation among the profiled vascular-enriched cells) showed trends across conditions: endothelial cells declined from 60.6 % to 47.5 %, whereas pericytes (15.8 % to 18.0 %) and immune cells increased in IDH-wild-type tumors (macrophages 1.3 % to 7.0 %; T cells 3.0 % to 7.5 %); astrocytes increased from 1.1 % to 4.5 %; these specimen-level trends were mostly not statistically significant (Supplementary Table S1). Cell-cell communication was predicted to be rewired, shifting from pericyte-smooth muscle cell crosstalk in non-tumor and IDH-mutant tissues toward pericyte-astrocyte and predicted vascular-immune interactions in IDH-wild-type tumors. Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified an IDH-wild-type vascular program dominated by extracellular matrix remodeling (COL1A1, COL3A1, COL4A1, LAMB1, TIMP1) and angiogenic activation (ANGPT2), with loss of quiescent endothelial markers (CA4, KLF2). Candidate markers (COL1A1, COL3A1, F3, S100A4, CSPG4, ANGPT2) showed no consistent prognostic association across independent cohorts. Conclusions This secondary analysis delineates transcriptional heterogeneity of BBB/BTB vascular cells and their inferred communication remodeling in glioma. The identified subtype markers are candidate biomarkers that require independent validation; our findings provide a framework for future studies-including spatial and protein-level validation of the candidate markers, functional permeability and coculture assays of the predicted vascular-immune interactions, and preclinical testing of BTB-modulating delivery strategies such as focused-ultrasound-mediated opening in glioma models.

papers.title: Thymic stromal defects and immune dysregulation in hypomorphic Rag deficiency: implications for hematopoietic cell transplantation.
papers.authors: Pala F, Oguz C, Corsino C, Lamborn I, Martins AJ, Tsang JS, Germain RN, Lack J, Notarangelo LD, Bosticardo M.
papers.abstract: Background Thymic epithelial cells (TEC) are essential for positive and negative selection during T-cell development. Hypomorphic RAG deficiency is characterized by T-cell lymphopenia and an increased risk of infections and autoimmunity. However, whether abnormalities of TEC composition and function also contribute to these clinical features is unknown. Objective Using a Rag1 hypomorphic (Rag1 mut ) mouse model, we examined composition and function of the TEC compartment, both before and after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Methods Flow cytometry, immunofluorescent imaging, and single cell RNA sequencing were used to characterize the TECs and thymocytes. Bone marrow transplantation studies were performed to define level of donor chimerism required to fully correct thymic abnormalities. Results The thymus of Rag1 mut mice is small, with an increased proportion of cortical and a severe reduction of medullary TECs, and reduced expression of tissue-restricted antigens. Transplantation of Rag1 mut HSCs into wild-type mice phenocopied the altered thymic architecture of Rag1 mut mice. Transplantation of wild-type HSCs into Rag1 mut mice fully corrected thymocyte development, and normalized the TEC phenotype. However, in competitive settings, lower levels of wild-type HSC engraftment were associated with persistence of mutant-derived double-negative thymocytes and of a low number of Itgβ4 + mTEC lo cells, incomplete restoration of the TEC compartment, and autoantibody production. Conclusion Impaired thymocyte development in Rag1 mut mice leads to abnormal TEC composition and immune dysregulation, whose correction requires robust levels of donor chimerism after HSCT.
papers.venue: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology

papers.title: Spatiotemporal mapping reveals microbiota-dependent maintenance of functional competence during postnatal immune maturation.
papers.authors: Wang X, Bao Y, Li W, Li H, Song J, Lan Z, Han D, Lin W, Huang W, Kang X, Cao P, Zeng F, Wu Z, Ye Y, Wang H, Ma D, Chen W, Li S, You S, Wu S, Sun X, Wang SY, Mao K, Li H.
papers.abstract: Postnatal immune maturation is commonly viewed as a developmental milestone associated with weaning. However, how postnatal microbiota exposure shapes immune cell heterogeneity across tissues, and whether this maturation is self-sustaining or requires continuous microbial input, remain unclear. Here, we conducted spatiotemporal single-cell transcriptomic profiling of 120,649 immune cells isolated from 10 tissues in both germ-free (GF) and specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice from weaning to adulthood. We demonstrate that microbial colonization drives the expansion and functional maturation of distinct monocyte, macrophage, and neutrophil populations, marked by enhanced antigen-processing capabilities across tissues. Simultaneously, commensal-derived signals reprogram lymphocyte metabolic and translational states, promoting oxidative phosphorylation and relieving PDCD4-mediated translational repression to sustain effector readiness. Notably, microbiota reconstitution through both co-housing and fecal microbiota transplantation demonstrated that immune competence is not a fixed developmental endpoint but instead requires continuous microbiota-derived input. Without sustained microbial signals, immune cells adopted a persistent hyporesponsive state rather than remaining developmentally immature. Together, these findings redefine immune maturation as a microbiota-dependent maintenance process, revealing potential strategies to restore immune competence through microbiota-targeted interventions.

papers.title: Metabolic immune checkpoints (MICs) in cancer: from molecular mechanisms to challenges and opportunities in clinical translation.
papers.authors: Yang J, Cai X, He F, Zhang J, Zhang Z, Yi Z, Xie C, Xu B.
papers.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a core feature of tumor cells in adapting to microenvironmental stress and acquiring malignant phenotypes. It not only supports rapid proliferation but also mediates immune escape by reshaping the immune microenvironment. In recent years, the "metabolism-immune axis", serving as a central hub for the crosstalk between metabolic regulation and immune suppression, has provided a new perspective for understanding tumor immune evasion. This review systematically discusses how metabolic pathways, including glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism, along with mitochondrial function and other related processes, shape the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by regulating immune cell function, immune checkpoint expression, and immune signaling networks, thereby promoting tumor immune escape. The concept of "metabolic immune checkpoints (MICs)" is innovatively proposed and classified into three categories based on their mechanisms of action: (1) MIC-I: metabolic modification-type immune checkpoints, exemplified by posttranslational modifications of immune checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1 lactylation, acetylation and glycosylation, etc.; (2) MIC-II: metabolic enzyme-dependent immune regulatory nodes, represented by enzymes such as indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 and others that directly influence immune cell function; and (3) MIC-III: microbial metabolite-coupled immune regulatory targets, including receptors for microbe-derived metabolites such as short-chain fatty acid receptors. By integrating molecular interaction networks of key targets such as lactate dehydrogenase A and ATP citrate lyase, this review explores synergistic therapeutic strategies that combine small-molecule inhibitors targeting MICs with immune checkpoint blockade. This highlights how metabolic intervention can restore immune cell function and reverse exhaustion. Current key challenges in clinical translation include limitations in metabolic dynamic monitoring technologies, lack of patient stratification biomarkers and insufficient specificity in microbiome regulation. Future directions will focus on personalized treatment guided by multiomics, integrating single-cell metabolic flux analysis, deep learning-driven target prediction, and synthetic microbiome engineering, driving tumor immunotherapy into the era of precision metabolic regulation. By integrating the fundamental mechanisms of MICs with translational medical research, this review not only provides a systematic paradigm but also establishes a foundation for the development of new-generation precision combination therapies.

papers.title: IGF2BP2 remodels the lung metastatic immune microenvironment to promote bladder cancer metastasis.
papers.authors: Bai M, Liu T, Wu H, Yang X, Yin Y, Sun Y, Li J, Zhou Z, Ma Y, Zhao Z, Wu X, Wu L, Chen Y, Liu S, Du X, Hao Z, Wang X, Li Z, Guo H, Fang F, Zen K, Yang R.
papers.abstract: Bladder cancer lung metastasis poses a major therapeutic challenge because of pronounced tumor heterogeneity. However, the mechanisms regulating bladder cancer metastasis remain elusive. Here, we established a lung-tropic bladder cancer subline through iterative in vivo selection, enabling stepwise enrichment of metastatic competence while minimizing intratumoral variability. Using integrated multiomics analyses combined with functional validation, we identified an IGF2BP2-m⁶A-complement axis that is progressively engaged during metastatic evolution and contributes to lung colonization by bladder cancer cells. IGF2BP2 expression increased stepwise during the metastatic cascade and selectively enhanced the translation of m⁶A-modified complement C3 mRNA through direct binding to its 3' region, without altering transcript abundance. Tumor-derived C3 is subsequently processed, thereby promoting neutrophil recruitment and phenotypic remodeling toward a prometastatic, T3-like state. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling revealed that loss of IGF2BP2 disrupted neutrophil recruitment and was accompanied by enhanced T-cell proliferative activity within lung metastatic lesions. Genetic ablation or pharmacological inhibition of IGF2BP2 attenuated neutrophil accumulation and significantly restricted metastatic outgrowth in vivo. Consistent with these experimental findings, elevated IGF2BP2 expression in clinical bladder cancer specimens correlated with advanced disease stage, increased metastatic risk, and poor patient survival. Collectively, our findings reveal a translationally regulated complement-immune circuit that shapes the lung metastatic microenvironment and identify IGF2BP2 as a potential therapeutic target in metastatic bladder cancer.

papers.title: From immune heterogeneity to targeted therapies in IgG4-related disease.
papers.authors: Hara S, Mizushima I, Iwata Y.
papers.abstract: Purpose of review Recent advances in single-cell, spatial, and multiomic technologies have provided new insights into the immunopathogenesis and clinical heterogeneity of IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD). At the same time, several mechanism-based therapies have entered clinical development. Recent findings Recent studies have identified distinct B-cell, T-cell, myeloid, and stromal populations and their interactions within affected tissues. Type 2 peripheral helper T-cell-associated, granzyme K+ cytotoxic T-cell-associated, and age-associated B-cell-related programs may contribute to tissue inflammation and immune dysregulation. Recent studies further suggest that immunopathogenesis varies across clinical phenotypes and may be shaped by additional axes such as allergy and malignancy. Clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy of the CD19-directed B-cell-depleting therapy with inebilizumab and the nondepleting B-cell modulator obexelimab, while Bruton tyrosin kinase inhibition and cellular therapies represent emerging therapeutic approaches. Summary IgG4-RD is increasingly recognized as an immunologically heterogeneous fibroinflammatory disease. Integrating immune pathotypes with clinical phenotypes and dynamic biomarkers may enable more individualized treatment and accelerate development of mechanism-based therapies.

papers.title: Extracellular matrix-targeted TNC-scFv armoring enhances CAR T cell persistence and antitumor activity in solid tumors.
papers.authors: Chen K, Fu Q, Zhang W, Lin Z, Chen L, Zhou Y, Huo Y, Gao Z, Wan H, Wang C, Huang X, Zhang S, Liu M, Ma X.
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR T cell) therapy has shown limited efficacy in solid tumors, largely due to physical and immunosuppressive barriers imposed by the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tenascin-C (TNC), an extracellular matrix protein highly expressed in multiple solid malignancies, contributes to immune exclusion and T cell dysfunction. Here, we engineer an armored CAR T cell platform that locally targets the extracellular matrix by secreting a TNC-specific single-chain variable fragment (TNC-scFv) linked to conventional CAR architecture. TNC-scFv-armored CAR T cells exhibit enhanced cytotoxic activity, improved persistence, and reduced exhaustion in vitro and in xenograft tumor models. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that TNC targeting reprograms the TME toward a CD8 + T cell-enriched and functionally active immune landscape. In humanized tumor models, TNC-scFv-armored CAR T cells mediate robust antitumor responses with minimal systemic toxicity. This extracellular matrix-targeted armoring framework is compatible with additional immunomodulatory payloads, as illustrated by combinatorial armoring with interleukin-2, which further enhances efficacy while mitigating cytokine-associated toxicity. Together, these results establish extracellular matrix-directed armoring as a generalizable strategy to improve CAR T cell therapy for solid tumors.

papers.title: An R-loop-related gene signature predicts prognosis and shapes the immune microenvironment in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.authors: Meng C, Su H, Yan R, Sun R, Yu Q, Meng Y, Xi Y.
papers.abstract: Background Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) features a poor prognosis and unclear pathogenesis, and the role of R-loops, key regulators of genome stability, has not been systematically characterized in this disease. Methods Transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing data of ESCC were integrated with published R-loop-related genes (RLRGs) to construct an RLRG scoring system. The associations between the RLRG score and prognosis, tumor immune microenvironment, and tumor stemness were analyzed via multiple bioinformatics algorithms. The expression of core genes was verified using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), Western Blot, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. Results Seven key RLRGs related to the prognosis of the ESCC patients were identified, among which three core genes-BRIX1, CHEK1, and NUP155-were significantly upregulated in ESCC tissues compared with controls, as confirmed by both bioinformatic analysis and experimental validation. Notably, BRIX1, CHEK1, and NUP155 were co-enriched in DNA replication, pyrimidine metabolism, RNA degradation, and MYC target pathways, which are closely linked to R-loop biology and suggest potential crosstalk between these genes and R-loop regulatory networks. Meanwhile, the low RLRGs score group exhibited significantly worse overall survival but displayed a more active yet dysfunctional immune microenvironment. Single-cell analysis identified SquamousEpithelium cells as the key cell type with the highest RLRG scores across five independent algorithms. Malignant SquamousEpithelium cells with high RLRG scores showed enhanced stemness and activation of pathways including JAK-STAT, hypoxia, and DNA repair. Conclusion This study provided the first systematic characterization of the R-loop landscape in ESCC, suggests that SquamousEpithelium cells may play a key role in R-loop-associated progression and are identified as potential prognostic biomarkers with possible therapeutic relevance that requires functional validation.

figure.caption: Identification of seven R-loop-associated key genes potentially driving the progression of ESCC. A Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes (DEGs1) between ESCC group and control group in the TCGA-ESCC cohort. B Heatmap of top 20 up-regulated and all down-regulated DEGs1. C Volcano plot of DEGs2 between ESCC group and control group in the GSE53625 cohort. D Heatmap of top 20 up-regulated and all down-regulated DEGs2. E Venn diagram of candidate genes. F Top 5 terms in Gene Ontology (GO) functions and top 5 terms in Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) functions enriched by 41 candidate genes. papers.title: Single-Cell and Bulk RNA-Seq Profiling Identifies Cell Adhesion-Related Gene Signatures in Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury.
papers.authors: Qian C, Qian L, Fang Z, Chen J, Peng C.
papers.abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) involves complex secondary damage mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and blood-brain barrier disruption, in which cell adhesion-related genes (CARGs) play a central role. Therefore, systematically elucidating the expression and regulation of CARGs is crucial for identifying new therapeutic targets to mitigate inflammatory infiltration and preserve barrier integrity. Both single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. The single-cell data were processed using Seurat, and CARG activity was comprehensively assessed using five scoring algorithms, including UCell and AUCell. A combined machine learning framework incorporating Boruta algorithm, LASSO regression, and random forest was employed to screen for reliable diagnostic biomarkers. Furthermore, immune infiltration profiles were evaluated using CIBERSORT, regulatory networks were constructed, and molecular subtypes were identified through consensus clustering. Single-cell analysis revealed high CARG activity in endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and astrocytes. Machine learning identified four robust diagnostic biomarkers (Itgb1, Fn1, Pdlim5, Kdr) with excellent predictive accuracy (AUC, 1) across multiple datasets. These biomarkers strongly correlated with immune cell infiltration, particularly macrophage polarization and mast cell activation, and successfully stratified CIRI samples into two distinct molecular subtypes. By integrating single-cell and transcriptomic data, this study systematically reveals the critical role of CARGs in CIRI. It identifies four core diagnostic genes that are closely associated with immune microenvironment remodeling and neuronal damage, thereby providing new molecular markers and a theoretical foundation for clinical diagnosis and treatment.

figure.caption: Single-cell characterization of CARG-related features in CIRI. A , t -SNE dimensionality reduction clustering map of single-cell transcriptome data. B , t -SNE distribution map from different samples. C , t -SNE distribution map of the CIRI group and the Sham group. D , t -SNE distribution map of 11 cell types. E , Bubble plot showing the expression of canonical marker genes in 11 different cell types. F , Relative proportion of different cell types in the CIRI group and the Sham group across different samples. G , CARG activity scores for different cell types as shown by the UCell, AddModuleScore, ssGSEA, AUCell, and Singscore methods. H , t -SNE distribution map of the total CARG activity score. papers.title: Chemokine-receptor axes in immune-tumor cell communication: spatial niches, immune exclusion, and therapy resistance.
papers.authors: Han Y, Liu Q, Ao F, Huang J, Lin H.
papers.abstract: Chemokine-receptor axes are traditionally viewed as leukocyte trafficking cues, but increasing evidence indicates that they also function as spatial and functional organizers of immune-tumor communication. In the tumor microenvironment, chemokine gradients determine which immune-cell subsets are recruited, where they are positioned, and whether they acquire antitumor or suppressive states. This review summarizes experimentally validated chemokine-receptor axes that shape spatial niches, immune exclusion, and therapy resistance in cancer. The CXCL12-CXCR4 axis serves as a prototype of stromal immune exclusion, particularly in pancreatic cancer, where CXCR4 blockade can improve immune accessibility but may require myeloid-directed combinations. CXCR2 ligand axes, including CXCL5-CXCR2 and IL-8/CXCR2 signaling, promote neutrophil-rich suppressive niches, CD8 + T-cell dysfunction, PD-L1 induction, and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade or chemotherapy. The CCL20-CCR6 axis recruits regulatory T cells and contributes to metastatic immune suppression, whereas CCL5-CCR5 signaling organizes perivascular macrophage niches and supports adaptive therapy resistance. CCL2-associated macrophage circuits further link monocyte recruitment, TAM polarization, and immunotherapy responsiveness. We discuss how single-cell and spatial technologies can validate these circuits and guide biomarker-driven therapies. Rather than targeting isolated ligand-receptor pairs, future strategies should reprogram chemokine-controlled immune ecosystems to overcome immune exclusion and treatment resistance.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: Conceptual framework of chemokine–receptor axes in immune–tumor communication. Chemokine gradients regulate three interconnected layers: immune-cell trafficking, spatial positioning within tumor niches, and functional reprogramming of immune and tumor cells. Representative axes, including CXCL12–CXCR4, CXCR2 ligand–CXCR2, CCL20–CCR6, CCL5–CCR5, and CCL2–CCR2, coordinate immune exclusion, suppressive niche formation, tumor adaptation, and therapy resistance.

papers.title: Tumor-associated macrophages in glioblastoma: implications for immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Lei J, Lao M, Ni Z, Chai W, Fang M, Wen Z, Lv X, Gao Y, Hu K.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 (GBM) is the most aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults, with a median overall survival of approximately 15 months despite maximal surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy with temozolomide. This therapeutic resistance is increasingly attributed to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), within which tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) represent the most abundant infiltrating immune cell population. GBM-resident TAMs originate from two distinct lineages: embryonic brain-resident microglia and bone marrow-derived monocytes. They exhibit substantial phenotypic and functional heterogeneity beyond the classical inflammatory versus immunosuppressive dichotomy. Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have identified multiple TAM states with distinct functional and spatial features, including GPNMB + and VSIG4 + marker-defined subsets as well as a mesenchymal transcriptional program predominantly associated with monocyte-derived macrophages, each preferentially enriched in distinct spatial niches with substantial overlap and plasticity, and driving context-dependent immunosuppression through distinct metabolic and signaling pathways. Mechanistically, TAMs promote GBM progression via metabolic reprogramming, cytokine-mediated functional adaptation, and direct suppression of adaptive immunity. TAMs are also directly implicated in resistance to temozolomide and immunotherapies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy. This review comprehensively summarizes recent mechanistic insights and translational advances in TAM-targeted strategies, including TAM depletion via CSF1R inhibition, functional reprogramming toward inflammatory phenotypes, metabolic intervention, and nanoparticle-mediated precision drug delivery capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier. Unlike earlier reviews that focused solely on TAM biology, this study explicitly connects the spatial distribution and functional heterogeneity of TAM subpopulations to therapeutic vulnerability, providing a practical framework for designing biomarker-driven, patient-specific combination immunotherapy trials.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: TAM-targeted therapeutic strategies in GBM. Four major intervention approaches are currently under investigation: (1) TAM depletion via CSF1R inhibitors (PLX3397, BLZ945) and CCR2 antagonists, which reduce TAM burden but are limited by compensatory recruitment and systemic toxicity; (2) functional reprogramming of immunosuppressive, tumor-supportive TAM states toward inflammatory, antigen-presenting functional programs using TLR agonists, CD40 agonists, or ITGA5 blockade, which harness macrophage plasticity to restore anti-tumor immunity; (3) metabolic interventions targeting PPAR-γ, arginase, or HIF-1α pathways to disrupt TAM immunosuppressive metabolism; and (4) nanoparticle-based precision delivery systems, including biomimetic and Janus nanoparticles, which enhance blood-brain barrier penetration and enable TAM-specific payload accumulation. Rational combinations of these approaches with immune checkpoint blockade and cellular immunotherapies are being explored to overcome compensatory resistance mechanisms.
