papers.title: CD14 Blockade Attenuates Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
papers.authors: Penna, V. R.; Ehle, E.; Farra, W.; Cannon, E. N.; Landim-Vieira, M.; Centner, A. M.; Owen, M. C.; Venkatesan, R.; Heo, G. S.; Das, A.; Liu, Y.; Appleby, M. W.; Crowe, D.; Ziegelaar, B. W.; Redlich, G. L.; Saffitz, J. E.; Chelko, S. P.; Lavine, K. J.
papers.abstract: Background: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) is a genetic and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disorder characterized by progressive cardiomyocyte loss, immune cell infiltration, and fibro-fatty replacement of the ventricular myocardium, with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD), predominantly caused by mutations in cardiac desmosomal genes including PKP2, DSP, and DSG2. We previously described the pivotal role of NF{kappa}B and CCR2+ cardiac macrophage-triggered inflammation in ACM pathogenesis. Methods: WT or Dsg2mut/mut mice were treated with either isotype control or anti-CD14 antibody once a week for the described treatment period (4 or 8 weeks). At the end of the treatment period, disease characteristics were assessed by echocardiography, electrocardiography, histology, immunofluorescence, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging and single-cell transcriptomics. Results: Here, we demonstrate the efficacy of neutralizing CD14 signaling, an important mediator of inflammatory macrophage activation, in attenuating ACM disease in vivo. Additionally, we elucidate shifts in the cellular and transcriptomic landscapes that occur following anti-CD14 antibody treatment in a well-established mouse model of ACM and identify substantial reductions in inflammatory macrophage and pro-fibrotic fibroblast populations. Conclusion: This study provides evidence that blockade of CD14 can attenuate the ACM disease phenotype. It may do so by inhibiting macrophage-based activation and inflammation, while also altering the transcriptional state of other important cell types. Collectively, these findings suggest that CD14 inhibition may be an effective option for ACM, which should be explored in early-phase clinical studies.

papers.title: IgG4 antibody repertoire diversity is stable over several years in health and autoimmune disease
papers.authors: Wollenweber, L.; Paardekooper, L. M.; Campman, Y. J. M.; van Bokkum, J. M.; Tannemaat, M. R.; Verschuuren, J. J. G. M.; Barendregt, A.; Heck, A. J. R.; Bondt, A.; Huijbers, M. G.
papers.abstract: Despite its relative anti-inflammatory nature, IgG4 is involved in a variety of pathological conditions such as autoimmune disease and cancer. To investigate whether the IgG4 repertoire presents any abnormalities in diseases where IgG4 autoantibodies predominate, we charted longitudinal IgG4 repertoires in health, in an IgG4-mediated autoimmune disease (AID; muscle-specific kinase myasthenia gravis (MuSK MG)), and in IgG1/IgG3 mediated AIDs (acetylcholine receptor (AChR) MG and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). In total, we assessed 218 samples of 69 donors using mass spectrometry-based antibody repertoire analysis, covering a timespan of up to eight years. Despite being superficially inconspicuous in clonal diversity and abundances, we detected a slightly elevated number of IgG4 clones in MuSK MG patients compared to healthy donors. Notably, this observation did not coincide with drastic repertoire changes during treatment, suggesting that a large portion of the IgG4 repertoire is not significantly affected by common MuSK MG treatment regimens. Comparing the IgG4 antibody repertoires of all donors, we found that they were exceptionally unique for each individual. Against what would be expected in the case of a constantly adapting antibody repertoire, a large portion of the IgG4 clones remained stable without any further maturation. This observation even extended to patients receiving B cell depleting or IgG modulating treatments. Our findings suggest that a dominating fraction of the IgG4 pool may be produced by long-lived plasma cells, which are unaffected by disease or medical interventions.

papers.title: Investigating the association between interferons and flares of systemic lupus erythematosus at a single cell level.
papers.authors: Faheem Z, Boukhaled GM, Nassar C, Manion K, Munoz-Grajales C, Kim M, Bonilla D, Gladman DD, Whitall-Garcia L, Touma Z, Brooks DG, Wither J.
papers.abstract: Background Elevated levels of interferons (IFN) are a hallmark of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and are linked to disease flares, but the precise mechanisms underlying this remain unclear. We examined the association between IFN-stimulated proteins (ISPs) and immune changes in flaring and quiescent SLE patients at single-cell resolution. Methods Using CyTOF, six ISPs were measured in PBMC populations from 18 healthy controls, 24 quiescent SLE patients, and 46 recently flaring SLE patients. Individual ISPs and a composite ISP score were assessed. Results Analysis of 29 immune populations revealed that mean ISP levels correlated with peripheral blood IFN-stimulated gene (ISG) expression and were higher in flaring than quiescent patients. Despite this correlation, ISP expression was heterogeneous between and within cell subsets. To identify factors contributing to this heterogeneity, we compared the top ISP-expressing cells with the remaining cells in each subject. High ISP-expressing cells had increased trafficking marker expression with distinct expression patterns suggesting that cells may have transited different tissues. Except for β7, these molecules were not induced by IFN in-vitro . Longitudinal analysis revealed that ISP expression gradually decreased in T and activated innate immune populations with flare resolution, whereas that in B cell populations remained stable with the baseline levels predicting sustained or recurrent disease activity one year later. Conclusion Although mean ISP expression in most cell populations correlated with global ISG expression, there is heterogeneity between and within immune populations in SLE, likely reflecting variable IFN exposure as cells traffic through inflamed sites within the body.

papers.title: γδ T cells in cancer immunotherapy, 2000-2025: A bibliometric analysis and clinical-trial evidence map.
papers.authors: Wang Y, He Y, Xu J, Wang Y, Su H, Zhang Y, Lv J, Chen H, Wang J.
papers.abstract: γδ T cells are promising cancer-immunotherapy effectors because they recognize tumors without major histocompatibility complex (MHC) restriction and carry low graft-versus-host-disease risk in allogeneic settings, yet few bibliometric studies have integrated immunotherapy-specific research trends with clinical-trial mapping and translational-gap analysis. We characterized the global research output, intellectual foundations, emerging frontiers, and clinical translation of γδ T cells in cancer immunotherapy (2000-2025) by combining bibliometric analysis of 3273 Web of Science publications (bibliometrix, VOSviewer, CiteSpace), a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR)-guided evidence map of 26 interventional cancer trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform [WHO ICTRP], regional registries), and an integrative step linking bibliometric hotspots to the pipeline. Annual output grew from 18 (2000) to 418 (2024) publications (compound annual growth rate [CAGR], 14.0%) across three phases; China (33.1%) and the United States (27.3%) led production. Co-citation analysis identified five intellectual pillars: phosphoantigen recognition, subset heterogeneity, clinical adoptive transfer, tumor-microenvironment suppression, and engineered γδ T therapy. Chimeric antigen receptor-engineered γδ T cells (CAR-γδ T cells), allogeneic platforms, and single-cell RNA sequencing were the leading 2022-2025 frontier terms. Trials shifted toward allogeneic cell sources; early-phase studies consistently met safety and feasibility endpoints, but monotherapy efficacy was modest. The LAVA-051 and LAVA-1207 programs were discontinued for disclosed business or internal-benchmark reasons, whereas allogeneic CAR-Vδ1 therapy (ADI-001) produced the most encouraging early signals before oncology reprioritization in 2024. Three persistent translational gaps-single-cell/T-cell receptor (TCR) profiling, metabolic reprogramming, and γδT17 biology-frame a proposed roadmap to convert bibliometric hotspots into mechanism-guided γδ T-cell cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics identify a JUNB+ neutrophil subset enriched in immune-excluded regions of lung adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Zhu Y, Shi D, Ji L, Wang B, Shen W, Liu F, Zhang S, Li X, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Background Tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) display functional plasticity in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), but subsets linked to immune exclusion are poorly defined. Methods We integrated single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and bulk multi-omics data to characterize neutrophil heterogeneity in LUAD. Key findings were validated by immunofluorescence co-localization and qPCR on clinical blood and isolated neutrophils. Results Neutrophils exhibited the highest scores for an EMT-associated transcriptional program and immune exclusion among all immune cell types. A distinct JUNB+ neutrophil subpopulation was spatially enriched in immune-excluded tumor regions and correlated with unfavorable prognosis. Spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between JUNB expression and neutrophil marker module scores across tissue spots (Pearson r = 0.216 and 0.205, P = 1.84 × 10^-10 and 9.06 × 10^-11). Immunofluorescence confirmed JUNB protein co-localization with CD66b+ neutrophils in LUAD tissues (54.3% ± 8.2% of CD66b+ cells JUNB +). qPCR revealed specific upregulation of JUNB mRNA in circulating neutrophils from LUAD patients, whereas no difference was observed in whole blood. Conclusion This study identifies JUNB as a marker of a neutrophil state associated with immune exclusion and poor prognosis in LUAD. The neutrophil-specific upregulation of JUNB highlights its potential as a circulating biomarker for TAN-mediated immunosuppression, which warrants validation in prospective cohorts.

papers.title: Integrated spatial and single-cell transcriptomics uncover IFI6⁺ regulatory T-cells and SPP1⁺ macrophages immunosuppressive niches in colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Miroszewska D, Song S, Urbiola-Salvador V, Cázares Olivera M, Jabłońska A, Bolcewicz M, Kalinowski L, Duzowska K, Drężek-Chyła K, Zdrenka M, Śrutek E, Szylberg Ł, Jankowski M, Bała D, Zegarski W, Nowikiewicz T, Filipowicz N, Piotrowski A, Dumanski JP, Li B, Chen Z.
papers.abstract: Background In colorectal cancer (CRC), tumor-immune interactions are critical drivers of tumorigenesis, immune evasion, and therapeutic response. Therefore, a deeper spatially resolved understanding of these interactions is urgently needed. Methods Spatial transcriptomics (ST) of CRC and matched normal samples was used to characterize cell populations and gene expression patterns associated with tumorigenesis and immune infiltration. An additional 41 publicly available ST slides, single-cell transcriptomics and bulk transcriptomics datasets from 472 and 617 CRC patients, respectively, were analyzed to validate the findings. Results Cancer regions exhibited profound molecular alterations with increased oncogenic pathways, immunosuppressors, and tryptophan deprivation via KYNU-AHR axis, inducing the macrophage attractant CXCL5, contributing to immune evasion. In tumor boundaries, SPP1⁺ macrophages fostered an immunosuppressive microenvironment with regulatory T-cells (Tregs) recruited via CCL18-CCR8 and CCL22-CCR4. SIT1 emerged as a potential anti-tumor T-cells suppressor within tertiary lymphoid structures, suggesting a novel immune regulator. We also uncovered a previously uncharacterized population of tumor-infiltrating IFI6⁺ Tregs associated with unfavorable prognosis and therapy response, defined by elevated interferon-related genes and LGALS9, a potential immune checkpoint target. Conclusion This study uncovered previously unrecognized immunosuppressive cell populations and key immune regulators that advance understanding of CRC immune evasion and highlight potential targets for personalized immunotherapy.

papers.title: Integrating deep learning model for precision design of MERS antibodies with augmented affinity against SARS-CoV-2.
papers.authors: Irshad A, Ur-Rehman A, Koser T, Alvi M, Usman H, Khalid RR.
papers.abstract: The rapid emergence of SARS-CoV-2 has renewed interest in cross-reactive antibody therapeutics targeting conserved epitopes across divergent coronaviruses. Building on our deep-learning driven protein engineering pipeline, we sought to redirect experimentally validated MERS-CoV antibodies toward the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain. A structural comparison identified a conserved Site 2 epitope capable of supporting cross-neutralizing interactions and three MERS-CoV antibodies showing measurable compatibility with this region were selected as templates. Using the customized ProteinMPNN based design framework, with multi-parameter biophysical filtering, we introduced context-specific substitutions to strengthen interfacial complementarity with the SARS-CoV-2 RBD. The study extends our earlier workflow by adding two evaluation parameters, antigen processing and T cell immunogenicity, to assess mutational impact on developability and immune compatibility. Top-ranked variants underwent molecular dynamics simulations and post-trajectory analyses, including stability profiling, hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic network evaluation, and per-residue binding energetics. Developability assessments, including aggregation propensity and immunogenicity profiling, were integrated to ensure therapeutic readiness. Across all scaffolds, several engineered variants, most notably D12(T721E), MERS27(D722N), and JC57-14(S618G), exhibited enhanced interface organization, favorable energy landscapes, and can improved structural stability relative to their parental antibodies. Many also showed reduced aggregation potential and lower predicted antigen presentation across MHC class I and II alleles, further refined by the added processing and immunogenicity metrics. Together, these findings suggest that MERS-CoV antibody scaffolds can be repurposed to target SARS-CoV-2 through a conserved epitope, highlighting a promising strategy for broad-spectrum coronavirus antibodies and providing strengthened leads for experimental development.

papers.title: Integrated multi-omic analysis characterizes an IFNγ-responsive-to-myeloid-suppressive immune continuum in immune-active hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Lin L, Weng N, Lai H, Wu G, Lin J, Wu X, Huang S, Chen X.
papers.abstract: Immune-active hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is commonly treated as a single inflamed phenotype, although its internal immune heterogeneity remains incompletely defined. We integrated public bulk transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, proteomic, phosphoproteomic, and treatment-cohort data to test whether this heterogeneity is better represented by discrete states or a continuous immune axis. In 112 checkpoint-high TCGA-LIHC tumors, an inflamed-minus-myeloid axis showed structured heterogeneity but no robust empirical bimodality: the observed kernel-density curve had one prominent mode and none of 1,000 bootstrap resamples contained two or more prominent modes. IFNγ-responsive-associated and myeloid-suppressive-associated labels were therefore retained only as operational summaries of opposing axis tendencies, and the biological polarity persisted across alternative definitions of immune-active entry. A fixed 10-gene within-sample rank template-contrast score transferred the axis to independent HCC cohorts. Transcriptomic analyses based on gene sets non-overlapping with the compact panel and original state-defining genes supported the IFNγ-oriented end, whereas spatial analyses showed local cross-end coexistence with reduced immediate-neighbor mixing relative to a count-preserving random-label null, and paired proteomic/phosphoproteomic analyses showed concordant myeloid-oriented associations involving macrophage, fibroblast/extracellular-matrix, hypoxia, SPP1-integrin-FAK, and myeloid-receptor programs. Direct application of the frozen transfer score to four public HCC immunotherapy cohorts yielded heterogeneous, imprecise response associations (pooled Hedges' g = 0.10, 95% CI -0.42 to 0.61) and did not establish clinical response prediction. These results support a structured IFNγ-responsive-to-myeloid-suppressive continuum within immune-active HCC. The framework is transferable across public datasets but requires prospective HCC-specific clinical validation, while functional perturbation studies are needed before causal or therapeutic claims.

papers.title: Integrated multi-omics and machine learning identify core mechanobiology-associated immune genes in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
papers.authors: Wang P, Zhao F, Yang T, Yuan Y.
papers.abstract: Background Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) involves vascular remodeling and altered mechanical signaling. The immune-associated transcriptomic changes accompanying this environment remain incompletely characterized. Methods We integrated bulk lung (GSE15197), PBMC (GSE33463), and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE169471) data using a curated set of 2, 537 mechanical-related genes. WGCNA, LASSO, random forest, and single-cell localization supported candidate prioritization. The four-gene panel was examined in a monocrotaline-induced PH rat model and PBMCs from 10 IPAH patients and 10 controls. Results PAH transcriptomes showed enrichment of stress-fiber, actomyosin, ECM, and immune-related programs. CD83, CD86, IL6, and TLR7 were prioritized, with compartment-dependent expression patterns. Single-cell data localized CD83/CD86 to myeloid/APC compartments and IL6 to endothelial/fibroblast populations; TLR7 was sparsely detected. In MCT-treated rat lungs, CD86 and TLR7 proteins increased, whereas CD83 and IL-6 decreased. Clinical PBMCs showed corresponding expression directions, and each gene had an AUC >0.7. The exploratory four-gene disease-state score achieved an internal cross-validated AUC of 0.765. Conclusions The four candidates provide a cellular and molecular context for investigating immune-stromal interactions in PAH, including responses to noninfectious vascular injury. The panel showed moderate internal discrimination. These findings support further clinical and functional investigation but do not establish direct mechanotransduction targets or a causal pathway linking mechanical stress to vascular inflammation.

papers.title: scTIME: single-cell-informed interpretable modeling of immunotherapy-associated immune states in non-small cell lung cancer.
papers.authors: Chen G, You C, Gao H, Xu C.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor response in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) reflects coordinated tumor and immune states that are not fully captured by single biomarkers. We developed scTIME, an interpretable model that translates single-cell immune programs into bulk transcriptomic scores, and integrated public single-cell, T-cell receptor, transcriptomic, survival, and proteogenomic cohorts. Response modeling used two cohorts with different endpoints (40 patients) and compared six algorithms. ElasticNet was selected as a sparse reporting model, achieving a pooled five-fold out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.810; nested model selection yielded 0.772. Matched held-out stratification identified response-enriched scTIME groups in a direct descriptive comparison with CD274, while the fitted score emphasized cytotoxic CD8, natural killer, SPP1 macrophage, interferon-response, and antigen-presentation programs. Single-cell analyses and external projections linked these programs to CXCL10-CXCR3 recruitment, exclusion-associated states, and T-cell receptor ecology across molecular contexts. Exploratory survival and cross-omics analyses extended the framework beyond the response cohorts but were interpreted as projection rather than independent validation. Together, the results show how cell-resolved immune biology can support transparent, multi-omic biomarker development without reducing response to a single pathway. scTIME remains exploratory because model choice was post hoc , cohorts were small and clinically heterogeneous, and endpoint-matched external validation was unavailable.

papers.title: Cross-Dataset Reanalysis of Mouse Alzheimer Disease Single-Cell RNA-Sequencing Data Reveals a Reproducible Innate Immune Activation Signature
papers.authors: Anand, A.; Natarajan, E.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies of Alzheimer disease (AD) mouse models have proliferated across independent laboratories, brain regions, and platforms, yet the cross-study reproducibility of transcriptional signatures derived from such data remains underexplored. We reanalyzed six publicly available mouse brain scRNA-seq datasets (GSE140399, GSE140510, GSE143758, GSE208683, GSE214244, and GSE296027; 360,620 cells, 102 annotated clusters) using a standardized pipeline (Figure 1) comprising quality control, Leiden clustering, confidence-tiered marker-based cell-type annotation, sample-level pseudobulk differential expression, cross-dataset consistency analysis, and pathway enrichment. Pseudobulk differential expression, performed on 32 samples (16 AD, 16 Control) from five of the six datasets, identified 301 significant genes (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05) out of 20,629 tested, of which 290 (96.3%) were upregulated and 11 (3.7%) downregulated in AD. The upregulated set was dominated by innate immune and interferon-response genes (Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl6, Itgax, Cst7, Tlr4, Trem2) and showed extremely strong enrichment for immune system and innate immune system pathways (Reactome, p {equiv} 1.9 x 10-43 and 2.1 x 10-29 respectively), phagosome and osteoclast differentiation (KEGG), and interferon alpha/beta signaling. Of the 301 significant genes, 235 (78%) showed the same direction of effect across all datasets in which they were tested. The sixth dataset, GSE296027, was excluded from differential expression analysis due to a gene-identifier corruption artifact introduced during pseudobulk aggregation (detailed in Methods and Limitations) but contributed valid cell-type composition and microglial subclustering data, independently recovering a disease-associated microglia-like state. These findings indicate that a reproducible, strongly immune/interferon-skewed transcriptional signature, rather than a balanced up/down transcriptional shift, characterizes the mouse AD models analyzed here.

papers.title: γδ T cells: bridging innate and adaptive immunity in development, tissue residency, and disease.
papers.authors: Lou J, Zou N.
papers.abstract: γδ T cells are a unique lymphocyte lineage that bridges innate and adaptive immunity through MHC-unrestricted recognition of phosphoantigens, lipids, and stress-induced proteins. Their tissue-resident subsets, shaped by Vγ/Vδ chain usage, play essential roles in barrier surveillance, tissue homeostasis, and host defense.This review synthesizes recent advances that fundamentally reshape our understanding of γδ T cell biology. We highlight two conceptual frameworks: (1) dual recognition modalities of γδ TCRs, distinguishing structurally resolved ligand interactions from functionally supported recognition; and (2) a developmental wave model in which TCR signal strength and transcriptional networks program effector fates. Mouse and human studies are presented in dedicated species-specific sections and tables, with explicit attention to species-specific nomenclature and evidence levels.We cover γδ T cell development, tissue-resident programs, antigen recognition mechanisms (including butyrophilin-mediated phosphoantigen sensing, antibody-like foreign antigen recognition, and intracellular self-protein recognition), and the dual roles of γδ T cells in infection, cancer, and chronic inflammation. Therapeutic applications-adoptive transfer, CAR-engineered cells, and extracellular-vesicle vaccines-are critically appraised against current clinical evidence.Finally, we identify major unanswered questions: the complete γδ TCR ligand repertoire, the mechanisms maintaining tissue residency, and the translational gaps between mouse models and human disease. This review provides a structured framework for understanding γδ T cells as pivotal connectors of innate and adaptive immunity.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: γδ T Cells: bridging innate and adaptive immunity. This new unifying figure visualizes the central conceptual framework of the review. A central green γδ T cell icon serves as the bridging hub, with three color-coded routes radiating outward to distinct immune compartments. Route 1 (blue, left) -- Antigen Presentation: γδ T cells act as professional antigen-presenting cells (HLA-DR upregulated, CD80/CD86 costimulation, MHC Class II induction) and prime CD4+ and CD8+ αβ T cell responses. Route 2 (orange, top-right) -- Cytokine Instruction: γδ-derived IL-17, IFN-γ, IL-21, IL-22, and GM-CSF instruct B-cell class switching, plasma-cell differentiation, neutrophil recruitment, and ILC3 modulation. Route 3 (magenta, bottom-right) -- Innate-Receptor Integration: γδ T cells integrate innate-receptor inputs (NKG2D, NKp30, CD16-mediated ADCC) to amplify dendritic-cell maturation and license NK-to-T-cell cross-talk. A bottom disease-context strip situates the bridging framework across four contexts -- Infection (CMV, influenza, bacterial clearance), Cancer (antitumor versus pro-tumor balance), Autoimmunity (psoriasis, colitis, spondyloarthritis), and Tissue Homeostasis (wound healing and barrier surveillance). The top banner emphasizes that the three bridging routes are non-mutually exclusive. Together, this figure serves as the conceptual summary of the entire review.

papers.title: CAR-engineered microglia harness phagocytosis to target brain tumor in organoid models.
papers.authors: Choe MS, Yang WS, Cakir B, Kiral FR, Kim J, Lo C, Cheng E, Ongnok B, Muthusamy V, Chattipakorn N, Chattipakorn SC, Park IH.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is among the most aggressive and lethal brain tumors, and standard treatment offers only modest survival benefits. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematologic cancers, but its efficacy in GBM remains limited. Here we develop a CAR-engineered microglia (CAR-MG) platform and an organoid-based framework to test whether programmable microglial phagocytosis can be directed against GBM. We isolate microglia (MG) from human cortical organoids and engineer them to express a CAR targeting EGFRvIII, a recurrent tumor-specific EGFR deletion variant in GBM. In a 2D co-culture, CAR-MG selectively eliminates GBM cells through phagocytosis. In a 3D GBM-cortical organoid model, CAR-MG infiltrates tumor sites and depletes GBM cells over extended culture. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) shows elevated phagocytic pathways in CAR-MG and detects internalized tumor-derived transcripts, which resolve phagocytosis-resistance programs. These results support CAR-MG as a myeloid CAR modality for human brain organoid models.

papers.title: Benchmarking sample preservation strategies for clinical single-cell proteomics.
papers.authors: do Amaral-Prado HM, Miyamoto JG, de Figueiredo D, Cardoso EC, de Sá Patroni FM, Domingues RR, Pauletti BA, Paes Leme AF.
papers.abstract: Single-cell proteomics (SCP) enables direct characterization of cellular states at proteome resolution but remains limited in clinical studies due to challenges in sample collection, storage, and transportation. Here, we systematically evaluated preservation strategies for SCP by comparing fresh, cryopreserved, and paraformaldehyde-fixed cells using HeLa cells as a benchmark model (n = 159 cells). Both strategies maintained comparable proteome coverage, but fixation altered protein abundance, whereas cryopreservation largely preserved the proteomic profile. To assess the translational applicability of this workflow, we analyzed single peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from one healthy donor, comparing freshly isolated cells (n = 77) with cells subjected to cryopreservation followed by extended-term storage (n = 75). In PBMCs, cryopreservation did not significantly affect protein group identifications, cellular morphology, proteome coverage, or global proteomic landscape. Together, these results demonstrate that cryopreservation provides a feasible strategy for preserving primary immune cells for downstream SCP under the conditions evaluated here, while comparative preservation strategies using single HeLa cells highlight the advantages and challenges of fixation and cryopreservation for future clinical applications.

papers.title: Fibronectin-guided immune-stromal cell crosstalk promotes angiogenesis in pulp-dentin complex regeneration.
papers.authors: Jeong S, Park SY, Ku H, Eom BS, Kim D, Kim JM.
papers.abstract: Macrophages are multifunctional immune cells that play crucial roles in immune regulation and tissue regeneration by interacting with various cell types. Although macrophage-stromal cell interactions are widely recognized as essential for tissue regeneration and homeostasis, their precise mechanisms in the pulp-dentin complex, a key functional unit for tooth maintenance, remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the interactions between macrophages and dental pulp stromal cells (DPSCs) within a dental pulp microenvironment in response to dental caries infection. As caries progressed, macrophage-DPSC interactions became increasingly prominent. Whole-transcriptome analysis revealed that these interactions are mediated by fibronectin-integrin engagement, which induces a phenotypic shift in macrophages from pro-inflammatory to pro-angiogenic, mediated by the upregulation of angiogenic chemokines. Integrated analysis of a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from human pulp tissue further confirmed that caries progression enhanced macrophage-driven angiogenic signalling in the endothelial cell population. Moreover, the altered secretome resulting from the macrophage-DPSC co-culture significantly enhanced in vitro endothelial tube formation and survival, indicating a strong angiogenic potential conducive to tissue regeneration. In a preclinical pulp revascularization model, the application of fibronectin during revascularization enhanced neovascularization, root dentin formation, apical maturation and organized pulp-dentin-like tissue formation. Collectively, these findings indicate that fibronectin is a key regulator that reprogrammes the damaged pulp environment into a pro-angiogenic and regenerative niche through coordinated immune-stromal interactions. This study provides a promising direction for the development of extracellular matrix-based therapeutic strategies in regenerative dentistry.

papers.title: Beyond the vessel wall: single-cell dissection of epicardial fat-myocardial crosstalk in coronary artery disease.
papers.authors: Puluca N, Vafadarnejad E, Saleem T, Rammoser C, Wirth F, Schwerdt V, Dreßen M, Gottmann I, Reiminger X, Yan Y, Seeler S, Bressem KK, Chen Z, Li S, Erhard N, Lahm H, Georgescu TC, Reiter A, Dzilic E, Günzinger R, Voss S, Herold U, Voss B, Vitanova K, Braun C, Leone V, Reichert M, Deisenhofer I, Hadamitzky M, Schunkert H, Krane M, Doppler SA.
papers.abstract: Aims Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) has emerged as an active regulator of cardiovascular disease, yet the cellular and molecular features of myocardial-associated EAT (mEAT) in coronary artery disease (CAD) remain incompletely defined. Methods and results We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of mEAT from patients with CAD (n = 9), nonCAD cardiovascular surgery patients (n = 9), and forensic controls without cardiac disease (n = 2), integrated with histology, CT-based EAT volume assessment, matched right atrial myocardium analysis, and functional in vitro assays. mEAT contained diverse adipocyte, stromal, immune, and vascular cell populations. In CAD, we identified two disease-enriched inflammatory cell states, inflammatory adipogenic cells (IAC) and inflammatory stromal cells (ISC), characterized by immune activation, stress-response signalling, extracellular matrix remodelling, and impaired adipogenic features. Histological analyses confirmed enlarged adipocytes, increased fibrosis, and higher abundance of IAC/ISC-associated markers in CAD-mEAT. Exploratory integration with CT imaging suggested a possible association between increased EAT volume and enrichment of inflammatory cell states. Comparative analyses with published adipose and cardiac single-cell datasets indicated that IAC and ISC share features with previously described inflammatory adipocyte and stromal populations, while displaying a distinct marker combination enriched in CAD-associated mEAT.Cell-cell communication analyses identified THBS1-CD36 and SEMA4A/SEMA3C-NRP1/PLXNA signalling as predicted CAD-associated communication axes involving inflammatory mEAT populations and myocardial cell types. Conditioned medium from CAD-mEAT-derived adipocytes/IAC altered contractile properties of human iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte (CM) microtissues, while simultaneously impairing endothelial tube formation and migration. Recombinant THBS1 and SEMA3C partially recapitulated selected effects, whereas combined CD36 and NRP1 blockade partially attenuated endothelial and CM responses. Conclusion Together, these data provide a high-resolution map of CAD-associated mEAT remodelling and identify IAC and ISC as inflammatory cell states linked to altered adipose-vascular and adipose-myocardial signalling. These findings support the concept that cellular and molecular features of mEAT may complement imaging-based EAT assessment and inform future studies on CAD-associated adipose tissue inflammation.

papers.title: Distinct chromatin landscapes dictate resident cardiac macrophage lifecycles and functions.
papers.authors: Wong A, Vohra S, Ellis K, Hamidzada H, Cordeiro B, Vanneste D, Bellworthy R, Arlidge C, Macklin J, Kantores C, Momen A, Dick SA, Clemente-Casares X, Marichal T, Langlais D, Wilson MD, Lupien M, Epelman S.
papers.abstract: Aims Three resident macrophage subsets co-exist in the homeostatic heart, exhibiting distinct origins transcriptional identities and functions. However, the underlying epigenetic architecture regulating resident cardiac macrophage subset heterogeneity is not known, which limits mechanistic understanding and therapeutic targeting. Methods and results We performed bulk and single-cell ATAC-seq to map the chromatin landscape of murine resident macrophage subsets. Integration of ATAC-seq with RNA-seq of each cardiac macrophage subset revealed two primary chromatin accessibility-based cell states that correlated with tissue residency - a CCR2- macrophage chromatin-based cell state that corresponded with resident TLF+ (TIMD4 + LYVE1 + FOLR2+) and CCR2-MHC-IIhi subsets that do not require monocytes for maintenance, and a CCR2+ chromatin-based cell state that corresponded to CCR2 + MHC-IIhi macrophages, which rely on monocyte input. Using footprint analysis, we identified subset-specific differences in transcription factor binding that explained transcriptional differences, including enriched AP-1 binding in CCR2+ macrophages and enriched MAF-family factor binding in TLF+ macrophages. Importantly, we demonstrate myeloid-specific loss of Mafb or Maf skewed macrophage subset composition toward CCR2+ macrophages and increased MHC-II expression in TLF+ macrophages. Furthermore, we identify a link between IRF8 and MHC-II, in which myeloid-specific loss of Irf8 abolished MHC-II expression exclusively in fate-mapped resident CCR2- subsets but not in CCR2+ macrophages, demonstrating a subset-specific dependency of IRF8 in modulating antigen-presentation. Conclusion Together, these data suggest tissue residency dictates chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding in cardiac macrophages, linking epigenetic structure to monocyte-dependency, distinct gene expression patterns and critical functions such as antigen presentation.

papers.title: A multiscale signaling-biophysical framework reveals mechanisms of macrophage-mediated RBC clearance in sickle cell and Gaucher disease.
papers.authors: Chai Z, Daryakenari NA, Karniadakis GE.
papers.abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) clearance by macrophages maintains blood homeostasis and is dysregulated in the hemolytic disorder sickle cell disease (SCD) and the lysosomal storage disorder Gaucher disease (GD), where biophysical and biochemical alterations promote premature phagocytosis. We develop a multiscale hybrid modeling framework integrating signaling dynamics, biophysical simulations, and machine learning to investigate the mechanisms governing RBC phagocytosis in these diseases. Our approach couples a systems biology model of macrophage-RBC signaling with dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations of molecular diffusion and membrane interactions, and leverages Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for simultaneous parameter inference, hidden-state reconstruction, and integration of multiscale mechanistic constraints. The DPD framework provides mechanistic insight into antibody diffusion, receptor engagement, and membrane-level interactions during macrophage-RBC contact, generating spatially resolved trajectories of CD47-SIRP α signaling and antibody-receptor binding that serve as intermediate observables constraining the signaling model. The model accurately captures differential phagocytic responses between healthy and altered RBCs, revealing diminished inhibitory signaling and changes in SHP1-mediated pathways in both SCD and GD. Identifiability analysis combining Fisher Information Matrix diagnostics and profile likelihood confirms that parameters governing the CD47-SIRP α -SHP1 axis are among the most robustly recoverable, and simulations of therapeutic perturbations with anti-SIRP α antibodies demonstrate modulation of engulfment outcomes. We further employ Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) as an alternative to standard PINNs, demonstrating improved robustness under noise and sampling variability. More broadly, our multiscale platform linking biophysical simulation with systems-level inference is generalizable, offering mechanistic insights and computational tools for therapeutic exploration in diseases involving dysregulated phagocytosis.

papers.title: TLR3-TRIF signaling in villus-like enterocytes drives type III interferon responses to enteroviruses.
papers.authors: Hare DN, Coyne CB.
papers.abstract: Enteroviruses initiate infection at the intestinal epithelium but can spread systemically to cause severe disease. Although both MDA5 and TLR3 have been implicated in enterovirus sensing, the mechanisms by which the intestinal epithelium detects these viruses remain poorly defined. To address this, we infected human intestinal organoids (enteroids) with the group B enterovirus echovirus 11 (E11) and compared responses in models differentiated to mimic either crypt-like or villus-like epithelium. Villus-like enteroids produced significantly more type III interferons following E11 infection and exhibited heightened responsiveness to type III interferon signaling. Single-cell RNA sequencing of infected enteroids revealed that E11 broadly infected epithelial cell types, but type III interferon expression was largely restricted to mature enterocytes. Notably, enterocyte differentiation was also associated with upregulation of TLR3 and other innate immune genes. Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout enteroids, we found that TLR3-TRIF signaling was essential for intestinal type III IFN responses to E11 infection, whereas loss of MAVS, the adaptor for MDA5, had no effect. Together, these data support a model in which mature enterocytes serve as key sensors of enterovirus infection via TLR3-TRIF signaling, triggering a localized type III IFN response that may help restrict viral spread. Importance Enteroviruses are commonly circulating viruses that can cause a broad spectrum of disease, particularly in pediatric populations. Innate immune sensing in the intestinal epithelium likely plays a critical role in determining the outcome of enterovirus infections. Deficiencies in TLR3 signaling, type III IFN responses, or crypt-villus architecture may contribute to severe disease presentations. Our findings highlight the importance of TLR3-mediated sensing in mature enterocytes, which may also have broader implications for other intestinal viruses, as well as for inflammatory conditions like inflammatory bowel disease. A deeper understanding of how TLR3 sensing and type III IFN production are regulated in the intestine could inform new therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating mucosal sensitivity to viral nucleic acids and enhancing antiviral defense.

papers.title: Epigenetic Priming Sensitizes Metastatic Breast Cancer to Checkpoint Blockade by Rewiring the Tumor-Immune Microenvironment.
papers.authors: Senent Y, Manguso RT.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has shown limited efficacy in metastatic breast cancer. Resistance mechanisms involve suppressive myeloid and stromal populations in the tumor microenvironment (TME). In this issue of Cancer Research, Gonzalez and colleagues integrate single-cell transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, functional immunology, and mathematical modeling to dissect how combined treatment with the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor entinostat and anti-PD-1/anti-CTLA-4 blockade (EPC) sensitizes these refractory tumors. Work using metastatic mouse models shows that the antitumor response is multifactorial, comprising downregulation of myeloid-mediated CD8+ T-cell suppression (via ICAM-1 and IFNγ signaling) along with increased B-cell and plasma cell activation, antibody production, and tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) maturation. Some of these findings are further validated in biospecimens from patients on a phase Ib trial treated with the EPC combination treatment. Mathematical modeling formalizes this insight, demonstrating that simultaneous modulation of T-cell activation and myeloid suppression, rather than either alone, is required to drive tumor eradication in silico. This work highlights the increasingly accepted idea that the answer to how current treatments modify and shape tumors is multifactorial. Thus, diversified strategies that include comprehensive analysis of the TME, mathematical modeling tools, and validation in human specimens are required to optimize treatment efficacy. See related article by Gonzalez et al., p. XX .

papers.title: Integrative Bioinformatics Identifies TTN as a Potential Diagnostic Marker for Rheumatoid Arthritis.
papers.authors: Fang Y, Li P, Zhu Z, Cao Z, Qu H, Wu W, Jing L, Li H, Xu J, Shu B, Mo W.
papers.abstract: Background Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, and its molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Objective To identify core genes associated with RA and evaluate their diagnostic utility, with an emphasis on immune relevance and causality. Methods Differential expression analysis and weighted gene coexpression network analysis were used to prioritize hub genes. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses supported biological interpretation. A nomogram and receiver operating characteristic analysis were used to evaluate diagnostic performance, and immune cell infiltration was analyzed to identify immune-associated core genes. The causal effect of titin on the risk of RA was estimated using genome-wide association study data and two-sample Mendelian randomization. Validation was conducted in independent public transcriptomic datasets and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of synovial tissue. Results Titin (TTN) was prioritized as an RA-associated core gene and demonstrated favorable diagnostic performance. TTN expression was consistently higher in RA than in controls across validation datasets. Public external validation datasets supported increased TTN expression in RA, and scRNA-seq analysis suggested enrichment of TTN expression in synovial T cells. Mendelian randomization supported a causal association between genetically predicted TTN and RA risk. Discussion Collectively, evidence from bulk transcriptomics, immune cell infiltration profiling, single-cell localization, external validation, and genetic inference supports TTN as a previously underexplored candidate RA-associated biomarker with potential immune relevance. These findings extend current RA biomarker discovery by linking diagnostic performance with immune context and genetic support. Further mechanistic studies are needed to clarify whether TTN is involved in RA immunopathology or reflects inflammation-related tissue remodeling. Conclusion Integrative analyses identify TTN as a potential RA-associated diagnostic biomarker requiring further experimental and clinical validation. Further studies are needed to clarify its mechanistic role and clinical utility in RA.

papers.title: Integrating Mendelian randomization with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to investigate gut microbiota-associated genetic signals and molecular characteristics in prostate cancer.
papers.authors: Qiu C, Zhang H, Du Z, Gao Y, Dai L.
papers.abstract: Background Prostate cancer (PRAD) represents one of the most prevalent malignancies among men globally. Accumulating evidence implicates gut microbiota dysbiosis in the initiation and progression of prostate cancer; however, the causal relationship and underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. This study integrated Mendelian randomization (MR), bioinformatics, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics to systematically investigate the genetic associations between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk and characterize the expression patterns of microbiota-associated candidate genes within the tumor microenvironment. Methods Two-sample MR analyses were performed using summary statistics from the OpenGWAS database to evaluate causal associations between gut microbiota and PRAD risk, with sensitivity analyses conducted to ensure robustness. Significant SNPs were functionally annotated and mapped to candidate genes using g:SNPense, and differentially expressed associated genes (DEAGs) were identified through integration with GEO datasets. Subsequent analyses encompassed immune infiltration profiling, machine learning model construction, and nomogram validation. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were employed to delineate cell type-specific expression and spatial distribution patterns of signature genes. Candidate gene expression alterations in prostate cancer cells were experimentally validated by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Results MR analyses identified significant positive causal associations between PRAD risk and Brevibacillaceae, Brevibacillales, CAG-110, and Pararhizobium, whereas Lawsonibacter sp000492175 exhibited a significant inverse association. A total of 21 differentially expressed genes were identified, with RASSF3, CROCC, UBE4B, SMOC2, and ACACA emerging as key signature genes. Immune infiltration analyses revealed a significant positive correlation between FRMD3 and regulatory T cells (Tregs), and a negative correlation between ACACA and neutrophil infiltration. The random forest classifier demonstrated optimal predictive performance, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.853 in the validation cohort. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses revealed cell-type-associated expression patterns of ACACA, SMOC2, and UBE4B across different cellular populations. These findings suggest potential associations between signature genes and specific cellular contexts, which require further experimental validation. qRT-PCR validated differential expression patterns of these candidate genes in prostate cancer cells. Conclusion This study provides genetic causal inference evidence supporting a close association between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk, and identifies multiple key signature genes implicated in immune microenvironment regulation and tumor progression. Integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses suggest that these genes exhibit distinct expression patterns among different cellular populations and may provide clues for understanding their potential roles in PRAD progression. These findings provide genetic evidence supporting the association between gut microbiota and prostate cancer risk and highlight potential microbiota-associated molecular signatures. Further functional studies are required to clarify whether these genes directly contribute to microbiota-related prostate cancer progression.

papers.title: TREM2 + macrophages mediate anticancer therapy-induced immune evasion in lung adenocarcinoma via the CCL5/CCL22-Treg axis.
papers.authors: Kim CY, Cha YJ, Park MK, Chang YS.
papers.abstract: Introduction Osimertinib and cisplatin are widely used as standard treatments for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, their effects on tumor microenvironment remodeling remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether TREM2-positive tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) promote immune evasion through the CCL5/CCL22-CCR5/CCR4-Treg axis under anticancer treatment. Methods The spatial and quantitative correlations between TREM2 + and FOXP3 + cells were assessed using NSCLC patient-derived single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets, human lung adenocarcinoma tissue microarrays, and cisplatin-treated mouse lung cancer models. Mediators linking TREM2 + and FOXP3 + cells were identified by cell-cell communication analysis using CellChat and gene expression profiling of THP-1-derived macrophages treated with osimertinib or cisplatin, with validation in bone marrow-derived macrophages. Results scRNA-seq dataset analysis showed significantly enriched TREM2 + and FOXP3 + cells in lung adenocarcinoma tissues compared with adjacent normal lung, with a significant positive correlation at the aggregated single-cell level (Spearman's rho = 0.7323, P + TAMs and FOXP3 + Tregs and were markedly induced by treatment but suppressed by TREM2 knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition. TREM2 overexpression further enhanced their induction. Mechanistically, CCL22 induction was broadly dependent on SYK, Src, AKT, NF-κB, or STAT3 signaling pathways, whereas CCL5 upregulation depended on Src, NF-κB, and STAT3, with SYK involvement varying by cell type. In the orthotopic Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) model, Trem2 inhibition reduced Treg infiltration and mitigated chemotherapy-associated immune evasion. Conclusion These findings indicate that TREM2 + TAMs drive CCL5/CCL22-mediated Treg recruitment and support targeting TREM2 to enhance therapeutic efficacy of standard NSCLC treatments.

papers.title: Genetic susceptibility and clinical validation of ICAM-5 in immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis.
papers.authors: Zhuang Z, Hu P, Hong X, Lin T, Yu Y, Jia X, Su X, Su B, Shi W, Hu J.
papers.abstract: Purpose To investigate genetically supported molecular factors associated with uveitis and to evaluate the clinical, transcriptomic, and retinal relevance of intercellular adhesion molecule 5 (ICAM-5) across major immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis subtypes. Methods Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was conducted using eQTLGen eQTL data and two independent pQTL resources (Icelandic SomaScan and FinnGen R10), with uveitis GWAS summary statistics as the outcome. ICAM5 was evaluated using complementary MR estimators, sensitivity analyses, reverse MR, and Bayesian colocalization. Plasma ICAM-5 concentrations were measured by ELISA in 90 patients with active non-infectious uveitis (30 each with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Behçet's disease-associated uveitis, and HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis) and 40 healthy controls using age- and sex-adjusted models. ICAM5 expression was further examined in the peripheral-blood transcriptomic dataset GSE194060, whereas retinal Icam5 expression and cellular distribution were evaluated using experimental autoimmune uveitis retinal single-cell RNA-sequencing data and GSE132229. Results Genetically predicted higher ICAM5 expression and ICAM-5 protein levels were associated with increased uveitis susceptibility in the eQTLGen dataset (OR = 2.46, 95% CI 1.48-4.11, P = 5.69 × 10 -4 ; nSNP =8), the Icelandic SomaScan cis-pQTL analysis (OR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.11-1.46, P = 5.30 × 10 -4 ; nSNP =89), and the FinnGen R10 cis-pQTL analysis (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.07-1.38, P = 3.13 × 10 - ³; nSNP =4). Sensitivity analyses showed no significant heterogeneity or horizontal pleiotropy, and reverse MR provided no evidence of an association from uveitis liability to ICAM-5 levels. Plasma ICAM-5 concentrations were higher in all three uveitis subgroups than in healthy controls and remained elevated after age and sex adjustment, with the greatest increase in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease. In the GSE194060 peripheral-blood transcriptomic dataset, ICAM5 expression was higher in the uveitis group. Analysis of the retinal single-cell RNA-sequencing data showed that Icam5 was predominantly detected in neuronal populations. Conclusion Multi-omics MR, clinical protein quantification, transcriptomic analysis, and retinal single-cell profiling provide convergent evidence linking ICAM-5 to immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis. These findings support ICAM-5 as a genetically supported candidate mediator and circulating biomarker.

papers.title: Metabolic reprogramming of NK cells in chronic brucellar arthritis: role of the HIF-1α/mTOR axis.
papers.authors: Sheng G, Li W, Liu D, Ren X, Wei M, Yang Z, Tian W, Zhang F, Zhu Y, Zeng F, Zhao Z, Xu P, Tian H, Pang N, Li C, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Background Brucellar arthritis is the most common complication of brucellosis, and its chronic progression is closely associated with immune cell dysfunction. Natural killer (NK) cells play a central role in anti-infective immunity; however, their functional status and regulatory mechanisms in brucellar arthritis remain poorly understood. Methods Peripheral blood and synovial tissue samples were collected from healthy controls, as well as from patients with acute-phase and chronic-phase brucellar arthritis. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), flow cytometry, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential assay, Seahorse metabolic analysis, and Western blotting were employed to systematically evaluate NK cell phenotypes, functions, metabolic profiles, and HIF-1α/mTOR pathway activity. In vitro , heat-killed Brucella melitensis 16M (HKBA) was used to stimulate NK-92 cells and HIF-1α-knockout (KO) cell lines, with mTOR inhibitor intervention, to dissect the regulatory mechanism of the HIF-1α/mTOR axis in NK cell metabolic reprogramming. Results scRNA-seq revealed enrichment of NK cells in the synovium of brucellar arthritis patients, with aberrant expression of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related genes. Clinical sample analyses showed that, compared with healthy controls, the proportion of peripheral blood NK cells increased in both acute- and chronic-phase patients; however, NK cells from chronic-phase patients exhibited significantly reduced IFN-γ, Granzyme B, and CD107a degranulation levels. HIF-1α protein was consistently overexpressed in patient NK cells, whereas phosphorylated mTOR-pathway proteins (p-PI3K, p-AKT, p-mTOR) were markedly suppressed. In vitro , HKBA treatment inhibited mTOR pathway activity in NK-92 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential as shown by JC-1 staining. HIF-1α knockout significantly restored NK cell cytotoxic function, upregulated OXPHOS- and glycolysis-related gene expression, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential. Transcriptomic sequencing confirmed enrichment of mTOR signaling and energy metabolism gene sets after knockout. Importantly, mTOR pathway inhibition completely blocked the HIF-1α-knockout-mediated restoration of NK cell function and mitochondrial fitness, indicating that HIF-1α primarily drives NK cell metabolic and functional abnormalities through mTOR suppression. Conclusions Brucella infection induces HIF-1α overexpression, which suppresses mTOR signaling and drives metabolic reprogramming of NK cells characterized by impaired OXPHOS and functional exhaustion, thereby promoting chronicity of brucellar arthritis. Targeting the HIF-1α/mTOR axis may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for brucellar arthritis.

papers.title: GULP1 Fuels Resistance to PD-1 Blockade through Lipid-Mediated Metabolic Reprogramming of Tumor-Associated Macrophages in Gastric Cancer.
papers.authors: Zhang Z, Xu W, Yu K, Bao A, Cao Y, Yu M, Yu Q, Zhao Y, Gong L, Xie P, Shen Z, Qin J.
papers.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) have substantially improved the treatment of multiple cancers; however, only a small proportion of gastric cancer (GC) patients achieve durable clinical benefit. The underlying tumor-intrinsic mechanisms driving resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify key regulators of immunotherapy resistance in GC and to elucidate their functional and mechanistic roles. Methods: Transcriptomic data from anti-PD-1-responsive and anti-PD-1-resistant GC patients were analyzed and integrated with mouse model data and publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Functional experiments, including in vitro assays and in vivo tumor models, were performed to validate candidate genes and explore their roles in tumor progression and immunotherapy resistance. Results: GULP PTB domain-containing engulfment adaptor 1 (GULP1) was identified as a key driver of resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy in GC. Elevated GULP1 expression was associated with poor prognosis and unfavorable clinical responses to PD-1 blockade. GULP1 promoted GC progression and attenuated the therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment. Functionally, GULP1 facilitated the accumulation and metabolic reprogramming of CD36 + programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) + tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) by shaping a lipid-enriched tumor microenvironment, thereby impairing CD8 + T-cell function. Mechanistically, GULP1 promoted insulin-induced gene 2 (INSIG2) palmitoylation through the recruitment of zinc finger DHHC-type palmitoyltransferase 8 (zDHHC8), resulting in sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1) nuclear translocation and enhanced de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of Gulp1 with glycyrrhizic acid significantly restored sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy in vivo. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings uncovered a previously unrecognized GULP1-fatty acid-CD36 + PD-L1 + TAM-CD8 + T-cell axis that drove resistance to PD-1 blockade in GC, highlighting GULP1 as a promising therapeutic target and predictive biomarker for immunotherapy responsiveness.

papers.title: Identifiable inverse optimal transport for single-cell state transitions
papers.authors: Dong, H.; Gong, Y.; Liu, Y.
papers.abstract: Signed effects of target-state programmes are unidentifiable in balanced optimal transport because fixed endpoint distributions make their contributions constant across feasible plans. We introduce UOT-IOT, a semi-relaxed inverse transport framework that restores measurable targetmass responses and provides a rank condition for local identifiability. It recovers coefficients inground-truth benchmarks (correlation 0.997 versus 0.081 for balanced transport), transfers frozen directions to six unseen samples with specificity controls, and achieves the lowest transition error against seven methods under matched evaluation conditions. GH-IOT separates shared directions from context and lineage-history offsets, revealing opposing history-associated effects. IFN/HLA is associated with patient treatment response, whereas EMT relates to drug sensitivity and perturbation-induced state changes. PERSIST-IOT improves future population-composition prediction in an independent experiment. Together, these modules distinguish current state,transition propensity and future population outcomes while supporting testable biological interpretations.

papers.title: Combined network pharmacology, transcriptomics and machine learning suggests Danggui Buxue Tang may suppress oxidative stress and inflammation through Nrf2/HO-1 and IL-17 pathways in pulmonary fibrosis.
papers.authors: Yang Z, Chen Y, Wen C, Chang Y, Zhang H.
papers.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevance Danggui Buxue Tang (DBT), a classical Chinese herbal formula of Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge and Angelica sinensis (Oliv.) Diels in a 5:1 ratio, has long been used for qi and blood deficiency. Its mechanism against pulmonary fibrosis (PF) remains unclear. Aim of the study This study examined how DBT treats silica-induced PF, combining network pharmacology, transcriptomics, machine learning and experimental validation. Materials and methods We built a rat PF model by intratracheal silica instillation. Network pharmacology and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified candidate therapeutic targets. Four machine learning algorithms screened diagnostic signature genes (DSGs). We profiled immune infiltration with CIBERSORT, modeled compound-target binding by molecular docking, and confirmed key genes and pathways by Western blotting. Results DBT treatment significantly attenuated silica-induced lung pathology, evidenced by improved pulmonary function, reduced alveolitis and fibrosis scores, diminished collagen deposition, and downregulated expression of α-smooth muscle actin, collagen I, and fibronectin. Furthermore, DBT markedly suppressed inflammatory responses (decreasing TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and TGF-β1 while elevating IL-10) and mitigated oxidative stress (lowering MDA levels while enhancing SOD, GSH-Px, and T-AOC activities). Bioinformatic analyses identified three core DSGs-MMP7, MMP13, and TNF-as candidate therapeutic targets. Enrichment analyses highlighted the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)/heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) pathway and IL-17 signaling as the primary mechanistic routes. Immune profiling revealed that DBT's therapeutic effects correlate with specific shifts in immune cell subsets. Ultra-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole-orbitrap mass spectrometry detected 11 prototype constituents in serum; notably, the Ononin, Methylnissolin-3-O-glucoside, and Isomucronulatol-7-O-glucoside exhibited strong binding affinities to MMP7, MMP13, and TNF. DBT inhibited the profibrotic IL-17 cascade while activating the antioxidant Nrf2/HO-1 axis. Conclusion Our data suggest that DBT may ease silica-induced PF through multiple targets that act on oxidative stress and inflammation. The DSGs (MMP7, MMP13, TNF) and pathways (Nrf2/HO-1, IL-17) help explain how DBT works and point to new targets for treating PF. The approach also provides a reusable workflow for studying other complex herbal formulas in fibrosis.

papers.title: Identification of plasma immune markers associated with latent tuberculosis conversion in HIV-infected individuals who received isoniazid preventive therapy.
papers.authors: Kumar NP, Mohan G, Vanamudhu A, K S, T K, Silvester YS, Kumar BS, M J, Kumar V, S V, Sekar, R K, Babu S, Hissar S.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis remains a major risk for people living with HIV, even those on antiretroviral therapy, due to increased susceptibility to latent TB infection. Identifying immune signatures that distinguish progression from resistance is critical for developing predictive biomarkers and targeted prevention strategies. In this study, 80 HIV-infected adults on antiretroviral therapy who received isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) were followed for six months and categorized as Progressors, Sustainers, Converters, or Resisters based on serial QuantiFERON-TB results. Plasma levels of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors were analyzed using a Luminex assay, alongside machine learning and pathway analyses. Progressors and Sustainers exhibited elevated proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors, while Resisters showed dynamic immune modulation following preventive therapy. Key predictors of progression included PD-L1, TNF-α, IL-17A, and FGF2. Network and pathway analyses highlighted persistent inflammatory signaling in Progressors and adaptive immune regulation in Resisters. Findings suggest distinct immune profiles associated with TB risk, offering potential for improved prediction and targeted interventions.
papers.venue: Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine

papers.title: Interpretable CT-Based Radiomics for Prediction of High-Affinity Neoantigens Associated Immunogenic States in Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma Treated with TACE Plus Targeted Therapy and Immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Bian C, Qin Y, Zou H, Fan W, Li J.
papers.abstract: Objectives: To develop and validate a CT radiomics-based machine learning model for the noninvasive prediction of HANS status in advanced HCC and to investigate the prognostic and genomic characteristics associated with HANS status. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included patients with advanced HCC treated with TACE-based triplet therapy. Patients were followed until death or last follow-up. Tumor tissue underwent whole-exome sequencing for HANS calculation, and arterial-phase CT images were used for radiomic feature extraction. A radiomics model (HANS-Rad), a clinical model (HANS-Clin), and a combined model (HANS-RC) were developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Calibration and decision curve analyses were performed to assess model reliability and clinical utility. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used for model interpretation. Genomic analyses were conducted to explore differences between predicted HANS subgroups. Results: A total of 129 patients were included (median age, 54 years; IQR, 44-62 years; 90% men). The HANS-High group demonstrated longer overall survival compared with the HANS-Low group (median, 23.0 vs. 10.0 months; hazard ratio, 0.60; p = 0.026). The combined HANS-RC model achieved the best performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.964 in the training set and 0.869 (95% CI, 0.716-1.000) in the test set, outperforming the radiomics-only and clinical models. The model also showed favorable calibration and net benefit. Genomic analyses revealed that HANS-High tumors exhibited higher tumor mutational burden and enrichment of immune-related and oncogenic pathways, whereas HANS-Low tumors were associated with distinct mutational patterns and pathway alterations. Conclusions: A radiomics-based machine learning model using CT images enables the noninvasive prediction of HANS status in advanced HCC, with strong prognostic relevance and biologic interpretability supported by genomic analyses.

papers.title: Metal-organic framework nanovaccines for systemic tumour regression.
papers.authors: Jiang X, Wang C, Yang K, Tillman L, Lin EJ, Piffkó A, Wen C, Germanas T, Li J, Ma X, Liang HL, Weichselbaum RR, Lin W.
papers.abstract: Cancer vaccines can elicit antigen-specific antitumour immunity, but their clinical efficacy is often limited by their inability to sustain T-cell activation in tumours. Here we report MOF-Vac, a nanoscale metal-organic framework (MOF)-based therapeutic vaccine platform that co-delivers peptide antigens and STING agonists with high loading capacity and phosphate-triggered intracellular release. This design enables coordinated antigen presentation and innate immune activation, resulting in sustained T-cell priming and intratumoural effector function. In murine models of melanoma, colorectal cancer, triple-negative breast cancer, lung cancer and oropharyngeal cancer, MOF-Vac induced tumour regression, immune memory and protection against metastasis. MOF-Vac also synergized with radiotherapy and immune checkpoint blockade to eradicate both primary and distant tumours. Single-cell RNA sequencing and immune depletion studies revealed that therapeutic efficacy predominantly depends on macrophage-mediated antigen presentation and remodelling of the tumour microenvironment towards a proinflammatory, immune-active state. MOF-Vac provides a modular platform for off-the-shelf and personalized cancer vaccination.

papers.title: Incision-triggered neuroimmune remodeling of nociceptor ion channels: from postoperative inflammation to pain chronification.
papers.authors: Song X, Feng M, Hao J, Luan Y.
papers.abstract: Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) arises after a known tissue insult, yet no intervention reliably prevents its development. This Review examines whether incision-triggered inflammation remodels nociceptor voltage-gated ion channels in ways that sustain peripheral input and favor pain chronification. We integrate human genetic and clinical evidence, incision-specific perturbation studies, functional work in non-surgical models, and expression-level associations distinguishing mechanistic strength from directness to CPSP. We focus on NaV1.7, NaV1.8, NaV1.9, and CaV3.2 within a broader network that includes peripheral transducing channels whose gating, trafficking, and abundance can be altered by TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, chemokines, p38 MAPK, NF-κB, and gp130/JAK signaling. Direct incision evidence now includes antisense and pharmacologic studies linking TNF-α/p38/NF-κB signaling to NaV1.8 and NaV1.9 expression and acute hypersensitivity, as well as single-cell maps showing insult-specific macrophage and neutrophil programs and protective immune-derived signals. Evidence from rare channelopathies does not establish population-level CPSP susceptibility. However, no human study has demonstrated the complete sequence from a defined postoperative immune signal to altered channel function and persistent pain. Sex, age, and hormonal context are plausible modifiers, but the strongest mechanistic evidence remains model-dependent and preclinical. Selective NaV1.8 inhibition validates peripheral channel tractability for acute pain but not prevention of CPSP. We therefore propose a testable, evidence-calibrated framework in which pathogenic and resolving immune programs act across peripheral, ganglion, and spinal compartments, and we define the experiments, biomarkers, and target-time-population alignment needed to determine whether this framework can guide mechanism-based prevention.

papers.title: Variant-informed multimodal tissue-state modeling reveals an NRF2 stress niche and dependency axis in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered cancer.
papers.authors: Kong M, Li Q, Zhao X, Wang Y, Luo Y, Yu Y, Zhang C.
papers.abstract: Introduction Cancer genotypes influence transcriptional programs, spatial organization, histopathology, and treatment-response states, yet these molecular and tissue-level features are often analyzed separately in public-data studies. VISTA was developed as a variant-informed, multimodal framework for modeling genotype-linked tissue states and prioritizing validation-ready biological hypotheses. Methods VISTA integrates somatic variants, protein-region and AlphaMissense-informed priors, RNA-state scoring, whole-slide image embeddings, immunotherapy cohorts, spatial and single-cell references, cell-line dependency maps, and pharmacogenomic screens. We evaluated the framework in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered lung cancer and melanoma, using the NRF2 stress axis as a biologically defined test case. Analyses incorporated project-adjusted modeling, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation testing, leave-project sensitivity analyses, independent tumor-level validation cohorts, fixed-effect external meta-analysis, model-system analyses using DepMap/CCLE, tissue-context analyses, immunotherapy cohorts, and exploratory whole-slide image analyses. Results In TCGA LUAD, LUSC, and SKCM pilot cohorts, KEAP1 and NFE2L2 alterations were consistently associated with NRF2 stress activation across project-adjusted models and sensitivity analyses. Independent analyses of CPTAC LUAD, CPTAC LSCC, and non-TCGA LUAD cohorts reproduced higher NRF2-state scores in KEAP1/NFE2L2-altered tumors. Fixed-effect external meta-analysis supported associations with both KEAP1 mutation and combined KEAP1-or-NFE2L2 alteration status. DepMap/CCLE analyses provided complementary model-system evidence: KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant models had higher NRF2 scores, while NRF2-high or KEAP1/NFE2L2-mutant contexts showed stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Tissue-context analyses positioned NRF2 stress near hypoxic, stromal, myeloid, and immune programs. Immunotherapy cohorts supported the relevance of NRF2-associated states to treatment-response biology, while also indicating limited utility for static pan-cancer prediction. Exploratory whole-slide image analyses using pathology foundation-model embeddings identified morphology associations with myeloid, hypoxic, and CAF/TGF-beta barrier programs. Discussion VISTA provides an evidence-layered approach to variant-informed tissue-state modeling. By integrating genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, spatial, cellular, dependency, and pharmacogenomic evidence, it can help prioritize genotype-linked cancer states and validation-ready hypotheses. VISTA is not intended to function as a stand-alone clinical predictor; its claims are bounded by the evidence available in each data layer and by the biological and clinical context of the analyzed cohorts.

papers.title: From CAF subtypes to clinically relevant states: cancer-associated fibroblasts in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Hao Y, Wang Y, Du Q, Li G.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) develops within a dense, poorly perfused tumor microenvironment (TME) in which cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are prominent cellular and structural components. Once viewed as a uniform population of activated matrix-producing cells, CAFs now include myofibroblastic, inflammatory, antigen-presenting and other populations identified by single-cell and spatial studies. These categories sharpen experimental resolution but do not form a stable hierarchy. CAF phenotypes overlap across spatial niches and disease stages, and they change under metabolic stress or treatment. We frame this heterogeneity as a set of context-dependent functional states. This review synthesizes evidence on fibroblast origins, canonical and recently reported states, and the signals that drive state transitions. It then examines CAF functions in extracellular matrix organization, tumor-cell plasticity and dissemination, metabolic support and immune regulation. Findings on tumor-restraining fibroblasts and protective collagen pools challenge indiscriminate stromal depletion. We also assess CAF states as prognostic and predictive biomarkers, their roles in treatment resistance and therapeutic strategies based on depletion, pathway blockade or stromal normalization. Failures of Hedgehog and hyaluronan-directed therapies show that target abundance alone cannot select patients. Clinical translation will require state definitions that integrate function, spatial context and treatment history, supported by reproducible markers, prospective validation and models that retain human stromal diversity.

The myCAF-iCAF relationship is supported by cytokine and metabolic perturbations in experimental PDAC; opposing directional arrows indicate context-dependent changes rather than universal reversibility in patients. Hypoxia and nutrient stress alter inflammatory and matrix-associated output. Therapy can induce adaptation or select pre-existing cells. Dashed relationships indicate proposed or model-dependent changes and do not imply lineage-traced conversion. Senescence is a potentially persistent stress response, and no reversal is assumed. Antigen-presenting CAF function depends on origin and immune niche. The diagram synthesizes the cited evidence and is not a measured lineage tree ( 13 , 14 , 16 , 17 , 22 – 24 , 28 ).
